studies.title: The Command Has Already Come
studies.meaning: The surah opens with a past tense for something still ahead. God's command has come. Early scholars read this as a certainty stated as fact. It answers listeners who kept demanding the promised reckoning on their own schedule. The order not to rush it comes straight after. Then the subject turns to what God does send down now. Angels carry the Spirit to servants he chooses, with one task attached. Warn that there is no god but him.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, from the later years in the city, when opposition had hardened into mockery. The classical sources describe opponents daring the Prophet to produce the punishment he warned of. They treated the delay as proof that nothing was coming. The surah opens by answering that taunt directly. Then it spends its whole first stretch on evidence already in front of them.

keyTerms.note: The word covers both an order given and the matter it concerns, so the phrase can mean the decree God has issued and the event that decree brings about. Early scholars keep both senses.
Read here as revelation itself, life-giving to hearts as breath is to bodies, or as the angel who carries it. The two readings sit together in the classical commentaries without conflict.
A form that means asking for something to be brought forward, not merely feeling impatient. It names a demand made out loud, which is what the opponents were doing when they called for the reckoning.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: In a society where few could read, a warning travelled by voice, and the word for warner named a real role. A man who spotted a raiding party from a ridge would run ahead of it into the settlement shouting, stripped of his cloak so that no one could mistake him for a traveller. Warning was urgent, unpaid and often unwelcome. The commission given in these ayat borrows exactly that role.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb that opens this surah is a perfect, the form Arabic uses for finished action. Yet the event it announces had not happened yet. Classical grammarians treat this as a way of stating a future certainty as though it were already done. Surah 21 opens with the same move. It announces that the reckoning of humankind has drawn near.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Two things are held together here. God's decree is fixed and its timing is not the listener's to set, which removes the argument that delay means absence. And revelation is described as something sent down by choice, on servants God selects, rather than earned or achieved. Prophecy is therefore not a rank a person climbs to. The content of every such sending is compressed into one sentence, so the message stays constant wherever the messengers differ.

crossReferences.why: Opens another surah with the same perfect-tense announcement of something that has not yet arrived.
Places the same construction at the head of a surah, saying the reckoning of humankind has drawn near.
Calls revelation a spirit sent by God's command to one who did not know the Book before.

studies.applyIt: Notice the next time you treat a delay as a cancellation. A reply that has not come, a result still pending, a change you were promised. Give it a name and set it down for a day without deciding what the silence means. The passage is not asking you for patience in general. It is asking you to stop reading absence into waiting.
studies.explainEasier: God says his order has already gone out, so there is no point asking for it to come sooner. He sends angels down with his message to the people he picks. Their job is to warn that there is only one God.

studies.title: From A Drop To Adversary
studies.meaning: Three acts of creation in three sentences, each smaller in scale. The heavens and the earth are made with truth, which means made on purpose and not as a game. Then the human being, traced back to a drop of fluid, who turns out to be an open arguer. Early scholars dwell on the jolt here. The lowest start there is, and then the nerve to argue against its Maker. Then livestock, where the stress moves from origin to use: warmth, benefits, food.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, part of the surah's opening catalogue of things its audience could check by looking. The argument being answered is not denial of God; the Meccans acknowledged a creator and attached partners to Him. So the passage does not set out to prove that God exists. It lists what He alone made, then names the human response as dispute, which is what the surah's first hearers were audibly doing.

keyTerms.note: The word names the small quantity of water left in a vessel or a skin, the residue rather than the pour. Choosing it sets the origin of a practised arguer at the smallest imaginable scale.

An intensive form. Not someone who happens to disagree but someone skilled at contention. Paired with a word meaning plain or open, it describes argument conducted in daylight rather than resentment held quietly.
A collective covering camels, cattle, sheep and goats together, the animals a household lived from. Its root carries softness and ease, and gives Arabic its ordinary word for a blessing.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A household's wealth was counted in animals, and one herd supplied nearly everything. Hair and wool became tents and cloaks, hides became water skins and sandals, milk and meat were the food, and dung was fuel where there was no wood. The word this passage uses for warmth points first at clothing. Losing a herd to drought or to a raid did not reduce a family's comfort; it ended it.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase translated as an open adversary occurs in only two places in the Quran, here and at 36:77. Both times it follows the same sentence about a human being made from a drop of fluid. The wording in the two surahs is nearly the same. Early scholars note this as a deliberate echo rather than a repeat.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Creation is said to be with truth. Early scholars gloss that as purpose and justice rather than accuracy. It rules out a world made for fun, and it makes a reckoning make sense. The human being is then set inside that ordered world at an odd angle. He is the creature with the smallest start and the loudest objections. Nothing is said about whether the dispute is fair. It is simply recorded as the human move.

crossReferences.why: Repeats the drop-to-adversary sentence and answers the argument it goes on to make about bones.
States directly that the heavens and the earth were not created in play, which is what creation with truth denies.
Returns to the same origin, a mingled drop, and reads it as the beginning of a test rather than an insult.

studies.applyIt: Pick one thing you argued about this week where you were sure you were right. Do not revisit whether you were. Instead spend a minute on the plain fact that the person holding that certainty began as almost nothing and will not be here in a century. The passage puts those two facts side by side without resolving them. Sit where it puts you.
studies.explainEasier: God made the sky and the earth for a reason. He made you from one small drop of fluid, and yet you stand up and argue with him. He also made the animals that keep you warm, help you and feed you.

studies.title: Beauty At Dusk And Dawn
studies.meaning: After the useful comes the beautiful. The same animals that gave warmth and food are now said to give beauty. The beauty is fixed to two hours: when the herd comes home in the evening, and when it goes out in the morning. Early scholars point out that no practical benefit is attached to this one. Then usefulness returns. The animals carry loads to places a person on foot would reach only at severe cost.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, inside the run of ayat listing what the audience already had, before the surah turns to argument. Mecca sat in a valley with no crops. It leaned on caravans for grain and on herds for nearly all the rest. These two ayat name the two things such a life ran on. The sight of the animals coming back at evening, and their power to cross ground people could not cross alone.

keyTerms.note: Not ornament but a beauty of proportion and fullness, used of a well-formed animal and of a scene in good order. The ayah lists it as a benefit in its own right, beside food and clothing.
From the root for rest and for evening. It names the hour when herds return to the fold, the one moment of the day when the whole flock is visible at once and a household counts what came back.
From a root meaning to split. The phrase pictures effort that divides a person, a cost paid out of the self rather than out of a purse, which is what a long march without an animal was.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Herding ran on two moments. At first light the animals were driven out to pasture, and at dusk they were brought back and penned, which was when losses showed. A camel could carry across a desert stage a load that would have killed the man carrying it himself, and the routes north to Syria and south to Yemen existed only because of that. Beauty and freight were the same animal.
studies.didYouKnow: The two verbs in this ayah each occur exactly once in the whole Quran. One means driving a herd out in the morning. The other means bringing it home at evening. Both of those single uses sit in this one sentence. The Quran has other words for morning and evening. These two belong to the movement of animals.
studies.theologicalSignificance: A list of benefits stops to name something that serves no purpose. Beauty is given as part of the provision, not a by-product of it. So the world is not arranged for use alone. The passage then closes with two names of God. One means tender kindness and the other mercy. They are attached to a line about freight and distance. Care of that quality is being claimed at the level of ordinary haulage.

crossReferences.why: Runs the same catalogue of livestock benefits and closes by asking why gratitude does not follow.
Names riding, eating, and reaching a need in the breast as purposes served by the herds.
Draws the same line from milk and meat to being carried, on animals and then on ships.

studies.applyIt: Find the hour in your day that corresponds to the herd coming home. The moment things stop moving and you can see what is there. Do not use it to plan or to review. Look at one ordinary thing in front of you and let it be pleasant rather than useful. That is the whole content of the middle of this passage.
studies.explainEasier: The animals are not only useful. There is something lovely about watching them come home at dusk and go out at dawn. They also carry your loads to places you could never walk to on your own.

studies.title: And He Creates What You Do Not Know
studies.meaning: Three more animals are listed, and this time riding and display are both named as purposes without embarrassment. The sentence then opens outwards: God creates things you have no knowledge of, which early scholars take as a standing clause covering whatever is not yet known. The second ayah turns from roads to the road. God undertakes to make the direct way plain, some ways deviate from it, and had He willed, everyone would have been guided.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The surah is still working through what its audience could check. Horses, mules and donkeys were closer to Meccan life than to the desert interior. They were animals of settled trade rather than long crossings. The turn in the second ayah is the surah's first move from evidence to response. It arrives with no bridge, which is how this chapter works throughout.

keyTerms.note: The word for what is added to make a thing look well. Listing it beside transport, with no criticism attached, sets the passage apart from the places where adornment is treated as a distraction.
From a root meaning to aim straight and to keep to a middle. The phrase pictures a road that goes where it says it goes, as opposed to one that bends away without announcing it.
Used of a road that leaves the true line and of a ruler who departs from justice. The same word covers both, so a crooked path and a crooked judgement are described identically.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Horses were expensive and scarce in Mecca, kept for prestige and for raiding rather than for haulage, while mules and donkeys did the short work between town and well. A man's mount announced his standing before he spoke. Meanwhile the caravan routes were real roads with real branches, and taking the wrong fork out of a valley could add days to a journey or end it. Guidance was first a matter of tracks.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase this ayah uses for the direct road occurs only once in the Quran. Elsewhere the same idea is carried by the word for a straight path, which appears dozens of times. Early scholars note that the unusual wording pairs a road with the human act of aiming. So the ayah is about the direction taken as much as about the route.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The closing clause is left open on purpose. God could have guided everyone and did not. The classical scholars handle that without flattening either side. The power is affirmed, and the choice not to use it is not explained away. Beside it stands the line that showing the direct way rests with God. So guidance is a gift and not a prize won. Between those two there is room for effort and for leaning on God, and that is where the tradition leaves it.

crossReferences.why: States the same possibility, that all on earth could have believed, and forbids compelling them into it.
Uses almost the same construction to say that guidance is upon God, and closes a different argument with it.
Contrasts one straight path with the many other paths that scatter a traveller away from it.

studies.applyIt: Think of one thing you own mainly because it looks well, and stop apologising for it. This passage lists display beside transport with no word of blame. Then notice where the apology really belongs in your week. It is usually somewhere else. Naming that difference is more use than a vague suspicion of everything pleasant.
studies.explainEasier: God made horses, mules and donkeys for people to ride and to look good on. He makes other things that you know nothing about yet. He also shows the road that runs straight, though some roads bend away from it.

studies.title: Water, And What Grows From It
studies.meaning: One substance is sent down and the passage follows it into two uses that do not look alike. First it is simply drink. Then it becomes the trees among which herds are pastured, and after that grain, olives, dates, grapes and every other kind of fruit. The list moves from what keeps a person alive today to what a farmer waits a season for. It closes by saying this is a sign, and specifies the audience: people who think.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Mecca had no farming of its own. The crops in this list belonged to Ta'if and the oases the Meccans traded with, not to the valley they lived in. The audience knew these fruits as goods arriving. That sharpens the point. The same water that fell somewhere else produced everything they bought, and nobody in the chain of purchase had made any of it.

keyTerms.note: A plain word for anything drunk, placed first and left undeveloped. The ordering matters: the passage gives water its simplest use before it gives the elaborate ones, and does not rank them.
A verb meaning to send animals out to graze freely, from a root connected with marking. It names a whole system of feeding that costs the owner nothing except the decision to open the pen.

A form suggesting turning something over repeatedly rather than a single insight. The sign is described as available only to sustained attention, which is why the audience is specified rather than assumed.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Water arrived twice a year at best, in short violent falls that ran off the rock and filled the wadis for a few hours. Wells were owned, named and fought over, and the right to water a herd could be inherited or bought. Grain, olives and dates came into Mecca on camels from Syria, Yemen and Ta'if. Nobody in that valley could imagine water as a background condition. It was an event that people watched for.
studies.didYouKnow: The formula that closes this ayah, calling something a sign for a people who use a named faculty, appears six times in the Quran with the singular word for sign, and five of those six are in this surah. The other stands in surah 27. Surah 16 uses it as a refrain, changing only the faculty it addresses each time.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Rain is the standing argument here, and its force is that no one can claim it. Nothing in the chain from cloud to fruit is a human product. Yet the result is described as being for you. So dependence and generosity sit in one sentence. Naming the sign for people who think also sets a condition. The evidence is public, and the conclusion is not automatic. Something is asked of the one watching.

crossReferences.why: Asks directly who sends the water down from the cloud, and offers to make it bitter.
Runs a nearly identical list of crops and closes it as provision for people and their livestock.
Follows the same water into grain, dates and olives, and asks the reader to look at the fruit ripening.

studies.applyIt: The next glass of water you drink, drink the first mouthful without doing anything else. Not as a ritual, just as an experiment in noticing. The passage puts drink first in its list and spends no words defending the choice. Most people find the ordinary things are the ones they have never once attended to, and water is the most ordinary of them.
studies.explainEasier: God sends water down from the sky. You drink it, and the animals feed on what it makes grow. Out of the same water come grain, olives, dates, grapes and every other fruit. People who stop and think will see the sign in that.

studies.title: The Sun, The Moon, The Stars
studies.meaning: The list rises from the ground to the sky. Night and day, sun and moon are put at the service of human beings. Then the stars come in a slightly different grammar. They are harnessed by God's command, which early scholars read as a way of stressing that nothing here runs itself. The second ayah drops back to earth, for the sheer range of colours scattered across it. Each ayah closes by naming a different faculty.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The audience lived by these bodies rather than looking at them: prayer times, market days, caravan departures and the pilgrimage season were all read off the sun and the moon, and night navigation across open country was done by stars. Nothing in the ayat asks for new information. They ask that things already used daily be counted as evidence, which is the method of the whole opening section.

keyTerms.note: Used of setting an animal or a worker to a task without payment. Applied to the sun and the moon it says they are working, on a schedule not their own, for a benefit that is not theirs.
A verb for creating by spreading widely, used of seed broadcast by hand. It implies profusion rather than assembly, which suits a sentence whose whole subject is variety.
From the root for remembrance. It suggests recovering something already known rather than learning something new, so the faculty addressed by the colours of the earth is recollection.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A caravan leaving Mecca for Syria travelled at night in summer to spare the animals, and the route was held by stars rather than by landmarks, which vanish in the dark. Guides who could hold a bearing across sand at night were paid well and remembered by name. The moon set the months and therefore the sacred seasons in which fighting stopped. Both bodies were instruments before they were ornaments.
studies.didYouKnow: The formula closing the second of these ayat, a sign for a people who take heed, occurs only twice in the Quran. This is one place, and surah 6 holds the other. Each ayah in this stretch of surah 16 closes with a different mental verb. They move through thinking, reasoning and remembering. The same evidence is offered three times to three faculties.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The heavenly bodies are placed under a verb used of hired labour. That empties them of divinity in one word, which mattered where the sun and the moon were worshipped elsewhere in the region. What is left is a working system, ordered and useful, and its usefulness is the argument. The range of colours then adds what order alone would not. The arrangement is not only efficient. It is richer than the job requires.

crossReferences.why: Forbids bowing to the sun and moon while pointing at the One who created them, on the same logic.
Uses the identical verb for the sun, moon and stars being harnessed by God's command.
Develops the theme of differing colours through mountains, people and animals, and links it to knowledge.

studies.applyIt: Go outside tonight and find one thing overhead you can name. The moon's phase will do. Then work out what it was doing for someone a thousand years ago in your position, with no clock and no calendar. The passage rests on things that were once instruments and have become scenery. Recovering one of them as an instrument takes about a minute.
studies.explainEasier: God set the night and the day to work for you. The sun, the moon and the stars all run on his orders. He also spread the earth with things in every colour there is. Both are signs for people who stop and think.

studies.title: The Sea Made To Serve
studies.meaning: One ayah takes the sea through four uses and ends by naming the response it expects. Fresh meat comes out of it, and ornaments people put on, and ships are seen cutting through it while human beings go looking for God's bounty. The last clause is the point of the sentence: so that you may give thanks. Everything before it is evidence. Early scholars note that seeking bounty is described as human work done inside a provision no one arranged.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, and worth noticing that Mecca is inland. The Red Sea coast was two days away at Jeddah and Shu'ayba, and Meccan trade reached the sea through those ports and along it toward Abyssinia. Pearls came up the same routes. The audience knew the sea as the edge of their commercial world rather than as daily scenery, which is why the ayah lists what comes from it rather than describing it.

keyTerms.note: A word for meat still soft and newly taken, used of fish. In a climate where meat had to be dried or eaten at once, freshness was the specific luxury, and the ayah names it rather than assuming it.
Covers pearls and coral brought up by divers. Adornment is listed as a benefit alongside food, without qualification, which early scholars read as an ordinary permission rather than an argument.
A form describing ships pushing water aside so that it parts audibly at the bow. The word carries the sound as much as the motion, which is why translators reach for ploughing.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Pearl diving in the Red Sea and the Gulf was old work. A diver went down on a held breath, with a stone to sink him and a rope to bring him back. The best beds were known and defended. Dried fish travelled inland, but fresh fish did not, so a Meccan tasted it only near the coast. Grain from Egypt and cloth from further off came by ship to Jeddah, then by camel up to the valley.
studies.didYouKnow: The word this ayah uses for ships cleaving the water appears in only two places in the Quran. This is one, and surah 35 is the other. Both passages pair it with the ornaments taken from the sea and with the search for God's bounty. Surah 35 adds one detail. Two seas, one sweet and one salt, both yield the same things.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The closing clause makes thanks the aim of the whole list. So gratitude is a way of seeing straight, not a mood. Seeking bounty sits in the same sentence as being given it. Human effort is not set against God's provision. It is placed inside it. The sea makes a useful case for this. It is the one setting where no amount of labour changes what is actually there to find.

crossReferences.why: Runs the same list of fresh meat, ornaments and cleaving ships, and extends it to two different seas.
States the principle the closing clause depends on, that gratitude is answered with increase.
Describes God driving ships at sea so that people may seek His bounty, in nearly the same words.

studies.applyIt: Take one thing you ate today and trace it back as far as you honestly can. The shop, the lorry, the field or the boat, the weather that season. Stop when you run out of knowledge, not at a tidy answer. The ayah does the same work in one sentence. Its point is the last clause, which arrives only once the tracing is done.
studies.explainEasier: God made the sea work for you. You eat fresh fish from it and wear pearls that are pulled out of it. Ships cut through it while people go looking for a living. All of that is there so you will give thanks.

studies.title: Is The Maker Like The Made
studies.meaning: Mountains are set into the earth so that it does not sway with its inhabitants, and rivers and roads are added so that people find their way. Then landmarks, and the star by which travellers hold a bearing. Having built the whole apparatus of orientation, the passage asks one question and stops: is the one who creates like the one who creates nothing. No answer is supplied. Early scholars treat the silence after it as the argument.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, closing the surah's long opening catalogue. The question at the end is aimed at one practice, not at unbelief in general. The Meccans acknowledged a creator and also served objects that had been carved. The ayah sets those two facts side by side. It is the hinge of the chapter. Everything after it argues from the ground this question wins.

keyTerms.note: From a root used of a ship riding steady at anchor. The word describes weight that holds something else still, so mountains are named by their function rather than by their height.
The verb for the unsteady motion of a ship or of a person about to lose their footing. It belongs to the same picture as the anchoring word beside it, and the two are usually paired.
Landmarks used for navigation, a rock or a ridge that tells a traveller where they are. The word shares a root with knowledge, so a landmark is literally a thing that informs.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Desert travel was navigation, not walking. A guide read dunes, rock formations and the colour of gravel by day, and at night held a course by particular stars near the pole. Losing the line by a few degrees over a long stage meant missing a well, which was fatal. Families paid for guides the way they paid for water. The ayat name exactly the tools of that trade and then ask who supplied them.
studies.didYouKnow: The ayah before this one used the plural for stars, calling them harnessed by God's command. This one switches to the singular. The singular form appears in four places in the Quran. This is the only one where it means the star a traveller steers by. The classical scholars note the shift and read it as pointing to whichever star holds a bearing.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The closing question defines God by an act, not by a quality. What marks the Creator off is not power in the abstract. It is the fact of having made something. The objects set against him are ones the audience had carved themselves. Putting the question after a list of travel aids is deliberate. The passage has just shown that finding your way rests on things you did not put there. Then it asks what you turn to.

crossReferences.why: Presses the same contrast further, saying the invoked objects could not create even a fly.
Has Abraham ask whether people worship what they carve, when God created them and their handiwork.
Uses the same image of the earth spread out and mountains set as pegs holding it steady.

studies.applyIt: Name one thing you rely on that you had no part in making, and one thing you rely on that you built yourself. Hold them next to each other for a moment without ranking them. This passage does not ask you to despise what people make. It asks you to keep straight which of the two you are leaning on when the ground moves.
studies.explainEasier: God set mountains in the earth so that it would not rock under you. He gave rivers, roads, landmarks and stars so you can find your way. Then he asks whether the one who makes all this is the same as one who makes nothing.

studies.title: The Dead Things People Call On
studies.meaning: The four ayat move by steps. Favours are declared past counting, and the sentence closes, against expectation, on forgiveness and mercy. Early scholars read that as covering the shortfall in thanks that must follow. Then comes knowledge of what is hidden and what is shown. Then the objects people call on are stripped of everything. They create nothing. They are themselves created. They are dead rather than alive. They do not even know when they will be raised.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, from a surah that spends its opening third listing what God has made and given: rain, cattle, the sea, mountains, stars for navigation. This passage is the turn from the list to its conclusion. The audience in Mecca maintained shrines and images that were tended, dressed and consulted, and the argument here works by taking them seriously enough to ask what they can actually do. No specific occasion is reported.

keyTerms.note: A singular noun given to a whole people to count, so the grammar sets one blessing against many counters and still says the tally fails. The root also gives the words for softness and ease.
From the root for a secret and for the innermost part of a thing. Placed against its opposite in the same clause, it covers the whole range from an unspoken thought to a public declaration.

The plural is the ordinary word for the dead, applied here to carved objects that were never alive. Using a word that implies a former life sharpens the contrast with the living God named throughout the surah.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: The sanctuary at Mecca held images that had names, histories and custodial families. People brought them offerings before a journey and consulted them by drawing marked arrows before a marriage or a raid. Caring for one was a paid office and a source of standing. To call these objects dead in front of the men who fed and clothed them was not an abstract argument; it named a household trade.
studies.didYouKnow: The surah is named for a creature that appears in only two of its ayat. That passage is about the bee, which is inspired to build in hills and trees. The surah is sometimes called the surah of blessings, because so much of it lists what has been given. This passage sits at the hinge where the listing turns into an argument.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The argument is made on the ground of what a thing can do, not on the ground of rank. Nothing is said about what the objects deserve. The question is what they are able to do. The answer works backwards: from making, to being, to life, to knowing. Set against that, the opening line about blessings beyond counting becomes evidence, not sentiment. The case for God rests on what has been given. The case against the idols rests on what has not.

crossReferences.why: The other place the uncountable-blessings sentence appears, closing on the human verdict instead.
Presses the same test further: they could not create a fly, or take one back.
Says the invoked ones do not hear, and would disown the association on the Day.

studies.applyIt: Take one thing you already own and trace it backwards. Your cup: clay or sand, a kiln, a driver, a shop, someone who chose it. Follow the chain until you get bored. Then notice that you did this for one object out of the several hundred in your house. That is the shape of the claim this passage makes about counting.
studies.explainEasier: Nobody could add up all the good things God has given. God knows what you keep secret and what you say openly. The things people pray to instead cannot create anything at all. They are not even alive.

studies.title: Hearts In Denial
studies.meaning: A short statement of oneness is followed by a diagnosis. Those who do not believe in the hereafter are described by two things at once. Their hearts refuse, and they are swollen with self-importance. Early scholars read the order as causal either way, since refusal breeds pride and pride breeds refusal. The striking part is where unbelief is placed. It sits in the heart rather than in the reasoning, and it is named as a posture, not a conclusion.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, right after the surah has dismissed the objects people called on as things that make nothing and are dead themselves. This ayah gives the positive statement those denials were clearing room for. The classical scholars tie the pride named here to the social place of the Meccan leaders. They stood to lose standing if the message were accepted. It is not arrogance as a general failing.

keyTerms.note: From a root meaning to find something unfamiliar and reject it. It describes a heart that does not merely disbelieve a claim but treats it as foreign, which is a reaction rather than a judgement.
A form meaning to seek greatness for oneself, to act big. The grammar implies claiming a size you do not have, so the fault is inflation rather than actual eminence.
The plain numeral rather than a term of praise. Its flatness is the point: the statement is offered as a fact to be registered, not as a slogan to be admired.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Meccan society ran on rank held between clans. Rank was kept up in public through hospitality, poetry, feuds and the care of the sanctuary. To accept a message that levelled that order was to take a demotion in front of everyone who mattered. Several early reports describe men who found the message believable in private and could not bear the public loss. The word for pride in this ayah names that exact situation.
studies.didYouKnow: The word this ayah uses for the denying heart occurs nowhere else in the Quran. The declaration that opens it, that your god is one god, appears in six places; three of those put it inside an instruction to the Prophet to say it. Only here is it followed straight away by an account of why people refuse it.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Denial is diagnosed here rather than argued with. The refusal is put in the heart, with pride beside it. So the obstacle to belief is often not a thought, and not every objection is a question that deserves an answer. That cuts both ways. It also means the cure the Quran offers for such refusal is not a better proof. It is a change in what a person is willing to be.

crossReferences.why: Describes those who behave arrogantly on earth being turned away from the signs themselves.
Says God seals the heart of every arrogant tyrant, linking the same two conditions in reverse order.
States the identical declaration of one God, followed there by the names of mercy rather than by denial.

studies.applyIt: Bring to mind an idea you dismissed quickly and recently. Ask yourself one narrow question about it: would accepting it have cost you anything in front of other people. You are not obliged to change your view. The passage is only pointing out that the answer to that question is often the real reason, and that most of us never check.
studies.explainEasier: Your God is one God. Some people will not take that in, because they do not believe there is a life after this one. Their hearts shut the idea out, and they think too much of themselves.

studies.title: Legends Of The Ancients
studies.meaning: Two ayat, and the join between them is the interesting part. The first says God knows what people hide and what they announce. It adds that he has no love for the self-important. The second gives an example of announcing. Asked what their Lord has sent down, they answer that it is old stories. Early scholars note that the reply is not an argument. It is a way of closing the subject, and the ayah before has already named what lies hidden underneath it.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The question in the second ayah reflects a real situation. Pilgrims arriving for the seasonal markets asked residents about the man preaching among them. The Meccan leaders had an interest in the answer given. Classical sources describe planned efforts to shape what visitors heard. A particular occasion may or may not lie behind this ayah. Either way, the exchange it records was ordinary in the pilgrimage months.

keyTerms.note: A fixed expression that opens a sentence with certainty, close to saying there is no escaping this. Grammarians have long debated how it is built, while agreeing on what it does.
A plural for things set down in lines, which is how the root also gives the word for writing. The charge is that the material is copied from older books rather than newly received.
The earlier generations. Attached to the word for tales it dates the material and dismisses it in one move, since what is old is being treated as already answered.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Mecca ran a yearly market season around the pilgrimage. Tribes arrived to trade, recite poetry and settle disputes. News moved faster in those weeks than at any other time, and reputations were made and broken in them. A visitor who asked about the new preaching got the answer the man he asked wanted him to carry home. Shaping that answer was worth real effort to men whose place rested on the sanctuary.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase translated as legends of the ancients occurs exactly nine times in the Quran. It is always in the mouths of opponents and never in a narrative voice. Few objections are quoted word for word this often. The nine are spread across surahs from the earliest Meccan period to the latest, which shows how long the charge lasted.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Divine knowledge of the hidden is set beside a dismissive public answer, and that makes a point. The sentence people say is not the whole of what they think, and both are known. So the reader is warned off taking stated objections at face value, including his own. The passage also does not argue with the charge of borrowed stories. The surah answers it later, with more material rather than with a defence.

crossReferences.why: Quotes the same accusation at length and answers that the One who knows the secret sent it down.
Records the identical phrase as the reaction of a man who hears the verses recited to him.
Puts the same question to a different group in this surah and reports the opposite answer.

studies.applyIt: Listen for the phrase you use to end a conversation you do not want to have. Everyone has one, and it usually sounds like a judgement while doing the work of a door. Catch yourself using it once this week and, instead of finishing the sentence, ask the person one real question. You can still disagree afterwards. You will simply have disagreed with something.
studies.explainEasier: God knows what people keep quiet and what they say out loud. When they are asked what their Lord has sent down, they brush it off as old stories from long ago. That answer is meant to end the talk.

studies.title: Loads Carried Whole
studies.meaning: The image is freight. Those who dismissed the message will carry their own loads whole, with nothing taken off. Alongside them comes a share of the loads of people they turned away without knowledge. Early scholars are careful about that second clause. It adds weight to the misleaders without lifting any from those misled, since the wording says some of their loads, not their loads. Responsibility is doubled at one end rather than moved.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, coming straight after the answer that the revelation was old stories. This ayah states what follows from giving that answer in public. The classical scholars tie it to the men who met arriving pilgrims and warned them off. A private opinion becomes another person's obstacle the moment it is broadcast. That is the exact case the ayah describes.

keyTerms.note: The word for a heavy pack, used of the loads carried in war and by animals. Applying it to wrongdoing turns guilt into freight, which is weighed and carried rather than felt.
An emphatic addition. The point of it is that nothing is quietly written off in transit, which forestalls the hope that some of a load might be lost between here and the weighing.
Attached to those being misled rather than to the misleaders. It marks them as people who did not know enough to judge, which is what makes turning them away a weight worth counting.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Caravan life gave the picture its edge. Loads were weighed at departure, and a driver answered for what he carried and for anything added to his animal by arrangement. Overloading a camel on a long stage ruined it, and everyone in a trading town had watched a beast go down under weight. The ayah takes words its first hearers used every week and applies them to speech.
studies.didYouKnow: The exact phrase this ayah uses, loads carried in full, appears nowhere else in the Quran. The same surah returns to the picture of weight later in a different key. Elsewhere the Quran states plainly that no bearer carries another's load. That is why classical scholars read the addition here as extra weight for misleading, not as guilt moved from one person to another.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Two principles are held together that look opposed. No one carries another's burden, and yet leading others astray adds to your own. The resolution is that influence is itself an act, so what is added is the misleader's own doing rather than someone else's debt reassigned. This makes speech consequential in a specific way. What you say about a matter you have not examined becomes part of your own account once it reaches someone who cannot check it.

crossReferences.why: States the principle this ayah must be read against, that no bearer of burdens bears another's.
Reports the same offer to carry others' sins and answers it with the same doubling of weight.
Shows the burdens being carried on the back on the day the reckoning arrives unexpectedly.

studies.applyIt: Think of an opinion you have passed on that you never actually checked. Not a lie, just something you repeated because it sounded right and it was easy. Find the person you said it to and correct it, briefly and without ceremony. The passage is concerned with what happens to a claim after it leaves you, and that is the only part still within reach.
studies.explainEasier: On the Day of Rising these people will carry the full weight of what they did. They will also carry part of the weight of those they led away from the truth. What they carry is a bad load.

studies.title: The Roof Came Down
studies.meaning: Earlier peoples schemed, and the answer came at their building from underneath. God took the structure from its foundations. The roof fell on them from above, and the punishment reached them from a direction they were not watching. Early scholars read the building two ways. It is an actual structure in the stories of past nations, and it is a figure for a scheme, since a plot is something built. Either way the point is the direction. The danger was below the part they were guarding.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, and pointed. The surah has just described people who dismissed the message in public and turned others away. This ayah tells them the pattern is old, and how it usually ends. It names no nation. Early scholars take that as deliberate. The audience knew the ruined sites along their own trade routes and could supply examples without being told which one was meant.

keyTerms.note: Planning carried out in secret, with the sense of turning someone aside from what they intend. It is not a moral word by itself; the Quran uses the same root of God's response to such planning.
The part of a building that sits in the ground, from a root meaning to sit. Attacking a structure there rather than at the walls is what makes the collapse total instead of partial.
A verb for fine awareness, from the same root as the word for a hair and the word for a poet. It names the alertness that catches small signals, and says even that failed here.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Building in Arabia meant dry stone and mud brick on shallow footings, and undermining a wall was a known way to bring a structure down without touching its face. Travellers on the northern routes passed the abandoned rock-cut dwellings of earlier peoples and the ruins of towns the caravan roads no longer served. Collapsed roofs were not a metaphor to that audience. They were a landscape feature on the way to Syria.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for foundations appears in only two places in the Quran. Here, where God takes a building away from them, and in surah 2, where Abraham and Ishmael are described raising the foundations of the House in Mecca. The same architectural term marks the one structure that is raised and the one that is pulled out from underneath.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The ayah says something exact about how consequences arrive. Not by beating a defence, but by taking away the assumption the defence was built on. And from a direction outside the plotter's view. That marks a limit on human planning that no cleverness closes, since the flaw sits in what the planner never thought to weigh. The passage does not offer this as unfairness. It offers it as the shape events take when they are answered.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same word for foundations of the House that Abraham raises, the opposite motion to this one.
Describes a scheme so great that mountains might move by it, and says God holds the answer.
Shows a plot answered by a plot the schemers did not perceive, ending in their own ruin.

studies.applyIt: Take a plan you are confident about and spend five minutes on a single question: what am I assuming that I have never checked. Not the risks you have already listed, which are the walls. The thing underneath them. Write down one answer, even a weak one. This passage is about the part of a structure nobody inspects because it is not visible.
studies.explainEasier: People before them made secret plans. God took their building away at the base, and the roof came down on them. The blow reached them from a side they were not watching at all.

studies.title: Where Are My Associates
studies.meaning: A scene rather than a statement. Disgrace comes first, then a question put by God with an edge in it: where are the partners you used to take My side against. The word for that disputing implies choosing an opposing camp. No answer is recorded from the people questioned. Instead a second group speaks, described only as those who were given knowledge, and their verdict is short. The silence of the accused is where the early scholars put the weight.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, following the ayat on schemes that fell in from the foundations. The surah has been arguing that consequences come from unexpected directions. This moves the argument to its final scene. The people addressed had spent years defending the standing of the Kaaba's idols in public argument. That is the activity the question names. The ayah pictures the moment that argument is asked to produce its subject.

keyTerms.note: From a root for public shame rather than private guilt. The humiliation described is social, which fits a group whose position rested on standing among people who are all present.

keyTerms.gloss: you used to oppose, take sides
keyTerms.note: From a root meaning a side or a split, so the verb pictures putting yourself on the far bank from someone. It describes not merely disagreeing but forming a party against.

The noun of the same root as the opening verb, repeated within a single ayah. Repeating it in the mouths of the knowledgeable makes their verdict an echo of the sentence rather than an addition to it.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Public dispute was a Meccan skill. Cases, feuds and reputations were settled in the assembly beside the sanctuary, and a man who could hold a position in front of the clans held real power. Poets were retained as weapons in those exchanges. To be shamed in that assembly cost a family for a generation. The ayah takes the whole apparatus of standing before a crowd and reuses it, with a different crowd and a different questioner.
studies.didYouKnow: The question at the centre of this ayah, asking where my associates are, is put in four places in the Quran. In two of them the reply is that no witness is left. The verb describing what the accused used to do, taking a side against, occurs in this form nowhere else. The ayah also uses the root for disgrace twice in one sentence.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Two things are set down here. Judgement includes exposure, not only penalty, so part of what is settled is the public record. And the wording about associates is pointed. They are called God's associates, the ones other people assigned to him, which quietly says the arrangement never existed outside human speech. Knowledge then gets the last word in the scene. That puts understanding, rather than force, at the close.

crossReferences.why: Puts nearly the same question, calling for the associates that people used to claim.
Asks where the partners are and records the reply that no witness remains among them.
Shows those given knowledge recognising the revelation as truth, the same group speaking here.

studies.applyIt: Think of a position you have defended more often than you have examined. Say out loud what it actually commits you to, in one plain sentence, with nothing rhetorical in it. Most positions survive that. Some do not, and it is better to find out now than to discover it while someone is waiting for your answer.
studies.explainEasier: On the Day of Rising God will shame these people. He will ask where the partners are that they argued for against him. They give no answer. The ones who were given knowledge say the shame today falls on those who refused.

studies.title: The Surrender Offered Too Late
studies.meaning: The moment of death is described as a negotiation that fails. Angels arrive, and the people being taken offer submission along with a denial: we were doing no wrong. The reply is a single word of contradiction, followed by the statement that God knows what they were doing. Early scholars note that the surrender itself is not refused for being a surrender. It is refused because it arrives attached to a lie. The gates named afterwards are for the self-important.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, in a passage that sets two deaths side by side, this one and the one two ayat later. The surah has been describing people whose refusal was tied to social standing rather than to evidence. It now follows them past the point where standing is worth anything. Nothing here is tied to a named occasion. Early scholars read it as the general end of the attitude the surah has been describing.

keyTerms.note: The word for laying down arms and accepting terms, from the same root as peace. Offering it at this point is a military gesture made after the outcome is already decided.
A particle used only to overturn a negative statement. Arabic has a separate word for ordinary agreement; this one exists specifically to answer a denial with a contradiction.
From a root meaning to stay put. It names a place of long residence rather than a stop, which is why it carries weight in a sentence about something without end.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Between tribes, a losing party could throw down its weapons and ask for terms. The customs around that were exact. What could still be claimed, who guaranteed safety, what a beaten group had to give up. Timing was everything. An offer made before a rout could save a clan. The same offer made after it usually could not. The passage borrows those customs and applies them to a moment when neither side is setting the terms.
studies.didYouKnow: This ayah and the one four lines later form a matched pair. The phrase describing those whom the angels take occurs in exactly two places in the Quran, both here in surah 16. The two are identical up to one word, the word for the state of the person dying. One says wronging themselves. The other says wholesome. Everything else in the two sentences parts from that word.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The line is drawn at the moment of death, not at the judgement, so the deadline falls earlier than a reader might expect. What is refused is not repentance. It is a claim of innocence offered in place of one. That distinction matters. The denial is what fails, not the lateness by itself. Behind it stands the assumption that the record cannot be revised by the person who made it.

crossReferences.why: States plainly that repentance offered when death arrives is not the repentance being asked for.
Shows belief professed at the sight of punishment and says it never benefited anyone before.
Repeats the same gesture of offering surrender in this surah, at the reckoning rather than at death.

studies.applyIt: Notice the difference between an apology and a defence dressed as one. Most of us make the second and hear ourselves making the first. Pick a recent example and rewrite it in your head with the explanation removed entirely. Whatever is left is the actual apology. If nothing is left, that is worth knowing before it matters more.
studies.explainEasier: When the angels come for them, these people suddenly offer to give in. They say they did nothing wrong, and they are told plainly that they did. God knows what they used to do. The gates ahead of them are the gates of Hell.

studies.title: They Will Say, Goodness
studies.meaning: The same question asked earlier in the surah is put to a different group, and the answer is one word: goodness. Where the first group had classified the revelation as old material, this one describes what it does. The sentence then widens past the answer into a promise with two halves, good in this world for those who do good, and a better home after it. The comparison is made without disparaging the first half.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The question fits the season when tribes came to Mecca for trade and pilgrimage and asked residents about the new preaching. The surah has already recorded the dismissive reply some of them gave. This ayah supplies the other reply visitors would have heard. It came from the smaller group who had accepted the message. That is why the two answers sit six ayat apart in one chapter.

keyTerms.note: A single word answering a question about content with a judgement about worth. It also serves as the comparative, so the same word returns later in the ayah meaning better, tying the answer to the promise.

From a root meaning beauty as well as goodness, and carrying the sense of doing something well rather than merely doing the right thing. The reward named uses the same root, so the return matches the act.
The word for a household's dwelling and the courtyard it encloses, not a house as a building. Applied to the hereafter it suggests belonging and settlement rather than accommodation.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: For an Arab of that period a home meant a compound of related families, with its animals, its dependants and its guests. To be without one was to be exposed. Exile from a clan's protection could be a death sentence, since nobody was bound to avenge or shelter you. The word the ayah picks for the hereafter is that word. So the promise is not of a better building. It is of belonging somewhere for good.
studies.didYouKnow: The question asked here, what your Lord has sent down, appears in exactly two places in the Quran, and both are in this surah, six ayat apart. It is put to two different groups and receives two answers of one word each. Nowhere else does the Quran stage the same question twice with opposite replies in a single chapter.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The good of this world is not treated as a consolation or a trap. It is granted first, plainly. Only then is it set beside something greater. That keeps the comparison from turning into contempt for the present. The passage also ties what a person says about revelation to how that person acts. Those who answered goodness and those who do good are described in one breath, and the link is never spelled out.

crossReferences.why: Puts the identical question to a different group in this surah and records the opposite answer.
States the underlying principle, that the reward of doing well is nothing but doing well.
Promises good in this world to those who do good, and adds that the earth is spacious.

studies.applyIt: Someone will ask you this week what you think of something you value. Answer in one sentence about what it does rather than what it is. The reply in this ayah is a single word and it describes an effect, not a category. Categories end conversations. Effects invite the next question, which is usually the one worth having.
studies.explainEasier: Ask the people who kept close to God what their Lord has sent down, and they answer in one word: good. Doing good brings good in this life, and the home waiting after it is better still.

studies.title: Gardens Of Perpetual Residence
studies.meaning: The home promised a line earlier is now named. Gardens of settled dwelling, entered rather than glimpsed, with water running underneath them. Then a clause that stops describing and hands the description over. They have there whatever they wish. Early scholars note the shift from a list to an open category. Anything named would be smaller than the promise. The ayah closes by putting the whole arrangement down to one act of repayment.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Descriptions of the garden in the Meccan surahs are short and concrete, drawing on what an audience in a dry valley would recognise as luxury: shade, running water, permanence. The elaboration found in later passages is not here. The ayah is a direct continuation of the one before it, supplying the content of the better home that had just been promised without description.

keyTerms.note: From a root meaning to stay in a place, which also gives Arabic the word for a mine, a thing fixed where it lies. Early scholars differ over whether it is also a proper name for a particular garden.
A verb of continuous motion, in a tense that keeps the action ongoing rather than completed. Running water, as opposed to stored water, was the mark of a place that would not fail.
From a root for settling an account in full. It presents the garden as a discharge of what is owed rather than a gift, which early scholars balance against the many ayat calling it grace.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: In Arabia a garden meant an enclosure with a water source, and the water was the whole of it. Wells and cisterns had to be lifted from, and a spring that ran on its own was rare and valuable enough to define a settlement's history. Ta'if and the oases north of Mecca were famous precisely for this. Shade, which the ayah implies rather than states, was the second scarce thing, and the two together were what wealth bought.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase used here for gardens of perpetual residence occurs in eleven places across the Quran, in Meccan and Medinan surahs alike. That makes it the most repeated of all the garden names. The next most common, the gardens of bliss, appears eight times. The clause about having whatever one wishes is far rarer. Early scholars treat it as the widest description given.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The description ends on an open clause, so no ceiling is fixed on what is promised. That does real work. It stops the garden being cut down to the pleasures one culture happens to prize. The language of reward is then set beside a picture of permanence. That answers the worry underneath most human striving. The worry is not that good things do not exist. It is that they do not last.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same clause about having whatever they wish, and calls it a promise to be asked for.
Names the same gardens and adds the entry of righteous relatives and the greeting of the angels.
Repeats the open promise, extending it to whatever the soul desires and whatever is called for.

studies.applyIt: Write down what you would actually ask for if the clause in this ayah were addressed to you. Not the answer you think is expected. The exercise is uncomfortable because most lists come back short and oddly specific, and noticing that is the point. What you would ask for tells you what you have been organising your week around.
studies.explainEasier: They walk into gardens where they will stay for good, with rivers running under them. Anything they want is there for them. That is how God pays back the people who kept close to him.

studies.title: Peace Be Upon You
studies.meaning: The second of two deaths described in this stretch, and the mirror of the first. The angels arrive again, and the people they come for are described with one word meaning wholesome or in good state. Early scholars read it of the condition of the soul and, in some reports, of the ease of the departure itself. There is no negotiation here because nothing is being contested. The angels speak first, with a greeting, and the entry is attributed to what the person had been doing.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, and deliberately placed. The surah has just shown a death that goes badly, then the reward promised to those who kept their duty, and it now returns to the same moment for the other group. Nothing suggests a specific occasion. The classical scholars treat the pairing as the surah's way of making the two outcomes comparable by describing them at the same instant rather than at the judgement.

keyTerms.note: A word covering what is clean, pleasant and fit for use, applied to food, soil and speech. Used of people at death it suggests something sound rather than merely blameless.
The ordinary greeting, offered here unchanged. Its plainness is the point: the first words spoken are the same ones exchanged between neighbours, which locates the moment inside familiar courtesy.

A small preposition doing large work. It attaches entry to prior action, and early scholars read it alongside the many statements that entry is by mercy, treating deeds as a cause God appointed rather than a price.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Arrival was a formal thing in that society. A traveller reaching a camp called out a greeting before coming closer. The answer decided whether he was a guest or a threat. Being received meant food, shelter and protection for three days by custom. Hospitality was the strongest social duty there was. The ayah has the angels use exactly that formula. It places the newly dead as a guest expected, not a stranger turning up.
studies.didYouKnow: This ayah and the one four lines earlier open with the same phrase about those whom the angels take. That phrase occurs nowhere else in the Quran. The two sentences part on a single word. One group is described as wronging themselves. The other is described as wholesome. The word chosen for the second group appears in the whole Quran only twice.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Putting a greeting at the moment of death changes what the moment is. It becomes a welcome rather than a seizure. The courtesy comes from the arriving side, which turns round the usual fear of being met by an unknown authority. Calling the person wholesome matters too. What is praised is a state, the thing a life settles into, rather than a tally of acts. The acts are still named in the same sentence.

crossReferences.why: Has angels descend on those who stood firm, telling them not to fear or grieve.
Addresses the settled soul directly at the same moment, calling it back to its Lord.
Gives the matching sentence in this surah for those taken in the opposite state.

studies.applyIt: Greet one person today whom you usually pass without speaking. A neighbour, someone at the same bus stop, whoever is behind the counter. Say the words properly rather than in passing. This ayah puts an ordinary greeting at the most serious moment there is, which suggests the small courtesies are not a lesser category of thing.
studies.explainEasier: Some people are in a good state when the angels come for them. The angels greet them with peace. Then they are told to walk into the Garden because of the way they used to live.

studies.theme: Time and the Brevity of Life
studies.title: What Are They Waiting For
studies.meaning: A question with only one answer available. If the evidence already given is not enough, what remains is the arrival of the angels or of the command itself, and by then the matter is closed. The passage then notes that earlier peoples did exactly the same, and forestalls the obvious complaint: God did not wrong them. What reached them was the consequence of their own acts, and the thing they had treated as a joke closed over them.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, following the two death scenes. The demand for a visible sign was a real and repeated Meccan objection, recorded in several surahs, and the classical sources describe specific challenges to produce angels or a punishment on demand. This ayah does not answer the demand. It points out what granting it would mean, and then observes that the pattern of asking is older than the people asking.

keyTerms.note: The verb covers both waiting and watching, so the sentence pictures people scanning for something rather than merely delaying. The English question loses the sense of eyes on the horizon.
A verb used of something surrounding a person on every side, with no sense of an impact. What was mocked does not strike; it settles over them, which is why translators reach for engulfed.
A form implying seeking amusement at someone's expense, done for an audience. It names a social act rather than a private opinion, which is why the response described is equally public.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Mockery was a weapon with rules. Satirical verse was made to order, memorised and carried between tribes. A well-made line could damage a clan's marriage prospects and trade for years. Poets who did that work were feared and paid. The early years in Mecca were fought partly on that ground. That is why ridicule, rather than argument, appears so often in these surahs as the shape opposition took.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb translated as engulfed occurs in this past-tense form six times in the Quran. In every one of them the subject is the same. It is what people used to ridicule, closing around them. The word is never given any other subject in that form. Classical scholars note that the Quran keeps it for the moment when mockery comes back on the one who offered it.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The clause denying wrong is doing careful work. It rules out reading the outcome as an extra penalty imposed from outside. What arrives is the deeds themselves. So justice and mercy stay in one frame, since nothing is added to what a person made. The question at the start makes a further point. A sign big enough to force belief would land when belief costs nothing, and then it would not be belief.

crossReferences.why: Answers the same demand by saying that when a sign arrives, faith will no longer benefit anyone.
States the same denial, that God does not wrong people, but people wrong themselves.
Uses the identical verb for what people mocked closing around them once the delay ends.

studies.applyIt: Find the thing you are waiting for before you make a change: a sign, a clearer moment, one more piece of information. Name it exactly, then ask whether you would actually act on it or move the marker again. Most people discover they have moved it before. That is worth knowing today rather than in the version of this where the waiting has run out.
studies.explainEasier: These people are waiting for the angels, or for God's order to land. By then it is too late. Others before them did the same. What came for them was their own doing, and the thing they laughed at closed in around them.

studies.title: Had God Willed, We Would Not
studies.meaning: An argument is quoted rather than paraphrased. God is able to stop anything. So the fact that we and our fathers served other objects, and set certain things off limits, must be what he wanted. The Quran gives no direct answer here. It notes that earlier peoples argued the same way. Then it closes with a question about the messenger's job, which is to deliver clearly. Early scholars read the silence as pointed. The argument is not answered because it was never used to find the truth.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The second half of the quoted speech points at a real Meccan practice. Certain animals and crops were set aside from ordinary use by custom, dedicated in ways the surah takes up elsewhere. So the argument recorded is not abstract. It defended a working system of religious practice. The ayah gives back the reasoning its holders really used to justify what they had inherited.

keyTerms.note: From the root that gives sanctuary and the sacred precinct. The verb means to place something outside ordinary use, which is what the Meccans did with certain animals dedicated to their objects of worship.
The noun for getting a message all the way to its destination, used of couriers. It defines the messenger's task as transmission complete, and stops there without extending to results.
An active form, so it means not merely clear in itself but clarifying. The delivery is required to make the matter plain, which sets a standard for the messenger while leaving the response to others.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Arabia before Islam had a system of animals set apart. Camels were marked and let off work. Produce was split between the sanctuary and the household. These customs came down from the fathers, and people defended them as such. No text held them in place. Community pressure did. Changing them meant breaking with fathers and grandfathers by name. In that world, family lines were the main form of memory. The words this ayah quotes defended that inheritance in part.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase describing the messenger's duty as clear delivery occurs seven times in the Quran. Two of those are in this surah, here and again near its end. In most of the other places it follows an order to obey. Here alone it follows a quoted argument. It works as a limit on what the messenger answers for.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage sets a boundary rather than settling the question of God's will and human action. Both are affirmed elsewhere in the Quran, and neither is folded into a tidy system. The classical scholars keep that tension rather than resolving it. What this ayah rules out is one use of the doctrine. Turning God's power into an excuse after the fact. The test it implies is practical. It asks whether the reasoning is applied to choices still ahead, or only to ones already made.

crossReferences.why: Quotes the same argument almost word for word and calls it conjecture rather than knowledge.
Records the identical excuse, that the Merciful would not have let them worship these.
Repeats the clause about clear delivery at the close of this surah, in a different setting.

studies.applyIt: Catch one explanation you give for something you keep doing, and test it the way this ayah does. Ask whether you would accept the same reasoning as a guide to a decision you have not made yet. If it only ever works backwards, it is not a reason. It is an account, and knowing which one you are holding is the whole of the exercise.
studies.explainEasier: Some people said that if God had not wanted them to worship these things, he would have stopped them. People before them said the same. The messenger's job is only to say the message clearly.

studies.title: A Messenger In Every Community
studies.meaning: One sentence covers all of history. Every community received a messenger with two instructions, one to do and one to avoid. The outcomes then split. Some God guided, and on others misguidance fell due. The reader is told to travel and look at what happened to those who denied. The second ayah turns to the Prophet's own eagerness for his people. It sets a limit on that eagerness, which early scholars handle with care, since the sentence does not say his concern is wrong.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, at a point where the message had been public for years and the response had settled into a pattern. The order to travel and look was literal for this audience. The caravan routes north passed ruined settlements, and Meccan traders made that journey twice a year. The ayah asks them to read as evidence what they already saw twice a year as scenery.

keyTerms.note: A people bound by something shared, not necessarily by descent or territory. Using it here makes the claim broad: wherever a group with a common life existed, a messenger came to it.
From a root meaning to overflow a limit. It covers idols, tyrants and anything given the obedience owed to God, so the word is defined by the position taken rather than the thing itself.
A verb of intense wanting, used of greed elsewhere. Applied to the Prophet's desire for his people's guidance, it describes an appetite rather than a duty, which is what the ayah goes on to bound.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: The road north from Mecca to Syria passed the rock-cut tombs of an earlier people at al-Hijr and the traces of settlements the trade had abandoned. Merchants camped near these places and the stories attached to them circulated as common knowledge. Southward lay the ruins of the dam country in Yemen. Nobody in the audience needed a library to check the claim in this ayah. They needed only to remember the last journey they had made.
studies.didYouKnow: The word this ayah uses for what must be avoided appears in eight places in the Quran. It is not a name for any particular idol. Early Arabic dictionary writers trace it to a verb meaning to cross a boundary. That is why classical scholars apply it to anything obeyed in God's place, a person or a custom included, and not to statues alone.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The claim that every community received a messenger has consequences the early scholars drew out. No people is left without address. The message given is always the same pair of instructions, so a difference between traditions is not a difference at the root. The second ayah then splits concern from responsibility. The Prophet is not told to care less. He is told the outcome is not his to produce. The tradition applied that line between duty and result widely.

crossReferences.why: States the same universality, that no community passed without a warner sent to it.
Gives the identical two-part message to every messenger before, worship Me and nothing else.
Addresses the same grief over those who refuse, in stronger terms, and gently checks it.

studies.applyIt: Take the person whose choices you have been trying hardest to change. Write down the part of it that is your work and the part that is not, in two short lists. Then act only on the first for a week. This passage does not ask you to care less. It asks you to stop paying for an outcome that was never on your side of the line.
studies.explainEasier: God sent a messenger to every people, saying the same thing: serve God and keep away from false masters. Some listened and some did not. You can travel and see what became of the ones who said no.

studies.title: Sworn With Their Strongest Oaths
studies.meaning: The denial of resurrection is reported as an oath, not as an opinion. The phrase used names the most binding kind of swearing there was. Early scholars note the oddity of it. God is called on to deny what God has undertaken. The answer overturns it with one particle, then restates the matter as a promise binding upon him. That shifts the ground. The question is no longer what is possible but what has been undertaken. The closing clause puts the disagreement down to ignorance rather than defiance.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Bodily resurrection was the hardest part of the message for its first audience, and the Quran returns to it constantly in the Meccan surahs. Classical sources report men bringing crumbled bone to the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) as an argument. Swearing by God while denying the resurrection was no contradiction to them. They accepted a creator God and denied only that he would raise the dead.

keyTerms.note: From a root for exertion to the limit. Attached to oaths it names the most solemn formula a person had, the one reserved for matters where their word had to carry alone.
A particle whose only job is to reverse a negative. Set against the heaviest oath in the language, its brevity is the response: no counter-oath is offered, only a contradiction and then a statement.

Placed with a word meaning binding upon, so the sentence describes God as having obliged Himself. Early scholars note that the obligation is self-imposed, which is the only sense in which anything is due from Him.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: In a society without courts or written contracts, an oath was the tool that settled disputes. Ownership of a well, the father of a child, a debt, a killing: all could turn on a formula sworn in front of witnesses. There were graded oaths for graded matters. A man known to have sworn falsely lost the ability to trade. Reaching for the strongest oath there was showed that a claim was being staked at the highest cost.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase for the most solemn kind of swearing occurs five times in the Quran. In every one of them it introduces something the speakers turn out to be wrong about, or fail to keep. Not one of the five is spoken by someone whose oath holds. Classical scholars point out the pattern. The Quran keeps pairing the heaviest oath with the weakest position.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The reply moves the argument from power to commitment. Resurrection is not defended here as something God could do. It is defended as something he has undertaken to do. So the issue is reliability rather than power. The last clause then declines to call the deniers liars. It says instead that most people do not know. That split between not knowing and defying runs through the Quran's treatment of unbelief, and it changes what response fits.

crossReferences.why: Records the same oath denying resurrection and answers with an instruction to say otherwise.
Answers the argument from crumbled bones by pointing back to the first origination.
Uses the identical phrase for the strongest oaths, sworn there over a demanded sign.

studies.applyIt: Notice how hard you swear when you are least sure. Most people raise the intensity of a claim exactly where the evidence thins, and it is audible if you listen for it in yourself. Next time you catch the phrase that means you are staking everything on something, stop and ask what you would actually accept as proof against it.
studies.explainEasier: These people swore their strongest oath that God would never raise the dead. They were wrong. God has promised to do it, and a promise from him holds. Most people simply do not know this yet.

studies.title: Be, And It Is
