studies.meaning: Two reasons are given for the resurrection just affirmed. It will settle what people disagreed about, and it will show those who refused that they were saying something false. Neither reason is about punishment; both are about the record being made clear. Then the difficulty is dismissed in one line. When God intends a thing, He says be to it, and it is. Early scholars note that the sentence removes any question of effort or material, which was the whole objection.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, answering the oath recorded two ayat earlier that God will not raise anyone who dies. The Meccan objection was practical, not philosophical. Bones decay, and nobody had seen the reverse. This pair of ayat answers first by saying what the raising is for. Then it puts the difficulty where the objectors had not looked, in their assumption that making needs a process.

keyTerms.gloss: so that He may make clear
keyTerms.note: From the root for separating one thing from another, which is how Arabic builds the idea of clarity. What is promised is not a verdict imposed but a distinction made visible.

A form suggesting mutual difference, people taking turns behind each other. It covers honest disagreement as well as dispute, which is why the promise here is of clarification rather than of sentence.
The shortest imperative in the language, two letters. Early scholars observe that the brevity is the argument, since a command needing no elaboration describes a making that needs no material.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Everything the audience made, they made from something. A tent was woven from hair that had been sheared, spun and dyed; a well was dug; a sword was traded for or beaten out of imported iron. Craft in that world was visible and slow, and it was the model people reasoned from. Bones that had gone to dust offered no material to work with, which is exactly why the objection felt decisive to the people making it.
studies.didYouKnow: The command translated as be, followed by and it is, occurs in eight places in the Quran. Three of them come in passages about Jesus. Two come in passages about the making of the heavens and the earth. Three more, this one among them, come in passages about giving life and raising the dead. The same two-word formula covers the start of the world, a birth, and the end.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Naming clarity as the purpose of the resurrection makes it an act of truth-telling before it is an act of judgement. That changes what the day is for. The second ayah then puts God's action outside the category of work altogether. Early scholars drew the consequence. Nothing is easier or harder for an act like that, so arguments from difficulty do not apply. What is left to discuss is only whether the thing was undertaken.

crossReferences.why: Repeats the same formula immediately after answering the argument from decayed bones.
Applies the identical words to the origination of the heavens and the earth without a model.
Uses the same command for the creation of Jesus, comparing it to the making of Adam from dust.

studies.applyIt: Think of something you have decided is impossible, and separate the two things hiding inside that word. One is that you cannot do it. The other is that it cannot be done. Write which of the two you actually mean. The passage is about the second kind, and most of what we call impossible turns out to be the first.
studies.explainEasier: God will raise the dead so that everyone can see the truth about what they argued over. Making it happen costs him nothing at all. He says be to a thing, and the thing is there.

studies.title: Settled In A Good Place
studies.meaning: A promise made to people who left. The clause specifying that they emigrated for God's sake after being wronged sets two conditions at once, a motive and a prior injury, and early scholars treat both as load-bearing. What is promised is a settling, in this world, in something good, and then a larger reward afterwards. The sentence closes with a conditional half-line that is left hanging: if only they knew. The subject of that clause is disputed among the scholars.
studies.historicalContext: The surah is Meccan, but many classical scholars hold this ayah and the one after it to come from a later stage. Some read them of the migration to Abyssinia during the Meccan years, when a group left to escape persecution. Others hold them to be among the Medinan ayat of this surah and read them of the move to Medina. The reports differ. The tradition keeps both readings side by side rather than settling on one.

keyTerms.note: From a root meaning to cut off or abandon, so the word carries severance rather than travel. It names leaving people and a place behind, which is why it also gives the word for parting speech.
A verb for assigning someone a dwelling and putting them in it, doubled here with emphatic markers. The word implies being housed by another's arrangement rather than finding a place yourself.
Deliberately unspecified. Early scholars list safety, provision, honour and victory among the readings, and note that leaving the noun open lets the promise fit whatever the emigrant actually lacked.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Leaving your tribe was close to unthinkable. Protection came from kin. A man outside that network had nobody to avenge him, nobody to stand surety for a debt, and no claim on hospitality past the usual three days. Emigrants arrived somewhere as dependants with no standing at all. The word this ayah uses for settling them is the word for being given a place by someone else. That is exactly the position such people were in.
studies.didYouKnow: The exact phrase used here, emigrating for God's sake, occurs nowhere else in the Quran. Other passages speak of emigrating in God's way or for his cause, with a different preposition. Classical scholars note the difference. They read this wording as naming God as the whole object of the move, not the direction of it.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The promise is double on purpose, and the order matters. Something good here first, and only then the greater reward. That refuses a comfort put off entirely to later, which would have been the easier thing to offer people who had lost houses and trade. The trailing clause about knowing then does something quieter. It hints that the hardship is not only material. What would make the loss bearable is something the sufferer does not yet know.

crossReferences.why: Makes the same promise to those who emigrated and were then killed or died on the way.
Describes the earth as containing many a refuge and abundance for one who emigrates.
Tells believing servants that God's earth is spacious, so worship Him wherever you are.

studies.applyIt: If you have moved away from somewhere, for whatever reason, name one good thing that came from the move that you could not have arranged yourself. Not to balance the ledger, and not instead of what was lost. This ayah puts the worldly good first and does not pretend it settles anything. Naming it accurately is different from being consoled by it.
studies.explainEasier: People who were badly treated and left home for God's sake are promised a good place to settle in this life. What is waiting for them after this life is better still. Most of them cannot see that yet.

studies.title: Ask Those Who Know
studies.meaning: The first line finishes the sentence before it. It names what those emigrants did. They held out, and they leaned on their Lord. The two come in that order, enduring first and reliance second. Early scholars read that as a sequence, not two names for one thing. The second line turns to an objection. The messenger was an ordinary man. The answer points outward: put the question to people who have the knowledge.
studies.historicalContext: The surah is Meccan. Many classical scholars hold that the ayat just before this one, about leaving home, belong to a later stage. The objection answered in the second line was a live Meccan complaint. A real messenger would be an angel, they said, not a man from a family they knew. The people to ask are usually understood as those who knew the earlier scriptures. They could confirm that every earlier messenger had been human too.

keyTerms.note: From a root meaning to confine or restrain. The word is closer to holding a position than to accepting a fate, which is why it also gives the word for binding an animal in one place.
From the root for appointing an agent to act on your behalf. The grammar implies handing a matter over after doing your part, not instead of doing it, which is how the early scholars read it.

Covers remembrance, mention and a revealed book. Attached to people it names those who carry the earlier revelations in memory, which is why the phrase is usually read as a pointer to earlier scripture.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Jewish and Christian communities lived within reach of Mecca, in Yathrib, in Yemen and along the northern trade roads. Meccan merchants dealt with them often. Monks and rabbis were asked as a matter of course about the earlier prophets, and stories from their scriptures passed around in Arabic by word of mouth. Telling an objector to ask them was practical advice, not a turn of phrase. The people meant could be found on the next trip north.
studies.didYouKnow: The order to ask the people of the reminder comes in just two places in the Quran. Here, and in surah 21. The two ayat are almost the same. Both open by saying that only men were sent before. Both add that those men were given revelation. Both close with the same clause about not knowing. It is one of the closest word-for-word echoes between two surahs.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Answering an objection by telling people to go and ask is unusual. Early scholars note what it takes for granted. The record of earlier prophecy is public, it can be checked, and it fits the claim being made. Revelation is treated as a line that continues, not as something new. The two words in the first line do separate work. Leaning on God can sit alongside strain, since the holding out is named as the thing being done while the reliance goes on.

crossReferences.why: Gives the same instruction in nearly identical words and adds that those sent ate food.
Answers the same objection by noting that every messenger before ate and walked in markets.
Sets out what reliance on God is promised to produce, a way out and provision unlooked for.

studies.applyIt: Pick one thing you have an opinion about but have never asked anyone qualified. Find a person who actually knows and ask them a single question, phrased so it can be answered. This ayah answers a serious objection by telling the objector where to look, which assumes the asking is available. Usually it still is, and we simply do not do it.
studies.explainEasier: Those who kept going through hard times put their trust in their Lord. Some people said a messenger should not be an ordinary man. The verse tells them to ask people who know. Every messenger before was a man too.

studies.title: That You May Clarify
studies.meaning: The ayah finishes the sentence started before it, about messengers sent with clear proofs and written books. Then it turns to the present task. The Reminder came down not only to be recited but to be explained. So the messenger's work includes making plain what the revelation says. Early scholars take that clearing up to cover both the wording and how it applies. The last clause puts the weight back on the hearers. Their reflecting is the point of the whole exchange.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, in a surah aimed largely at people who denied that an ordinary man could carry revelation. The ayat just before answer that by pointing to earlier communities, who also received men as messengers. This ayah names what those messengers carried, and why the present one has been given the same. No particular occasion is reported for it. It belongs to the long Meccan argument about prophecy.

keyTerms.note: A name for the revelation that presents it as recall rather than novelty. The root covers both mentioning aloud and holding in mind, so it names the text and the effect it is meant to have.
An intensive verb for making something distinct and unmistakable. It assumes the text can be misread, and treats explaining it as part of the message rather than an addition to it.
A reflexive form suggesting sustained turning over rather than a single thought. The grammar makes reflection something the hearers do to themselves, which no messenger can do on their behalf.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Mecca was mostly an oral culture. Authority moved by memory and by reciting aloud. A poet or a speaker gave his lines, then explained them if someone pressed him. Written scripture belonged to the Jewish and Christian communities to the north. Meccan traders had seen their scrolls on the Syrian roads. Naming both clear proofs and written books set this recitation beside something the caravans already knew was there.
studies.didYouKnow: The word rendered as the Reminder appears twice in a row here. The ayah just before it tells objectors to ask the people of the Reminder, and this one says the Reminder was sent down to the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him). One term names an older body of scripture and the new revelation within two consecutive lines.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Revelation is shown as needing a human being to explain it. Prophecy lies in the explaining as well as in the delivering. That rules out a text working on its own, with nobody standing behind it. The last clause refuses to make understanding automatic. The clearing up is done, and the reflecting is still left to the hearer. Guidance is offered, not installed.

crossReferences.why: Runs straight into this ayah, naming the people of the Reminder just before the Reminder itself is named.
States that every messenger came in his own people's tongue, which is what makes clarification possible.
Describes a covenant to make scripture clear to people and not to conceal it.

studies.applyIt: Take one ayah you have heard many times and read a short explanation of it this week, from a source you trust. Notice whether the explanation changes anything or only confirms what you had assumed. The last word of this ayah is about reflecting, and reflection needs something to work on besides the sound.
studies.explainEasier: God sent messengers before with clear proofs and books. Now this Reminder has been sent down too. It is here so that people can be shown plainly what was sent to them, and so they will stop and think about it.

studies.title: Do They Feel Secure
studies.meaning: A question opens a short list of possibilities. Each one names a different way ruin could arrive. Early scholars note that the schemers are asked about their confidence, not about their guilt. Nothing here says any of it will happen. The question takes apart the assumption under the plotting. The plotting assumes the ground is steady. It assumes consequences give notice first. It assumes a plan made in secret can be made safe.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. By this stage the opposition had moved past argument into planned scheming against the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) and those who followed him. The surah has just recalled peoples before them whose plotting was answered from a side they had not watched. The classical scholars tie this warning to the general Meccan situation rather than to one named plot. They report no particular occasion.

keyTerms.note: A verb for a plan whose success depends on staying hidden. Across the Quran it usually pairs human scheming with a counter-move, so the word tends to carry its own answer with it.
Used of ground giving way and swallowing whatever stands on it. The image belongs to earthquake and sinkhole rather than to storm or flood, so the danger named comes from below.
From a root for fine, intuitive awareness rather than deliberate knowledge. Denying it says the harm would arrive below the threshold at which they might have sensed it coming.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Arabian trade ran on secrecy. A caravan kept its route and its hour of leaving close. Alliances were settled quietly. A boycott could be agreed before its target heard of it. Meccans had also inherited stories of towns in the north that were swallowed or buried. The northern roads went right past those ruins. Ground that opens was not a figure of speech to people who travelled by them.
studies.didYouKnow: The sentence that starts here does not finish in this ayah. It runs on through the next two. Each one adds another option, joined by the same short word for or. It never states an outcome. Classical scholars read the piling up as the argument itself. The list is not complete, and that is the point. No direction has been covered.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage separates the feeling of safety from safety itself. Nobody here is told they are about to be destroyed. They are told that their sense of being out of reach rests on nothing. So the warning aims at an inner state, not at an event. It also puts the timing and the direction of consequence outside any human sum. That is what makes scheming, as a way of living, unworkable.

crossReferences.why: States the same principle directly, that only those already losing feel secure from the planning of God.
Narrates a case in which the earth actually caves in, giving this warning a precedent.
Shows human scheming answered by a better plan, which is the pattern this question assumes.

studies.applyIt: Notice the next time you catch yourself thinking a situation is handled. Not that it will go badly, only that you have counted every direction it could come from. Ask honestly how many of those directions you actually checked. The ayah is not asking you to become anxious. It is asking you to stop treating a plan as a guarantee.
studies.explainEasier: Some people made secret plans to do harm. The verse asks them if they really feel safe. God could make the ground cave in under them. Trouble could come from a side they never thought to watch.

studies.title: Or While In Dread
studies.meaning: Two more possibilities close the series. God could seize them in the middle of ordinary movement. Or he could seize them while they are already afraid. Then the sentence turns with no warning. Instead of naming a punishment, it names God as Gentle and Merciful. Early scholars read that ending as the reason the warning was issued and not carried out. Scholars differ over the second phrase. Some take it as slow loss, others as fear of a blow to come.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The surah is arguing with people who had grown sure that nothing would interrupt their arrangements. These two ayat finish a question begun above, then break its momentum completely. The classical scholars report no particular occasion. They read the pair as part of the surah's steady swing between warning and the naming of God's kindness. That rhythm runs through its Meccan sections.

keyTerms.note: A word for turning back and forth, used of travel and of the ordinary busyness of trade. It places the possible seizure inside routine rather than at some singled-out dramatic moment.
Scholars differ over the sense. Some read a gradual diminishing, others a fear that precedes a blow, and both readings survive in the classical commentaries without either being settled.
A name for tenderness that shrinks from causing hurt. Placed after a list of ways ruin might arrive, it explains why the list stays a possibility instead of becoming a sentence.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A merchant's life was movement: loading before dawn, weeks on the road, settling accounts in a market town, turning round again. Sudden death on the route was common enough that wills were made before departure. So was the slower ruin, a season of raids or collapsed prices eating a family's holdings until nothing remained. Both kinds of ending were familiar, and neither announced itself.
studies.didYouKnow: The two divine names that close this passage, Gentle and Merciful, occur as a pair nine times in the Quran. This surah uses that pair once before, near its opening, where it describes the animals that carry loads to towns people could not otherwise reach. The warning and the kindness are given the same closing vocabulary.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage refuses to let power and tenderness stand as alternatives. One sentence lists three ways a life could end without notice. The same sentence ends by naming God as the one who is gentle. Neither half softens the other. What the arrangement shows is that delay is not indifference and not weakness. It is a quality of the one who delays, set down here so that it can be leaned on.

crossReferences.why: Closes with the identical pair of names, there attached to the animals that carry burdens for people.
Repeats the point that no creature would remain on earth if consequence were not deferred.
Lists directions from which trouble might come, in the same open-ended way this question does.

studies.applyIt: Think of a fear you carry that is about slow loss rather than sudden disaster, the kind that erodes. This passage names that kind separately, which means it is not too small to be taken seriously. Bring that particular fear into your prayer tonight in plain words, and end it with the two names this passage ends with.
studies.explainEasier: God could take these people while they go about their day, or while they are already afraid. Nothing they do would stop it. Then the verse says something else. Your Lord is gentle and kind.

studies.title: Shadows Leaning Away
studies.meaning: The argument switches from warning to observation, and asks whether anyone has actually watched. Shadows move. They lean one way in the morning and the other in the afternoon, and the passage reads that movement as prostration. Early scholars note that the verb describes a shadow returning, so the daily circuit itself is the act rather than any single position. The closing word says the bowing is not chosen.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, in the middle of an extended argument that runs from the objections of the deniers to the evidence lying in plain sight. The surah has already used rain, cattle, the sea and the stars in this way. Here it turns to something with no obvious usefulness at all, which is part of the point being made. The classical scholars report no specific occasion for the ayah.

keyTerms.note: A verb for a shadow returning after the sun has moved it. The form suggests repetition, so the prostration described is the whole daily circuit rather than one fixed posture.
A plural used of a single created thing. Early scholars read it as the shadow being counted at each hour it occupies, which keeps the emphasis on movement rather than on shape.
A word for being lowered against one's own inclination. It ends the ayah on a submission that is not voluntary, which is what distinguishes what shadows do from what a worshipper does.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Before clocks, a shadow was the instrument. Prayer times, market openings and the hour to move a herd were judged by the length of a man's shadow measured against his own foot, a reading anyone could take anywhere. Travellers found direction by it at midday. Watching shadows was not contemplation for the first hearers. It was the ordinary skill by which a day was divided.
studies.didYouKnow: This is one of a small group of ayat that describe things without will as prostrating, and the surah places it immediately before the only prostration marked for recitation in its hundred and twenty-eight ayat. There are fifteen such marks in the whole Quran. A reader following them will bow at the passage that comes next.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Prostration is redefined by being extended to things that have no will, and that does two things at once. It says the universe is already in the posture human beings are asked to take, so worship is joining something rather than beginning it. And it makes human prostration distinctive precisely because it can be refused. The shadow has no say in the matter, and the reader does.

crossReferences.why: Says the same of shadows in the mornings and evenings, and carries a prostration mark of its own.
Pairs stars and trees as things that bow, extending the same category in a different direction.
Widens it to a praise offered by everything, which human beings are said not to understand.

studies.applyIt: Step outside once tomorrow around midday and look at your own shadow, then look again in the late afternoon. It will have crossed to the other side. That is all this ayah asks anyone to notice. Spend the thirty seconds it takes rather than agreeing in principle that shadows move.
studies.explainEasier: Look at what God has made. Shadows move all day long. They lean one way in the morning and the other way later on. As they do that, they are bowing low to God.

studies.title: And They Are Not Proud
studies.meaning: The scope widens from shadows to everything that moves in the heavens and on the earth. Then the angels are named on their own, and it is said of them that they are not proud. Two short clauses follow. They fear their Lord above them, and they do what they are told. Only after all that does the instruction arrive. It comes as a ban on a number. Early scholars read that order as chosen, not accidental.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The surah has been building a case from observable creation towards the single claim its audience rejected, and these ayat complete that movement. The address at the end shifts into direct speech reported as God's own words, which the classical scholars treat as a change of register rather than the mark of a new occasion. No particular event is reported for the passage.

keyTerms.note: From a root for treading or crawling. It covers everything that moves under its own power, so the sentence sweeps in animals the audience never considered alongside the angels named next.
A reflexive form meaning to make oneself great. It presents pride as a claim a creature makes about itself, which is why denying it of angels is a statement about accuracy rather than manners.

The dual form. The prohibition is framed against exactly two rather than against many, which early scholars read as striking at the idea of a rival at all, since two is the smallest possible plurality.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: The sanctuary at Mecca held a great many tribal images. Pilgrimage to it was the income of the city. Each tribe kept its own image, and the system worked because no one image claimed to be the only one. A household could add a god without dropping one. Against that, a ban built around the number two lands exactly where the practice stood.
studies.didYouKnow: The middle ayah here carries one of the fifteen prostration marks in the Quran. It is the only one in this surah of a hundred and twenty-eight ayat. In many reciting traditions, a reader who reaches it stops and bows down. So a passage about creatures bowing makes the reader bow too.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Pride is treated as an error of fact, not a flaw of character. The angels are not praised for holding back. They are described as accurate about where they stand. That is why the lack of pride sits beside obedience as one thing rather than two. Putting the ban after the survey matters as well. The oneness of God arrives as the end of an observation, not as a demand made before one.

crossReferences.why: Describes those near God as free of pride and prostrating, using the same two ideas together.
Adds that the angels never tire of praise, extending the description of them given here.
States the same oneness positively, where this passage states it as a prohibition against two.

studies.applyIt: Notice one place today where you would rather be right than accurate. A small one works better for this. The passage does not describe angels as humble by effort; it describes them as not overstating their position. Try saying out loud, to one person, a sentence that gives up a little of the standing you had claimed.
studies.explainEasier: Everything in the sky and on the earth bows down to God. Every living creature does, and the angels do too. They are never proud. They do what they are told. God says to take one God only.

studies.title: Obedience Owed Without Interruption
studies.meaning: Ownership is stated first. The second clause draws the conclusion with one adverb. What is owed to God is owed without a break. Early scholars take that word to cover both steadiness and certainty. So the obedience meant is not seasonal and not a bargain. The closing question then presses on what the hearers actually did. They spread their fear among several powers, and kept the largest share for whichever one seemed nearest.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. It closes the section that began with shadows and reached the ban on taking two gods. The question at the end is aimed at people who agreed that God was the creator, while spreading their caution among lesser powers. The classical scholars treat the ayah as gathering up the argument rather than answering one incident. They report no occasion for it.

keyTerms.note: The word later comes to mean religion, but its older sense is what a lower party owes a higher one. Reading it as a debt keeps the sentence tied to the ownership clause before it.
From a root for something continuous and also for wearing effort. Early scholars give both permanence and obligation, so the word says the debt neither lapses nor pauses at any point.

A verb for taking protective care, which in practice means arranging your life around avoiding something. The question asks what the hearers actually organise themselves around, not what they profess.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Fear in that society was practical and distributed. You feared a stronger tribe, a creditor, a season of drought, the displeasure of a shrine's guardians. Protection was bought with alliance and gift, and a man who offended the wrong power lost the safety of the road. Asking whom the hearers feared was asking whose favour their travel and their trade depended on.
studies.didYouKnow: The word rendered here as constant comes up only twice in the Quran. The other place describes a punishment, not a duty. So one term for something that does not let up is used once for what is owed to God. It is used once more for what waits for those who turn him down. The balance is deliberate.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The ayah draws the duty from ownership, not from benefit and not from threat. That is a specific move. It means the claim on a person does not rise or fall with how life is going. It also names divided fear as the working form of setting partners beside God. What a person guards against shows who they think holds their outcome. It shows it more reliably than what they say.

crossReferences.why: Argues from the same premise, that everything already submits, towards the same conclusion about what is owed.
Answers this closing question in the first person, with devotion made deliberately exclusive.
Asks directly whether people are more deserving of a person's fear than God is.

studies.applyIt: Make a short list tonight of the three things you are most careful never to provoke. A person, an institution, an outcome. Do not judge the list. Just notice how much of your week is shaped by it, and set beside it how much is shaped by the one this ayah names. The comparison is the whole exercise.
studies.explainEasier: Everything in the sky and on the earth belongs to God. What people owe him never stops and never takes a break. The verse then asks why anyone would be more careful of some other power than of God.

studies.title: The Cry And The Forgetting
studies.meaning: A sequence rather than a rule. Every blessing is traced to one source. Then harm arrives, and people call out to that source with a word that means bellowing, not praying. Then the harm lifts, and some of them attach partners to their Lord again. Early scholars note the careful limiting word, some, which keeps the description from becoming a charge against everyone. The closing line is left short and heavy.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The surah has just stated that everything in the heavens and the earth belongs to God and asked why anyone would fear another. This passage answers by describing behaviour rather than argument. Mecca depended on trade routes that ran through drought, raiding and storm at sea, so the experience being described was common: vows made in danger and quietly dropped on arrival. No specific occasion is reported.

keyTerms.note: The verb is used of cattle lowing and of a wounded animal's noise. It is not the word for a composed prayer; it names the sound made when composure is gone.

A verb of removing a covering rather than of curing. The harm is treated as something laid over a person and taken off, which makes relief an act performed on them rather than a change in the situation.
An imperative that is not a permission. The same root runs through the Quran for temporary provision, and here the command is a way of leaving people to a course whose end the next clause withholds.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Sea travel to Abyssinia and the Yemen was the most frightening thing most Meccans did. Ships were small, crews prayed aloud in storms, and men made vows at the rail that they told stories about afterwards. On land the equivalent was a caravan caught without water. Everyone in the audience had heard someone swear an oath in fear and had watched, weeks later, as it quietly went unmentioned.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb used for the cry in distress appears only a handful of times in the Quran. It always shows up in this setting, of people calling out under pressure. It belongs to animal sound, not to speech. So the passage is not describing insincere prayer. It is describing prayer that is fully sincere and fully short-lived.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage makes a claim about human nature that is both very kind and very hard. Kind, because it grants that the cry in distress was real and aimed the right way. That means the knowledge of God is already there. Hard, because it shows how fast relief wipes it out. What is laid bare is not disbelief. It is a memory that works only under pressure, and that is harder to fix.

crossReferences.why: The same pattern at sea: sincere calling in the storm, association again on dry land.
Extends the scene, adding the promises made during the storm and broken after it.
Describes a man calling on his Lord in affliction and forgetting what he called for.

studies.applyIt: Think back to the last time you were genuinely frightened and prayed. Try to recall what you promised, in words or half-words. Most people cannot. Write down one thing you would want to have promised, and do it this week, now that nothing is wrong. The passage is not really about the cry. It is about the fortnight afterwards.
studies.explainEasier: Everything good you have comes from God. When something hurts you, you cry out to him. Then, once he takes the trouble away, some people go back to treating other things as if they were God.

studies.title: A Share For What They Do Not Know
studies.meaning: A practice is described rather than argued with. A portion of harvest and livestock was set aside for objects of worship, and the passage attacks the custom at one precise point. What receives the share is called something they do not know, and what is handed over was provided by God in the first place. The oath that follows attaches the coming questioning not to the giving but to the inventing.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Arabian tribes split their produce between God and their gods by a customary share. The surah comes back to that practice more than once. Early scholars describe the arrangement in general terms. They differ over how the shares were kept apart, and over what happened when one spilled into the other. The ayah addresses a custom its first hearers already knew, not a single incident.

keyTerms.note: The ordinary commercial word for a part of something divided among claimants. Using it keeps the practice in the register of accounting, which is exactly where the objection is aimed.
The verb names the giver of the produce before the share is mentioned at all. The grammar leaves nothing that belonged to the allocators, which compresses the whole argument into one word.
A verb for cutting or fashioning something new, used of lies. It presents the deities not as mistaken beliefs quietly inherited but as things actively manufactured by the people now offering to them.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Farming and herding communities divided every yield. A portion for the household, a portion for guests and those they kept, a portion set aside at a shrine. The dividing happened at the threshing floor or at the pen, in front of witnesses. Within a clan it worked as a public record. Moving a share elsewhere was something the neighbours could see, and would remember.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb rendered as they allocate opens three ayat in this surah. Each one names a different thing people assign away. The three sit within seven ayat of one another, and those are the only times the word appears in the surah. The repeating builds a short list of things wrongly given, held together by one word.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Giving to what does not exist is treated as stealing the credit, not as wasting goods. The passage never says the produce was needed somewhere else. It says the produce was never theirs to assign. So the error is a bookkeeping error about where things came from. And the coming questioning is tied to the inventing. What a person answers for is the claim, not the ritual built on it.

crossReferences.why: Describes the same division of crops and cattle in detail, including how the two shares were handled.
Presses the same point by noting that what they call upon provides them with nothing at all.
Asks who authorised the categories people invent about the provision given to them.

studies.applyIt: Look at where your money actually went last month and pick out one line you would struggle to explain as anything but habit. Not necessarily a wasteful line. Just an unexamined one. The objection in this ayah is to allocation on autopilot, towards something whose claim on you has never once been checked.
studies.explainEasier: These people took part of the food and animals God gave them and set it aside for things they know nothing about. God says they will be asked about the stories they made up.

studies.title: News Of A Daughter
studies.meaning: Two claims are set side by side and the contradiction between them is left to do the work. Daughters are assigned to God; the speakers keep for themselves what they actually want. Then the passage follows one of those men home and describes his face at the news of a girl. Early scholars note that the second ayah does not argue at all. It reports a physical reaction, and the reaction is the refutation.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Some Arabian tribes called certain worshipped figures daughters of God, while putting little value on daughters of their own. The surah exposes that pairing more than once. The classical scholars describe the attitude to baby girls as varying between tribes and households, not as universal. The Quran still names the practice directly, as something serious enough to say out loud.

keyTerms.note: The verb normally announces something welcome, and it comes from the word for skin, because good news shows in the face. Followed here by a darkening face, the word is turned against the man.
A form describing a colour deepening as it happens rather than a fixed state. The choice makes the change something the hearer watches, so the news is seen landing on him.
From a root for closing a waterskin tight. It describes swallowing an emotion rather than voicing it, so the man is full of something he has decided not to say aloud.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A birth was announced in public, and a man got the news in company. Sons meant fighters, herders and heirs who kept property inside the line. Daughters married outward and carried a settlement with them into another clan. The money side was real. An honour system also left a family open through its women, year after year. The news came where everyone could watch the father's face.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb used for the announcement here is the same one the Quran uses elsewhere for the good news brought to Abraham about a son and to Mary about a son. The vocabulary does not change when the child is a girl, and neither does the word for the news itself. Only the man's face changes.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage exposes a belief through behaviour rather than through logic. Daughters are assigned to God as a way of handing him something lesser. In doing that, the man has already said what he thinks of God. The method runs through the whole surah, past this one practice. What people do with what they claim to honour is treated as evidence about belief. It is allowed in as evidence.

crossReferences.why: Puts the buried girl herself in the courtroom, asked for what offence she was killed.
Repeats this darkening face almost word for word, inside the same argument about attribution.
Names daughters first when describing what God grants, reversing the order this passage assumes.

studies.applyIt: Think of something you say you value, then check one recent decision against it. Not a large decision. This passage works by setting a stated belief beside a face at a doorway, and the gap between them is the whole point. Give yourself the same test once, in private, and do not argue with the result.
studies.explainEasier: Some people said God had daughters, while keeping the sons they wanted for themselves. When one of these men was told his new baby was a girl, his face went dark and he swallowed his grief.

studies.title: Keep It Or Bury It
studies.meaning: The scene goes on and narrows. A man keeps away from people. Then come the two choices he turns over. Both sit in his own head, and neither is good. Keeping the child means keeping her in shame. The other way is covering her in earth. Early scholars read the wording as a refusal to offer him a third way, since his own starting point has already removed it. The verdict at the end lands on the reasoning.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The classical sources report the burial of baby girls as the practice of some Arabian groups. Poverty drove it, and so did the fear of dishonour. It is not described as universal. The Quran raises it several times in the Meccan years. Early scholars treat this passage as describing the mindset that made the act thinkable, not as reporting one case.

keyTerms.note: A verb for going behind something out of sight. It puts shame before any decision, so the passage shows him managing what others can see before he has considered the child at all.
From a root for lightness and low worth. The word names what he would be keeping her in, which means the option he calls keeping her is already a form of harm.
A verb for thrusting something down out of view, used of concealing rather than of any burial rite. The word does to the child in language what the act does in fact.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Honour in that society was shared and easily broken. A family carried its name into every deal over trade, marriage and protection. How a daughter later behaved, or her capture in a raid, could be talked about for a generation. Poverty made all of it sharper. Refusing the practice meant taking on a cost, and the whole clan paid it, not the man alone.
studies.didYouKnow: In both options the pronoun for the child is masculine in form. In the grammar of the sentence it agrees with the word for the news, not with the girl. Classical grammar writers discussed the choice at length. Several read it as holding the reader on how the father is thinking, rather than on the child herself.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The verdict at the end falls on the judging. It does not fall on the man's grief or on his poverty. That difference matters. Weighing up a human life can be simply wrong, the way a sum is wrong. It is not one custom to be set against other customs. The passage also shows that a child's worth does not come from what she will one day contribute.

crossReferences.why: Supplies the news and the darkened face that this ayah continues without any break in the sentence.
Returns to the buried girl on the Day of Judgement, and gives her a question of her own.
Names the killing of children out of fear of poverty, and answers that fear directly.

studies.applyIt: Think of someone whose value in your mind is quietly attached to what they provide. A colleague, a relative, a person you find hard work. Say one thing to them this week that has nothing to do with their usefulness to you. The charge in this ayah is against a way of counting, and that is where it can be answered.
studies.explainEasier: The man hides from people because of the news. He wonders whether to keep the girl and treat her badly, or bury her in the dust. God says the way they decide is evil.

studies.title: The Highest Description
studies.meaning: A short ayah with a comparison folded inside it. What it sets out is not a moral contrast between two groups. It is a contrast of descriptions. People who do not expect an afterlife are said to have the description of evil, and God has the highest one. Early scholars note that the word covers a likeness, a proverb and a set of qualities at once. Two names close the ayah, might and wisdom, and they say what the highest description holds.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, closing the passage about attributing daughters and following it with a general principle. The surah has been showing what people say about God and what they quietly keep for themselves. This ayah names the deeper error, which is that a description of God had been produced at all, assembled out of human preference. No occasion is reported for it in the classical sources.

keyTerms.note: The word covers a comparison, a proverb and a set of attributes. Its width is useful here, because the passage concerns both the pictures people make of God and the ones they make of themselves.
A superlative from a root for elevation. Set against the description of evil rather than against a merely lower one, it puts the two on a single scale with nothing standing between them.
From a root for being rare, strong and out of reach. It names power that cannot be diminished, which is the quality a description assembled out of human wishes would never think to include.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Arabian society ran on likenesses. A poet could fix a tribe's name with one comparison. A proverb repeated at a gathering settled arguments or ruined families. Descriptions were the coin of honour. Travellers heard them once, learned them by heart and carried them between towns. Claiming the highest description there was a claim made inside a real market of speech, where others competed.
studies.didYouKnow: This surah is unusually full of comparisons. After this ayah it builds three long ones, each opened by the same phrase. A slave who owns nothing is set against a man who spends freely. A mute man who is a burden is set against one who commands justice. Then a safe town that turned ungrateful. The highest likeness is announced first, and the human ones follow.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The ayah moves the argument from what people worship to how they describe. That is a quieter charge. A description built to comfort, or to justify what its maker already wanted, ends up describing the maker. Might and wisdom are then attached to the highest description. That rules out two familiar stand-ins at once. A God who can be managed, and a God who acts on nothing but whim.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same phrase for the highest description, inside an argument from creation to re-creation.
States the denial that makes this comparison work, that nothing whatever is like Him.
Warns against striking likenesses for God, applying immediately the principle set out here.

studies.applyIt: Write down in one sentence what you assume God is like when you are not thinking about it carefully. The version running underneath your reactions. Then read it back and ask which part came from a verse and which part came from your own hopes or fears. Do not correct it yet. Seeing it clearly is enough for one day.
studies.explainEasier: People who do not believe in the life to come have a bad description. God has the highest description of all. He is strong and cannot be beaten, and he is wise.

studies.theme: Time and the Brevity of Life
studies.title: Postponed To An Appointed Term
studies.meaning: The ayah opens with an if, set on a deliberately huge scale. If wrongdoing were answered at once, nothing that moves would be left alive. Early scholars note that the sentence takes in animals. So the result would not stop at the wrongdoers. Then it turns to what actually happens, which is delay. The last clause shuts the other direction too. When the appointed term arrives, it cannot be moved by an hour either way.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The surah has just described people assigning to God what they themselves dislike. This ayah answers an objection nobody has said out loud, that if all this is true, nothing seems to be happening. The classical scholars treat it as a general statement about how the world is run, not as a reply to a named incident. They report no particular occasion.

keyTerms.note: A reciprocal form of the verb to take, used for calling in what is owed. It belongs to the language of debt and contract, so the sentence describes a claim being enforced rather than anger being expressed.
A fixed period with a known end, used in that society for the due date on a loan. The word holds both the span and the deadline, so the delay described is already measured out.
The smallest unit the sentence could have chosen. Naming it makes the fixity precise in both directions, since the verbs that follow deny delaying the term and bringing it forward alike.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Credit ran the caravan economy. Goods went north against a promise, and a term was set for repayment, witnessed and remembered. Everyone knew what a due date was and what asking for an extension cost a man in standing. A creditor who did not call in a debt immediately was understood to be showing forbearance rather than forgetting. The vocabulary of this ayah belongs to that world.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for a creature that moves, used here for what would be wiped out, occurs twice in this surah and only twice. The other occurrence, a dozen ayat earlier, names everything in the heavens and the earth that bows to God. The same term marks the whole of animate creation once as worshipping and once as at risk.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Two things are set out together, and they pull against each other. Delay is real. So the lack of a visible result proves nothing about whether wrongdoing is registered. The term is also fixed. The delay has an end, and it is not a bargain anyone can enter. Between them, the ayah takes away two things. The comfort of thinking nothing is counted, and the panic of thinking anything might land at any moment.

crossReferences.why: States the same conditional almost word for word, then names the term and describes its arrival.
Applies the fixed term to whole communities, with the same denial that it can be moved.
Explains the deferral as mercy, supplying the reason this ayah leaves unstated.

studies.applyIt: Think of a consequence you have quietly decided is not coming, because enough time has gone by. A conversation you owe, a debt, a habit. You do not need to panic about it. Just move it back from the settled column into the open one this week, and take the first small step you have been putting off.
studies.explainEasier: If God punished people as soon as they did wrong, no living thing would be left on the earth. Instead he gives them time, up to a set day. When that day comes, it will not move.

studies.title: What Their Tongues Describe
studies.meaning: The last and sharpest of the three allocations in this surah. Something is assigned to God that the assigners themselves would not want. In the same breath, their tongues claim the best outcome for themselves. Early scholars read the two halves as one gesture. The false attribution and the self-flattery are a single act, seen from either end. The response follows with no argument, and the wording marks it as beyond dispute.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. It ends a run of three ayat that each open by describing what people allocate. The surah has moved from a share of produce, to daughters, to this. The classical scholars tie the passage to a Meccan confidence, that whatever came after death, the speakers would be fine. No specific occasion is reported. The attitude is treated as general among the objectors.

keyTerms.note: The verb for giving an account of something's qualities, used of a witness or of a merchant describing goods. Attaching it to tongues makes the lie a piece of testimony rather than a private opinion.
A feminine superlative, the finest of something the sentence never names. That vagueness is part of the claim, since what is being asserted is a general confidence about how things will turn out.
Scholars differ over the reading. Some take it as being driven forward into the Fire, others as being neglected and forgotten there, and the classical commentaries preserve both without settling it.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Reputation was made and unmade by speech. A man's word in the market was his credit, and a merchant who described his goods falsely lost the trade of a whole route. Poets were paid to describe, and their descriptions travelled with the caravans. In a culture where a spoken characterisation carried that kind of force, a tongue describing a lie was doing measurable damage.
studies.didYouKnow: The short phrase that introduces the verdict here means without doubt, or no escaping it. It occurs five times in the Quran, and three of those five are in this surah. One comes earlier, about God knowing what people hide. One is here. One comes again near the end of the surah.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Judging yourself is treated as a claim about God, not as a mood. To be sure of the best outcome, while handing God what you would refuse for yourself, is to settle both ends of the account in your own favour. The passage does not answer by disproving the confidence. It answers by naming who holds the verdict. What is at stake is where judgement sits.

crossReferences.why: Opens with the same verb of allocating, beginning the short sequence that this ayah closes.
Records the identical confidence, that things will turn out well, in the mouth of a similar speaker.
Dramatises the assumption as a story, with a man certain his garden and his standing will hold.

studies.applyIt: Listen this week for the sentence you use to reassure yourself about how things will end. Most people have one and say it often. Write it down word for word. You do not have to reject it. Just notice that you are the one who said it, and that saying it is not the same as knowing it.
studies.explainEasier: These people give God what they would hate to have themselves. At the same time they say out loud that the best is waiting for them. It is a lie. The Fire is what waits for them.

studies.title: Made Alluring To Them
studies.meaning: An oath opens the first ayah, and what follows is a pattern rather than an accusation. Messengers were sent to earlier communities, and something made their own conduct look attractive to them. Early scholars note that nothing was added to those deeds; only the appearance changed. The second ayah then names the book's function against exactly that problem. It is sent to settle what people disagree about, and it arrives as guidance and mercy for those who accept it.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) was meeting the same rejection earlier messengers had met. The surah keeps setting the present opposition inside that longer series. The classical scholars read the pairing here as comfort and instruction at once. No particular occasion is reported. The two ayat belong to the surah's argument about how communities receive a message.

keyTerms.note: An intensive verb for decorating a surface. It leaves the thing itself untouched and alters only how it looks, which is why early scholars describe this as a failure of judgement rather than of information.

The word for a protector who holds authority and gives support in return for loyalty. Applying it here inverts a relationship the audience valued, since patronage was the very thing that made life safe.

A reciprocal verb suggesting people pulling in opposite directions rather than holding calm opinions. It names disagreement as a condition the scripture arrives into, not one that the scripture creates.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Patronage held Arabian society together. A man with no protector could be killed on the road and nothing would follow. So alliances were formal, declared in public, and worth more than property. Freed slaves and newcomers to a town needed one before they could trade at all. Naming a patron for a whole community meant naming who would answer for them when something went wrong.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb rendered as clarify is used twice within these few ayat, with the same person as its subject. Earlier the Reminder is sent down so the messenger may make clear to people what was revealed to them. Here the scripture is sent down so he may make clear what they dispute. The task is stated twice, and only the second half changes.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage puts the difficulty of belief in how things look, not in the evidence. If a person's own deeds can be made to look good to him, more argument will not always help. That is why the answer given is a book that settles disputes, rather than another proof. Guidance and mercy are then named together at the end. Being shown where you are wrong is presented as a kindness.

crossReferences.why: Says that every community has had its own conduct made to look good in its own eyes.
Describes scripture given to a people who then disputed only after clear knowledge reached them.
Sets out the same purpose for revelation, sent to judge between people over what they differed about.

studies.applyIt: Name one thing you do that you have never seriously questioned, because it has always looked obviously fine. Ask someone you trust what they see in it. The warning in this ayah is not about doing wrong knowingly. It is about the way a habit stops looking like a choice, and a person outside your head can usually still see it.
studies.explainEasier: God sent messengers to peoples long before this. Satan made their own deeds look fine to them. The Book was sent down to make clear what people argue about, and to guide those who believe.

studies.title: Revived After Its Death
studies.meaning: One sentence, one image, then a closing clause that names its audience. Water comes down, and dead ground becomes living ground. Early scholars read this as the standard Quranic argument for resurrection. It is offered not as proof but as a yearly showing that nobody disputes. What is unusual is the last word. It names people who listen rather than people who think. So the sign is filed under hearing, not under reasoning.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. It opens a run of ayat that move from rain to cattle to fruit to bees. Each one closes on a different kind of person. The surah is answering people who accepted God as creator while denying that he would raise the dead. The classical scholars treat the sequence as one building argument, not as a set of separate occasions. They report no specific event behind it.

keyTerms.note: A causative of the verb to live. It is the same verb used across the Quran for raising the dead, so a sentence about a field is already carrying the vocabulary of the argument it serves.
Land is given an actual death rather than dormancy. The choice of word makes the yearly recovery an instance of the thing being denied rather than a comparison drawn loosely.
The verb for hearing, used here of taking something in and letting it register. It implies a sign that works on a person willing to attend, not one who must first be argued into position.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Rain in Arabia was rare, local and dramatic. A valley could stay dry for years and then flood in a night, and within days ground that had been bare would carry grazing. Tribes moved herds towards reported rainfall, and news of it travelled fast between camps. Everyone in the audience had watched a landscape come back, and had staked a season on it happening.
studies.didYouKnow: The exact closing phrase here names one sign for a people who do something. It occurs six times in the Quran, and five of those six are in this surah. The last word changes each time. Those who reflect, who remember, who listen, who understand, and who reflect again.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The argument treats resurrection as a question about power, and one already answered in public. If bringing dead things back were impossible, it would not happen every spring in front of the people objecting. The passage adds one thing. The sign is open to whoever will listen. So the obstacle sits in attention, not in cleverness and not in reaching the evidence.

crossReferences.why: Draws the conclusion this ayah leaves implicit, naming the reviver of the earth as the reviver of the dead.
Uses the stirring of dry ground as a direct answer to a question about being raised.
Sends winds driving cloud to dead land, and calls the resurrection just such an emergence.

studies.applyIt: The next time it rains where you are, go to a window and stay there for one minute without doing anything else. That is the whole exercise. The closing word of this ayah is about listening, and rain is one of the few signs that arrives with a sound. Let it be a sign once instead of weather.
studies.explainEasier: God sends water down from the sky. The dry ground comes back to life after it was dead. That is a sign for people who will listen to it.

studies.title: From Between Waste And Blood
studies.meaning: The passage announces a lesson and then shows its working, which is unusual. It traces milk back to where it comes from, and it does not soften the description. Something clean and pleasant comes out of a place that is neither. Early scholars read the point as separation rather than change. What is produced is kept distinct from what surrounds it. The word for pure carries that argument.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, inside the run of signs drawn from ordinary life. Herd animals were the wealth of the audience. Milk was a daily staple, not a luxury. The classical scholars note that this ayah and one elsewhere in the Quran open with the same wording before they part. No specific occasion is reported. The surah is reasoning from what its hearers handled every morning.

keyTerms.note: From a root for passing from one bank of a river to the other. The word names a thought that carries you from what you see to what it implies, which is what the rest of the ayah then performs.
A word for something separated out and left free of any admixture. Placed immediately after the two things named beside it, it insists on distinctness rather than on cleanliness.
From a root for going down the throat without resistance. It adds the drinker's own experience to the description, so the sign includes how the thing feels and not only what it is.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A herd was a family's bank. Camels and goats were counted as wealth, given as bride price, paid as compensation, and milked twice daily for the household. Milk was drunk fresh, soured for keeping, and thinned with water on journeys when nothing else could be carried. A poor season showed first in the milk, so anyone could read an animal's condition at a glance.
studies.didYouKnow: This ayah and one in a later surah begin with the same clause, word for word, about cattle and a lesson. Then they go different ways. The pronoun attached to the bellies of the animals differs between them. It is masculine here and feminine there. Classical grammar writers wrote at length about which noun each one agrees with.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The example is chosen so that the process carries the argument, not only the product. Anyone can be grateful for milk. This ayah insists on where it comes from. So what God provides works through ordinary biology rather than around it. It also sets a pattern the surah repeats. What is valuable is often made quietly inside something a watcher would rather not look at.

crossReferences.why: Opens with identical wording about cattle and a lesson, then turns to their other uses instead.
Introduces the same animals earlier in this surah, listing warmth and food among their benefits.
Returns to livestock as something people did not make, and asks why gratitude does not follow.

studies.applyIt: Drink something slowly today and notice the moment it goes down easily. That specific quality is named in this ayah, and it is there because the sign is meant to include the drinking and not only the milk. Most gratitude fails at the point where a thing is too ordinary to register. This is one attempt at catching it before it slips.
studies.explainEasier: There is a lesson for you in cattle. Milk comes out of their bodies, from between waste and blood. It is clean and pure, and it goes down easily for anyone who drinks it.

studies.title: Inspired To The Bee
studies.meaning: Fruit is named first. The passage notes, without comment, that people take two different things from it. One makes a person drunk. The other is wholesome food. Early scholars read the pairing as a contrast drawn on purpose and left open at this stage. Then the direction changes completely. An instruction is given to an insect, in the feminine singular, telling it where to build. What is described is guidance reaching a creature with no language.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The surah takes its name from this passage. The classical scholars note that the ayah about grapes and dates came before the later Medinan passages that address intoxicants, which is why it can describe the practice plainly. Beyond that they report no particular occasion. The section belongs to the surah's run of signs drawn from familiar agriculture and familiar animals.

keyTerms.note: Named beside wholesome provision with no verdict attached. Early scholars note the plain contrast between the two words, and read the ayah as describing what people do rather than evaluating it.

The verb ordinarily used for revelation given to prophets. Applied to an insect, it names an instruction arriving without language, which is why early scholars call it a different mode of the same thing.
A feminine singular imperative, addressed to the bee the way one addresses a person. The grammar makes the instruction direct rather than general, and the bee is the one being spoken to.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Wild honey was gathered from cliffs and hollow trees, and it was valuable enough to trade and to give as a gift. Date palms and vines were the two great cultivated crops of the oases, and both were pressed. A household's year ran on the date harvest, which was counted, stored and borrowed against. Bees, palms and vines were the ordinary furniture of an oasis economy.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for the bee occurs exactly once in the whole Quran. It is in this passage. The surah is named after it, though it runs to a hundred and twenty-eight ayat on many other subjects. The same verb of inspiration is used elsewhere of the mother of Moses. It is used of the heavens themselves.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Using the words of revelation for an insect does something careful. It says guidance is wider than prophecy. The world is full of creatures being told what to do, in ways they never feel as instruction. So prophecy is the human form of something general. It is not an exception in an otherwise silent universe. And the skill of the bee becomes evidence rather than charm.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same verb of inspiration for the mother of Moses, outside the line of prophets.
Applies the same verb to the heavens, extending it to something further still from speech.
Returns to these two products of the vine and weighs their benefit against their harm.

studies.applyIt: Watch a bee or an ant for one minute this week without interrupting it. You will see competence nobody taught it and it cannot explain. The claim in this passage is that the competence is instruction, arriving in a form the creature never recognises as instruction. Sit with that for the length of one small animal's errand.
studies.explainEasier: People get two things from dates and grapes. One of them makes you drunk. The other is good food. That is a sign. God also told the bee to make its home in the mountains, in trees and in what people build.

studies.title: The Pathways Of Your Lord
studies.meaning: The instruction to the bee continues: eat from every fruit, then travel your Lord's paths, and a single word describes the manner. Scholars differ over whether it describes the paths as smoothed or the bee as compliant, and both readings are old. What follows is stated as fact rather than promise. A drink of varied colours emerges, and in it is healing for people, which the sentence leaves unqualified.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, completing the passage that gives the surah its name. Honey was a known remedy in Arabia long before this ayah, used on wounds and for stomach complaints, so the statement would not have startled the first hearers. The classical scholars report no specific occasion. They read the closing phrase about reflection as marking the end of the whole run of signs.

keyTerms.note: The plural of a road or track. Attaching it to the Lord makes the bee's foraging routes something assigned rather than chosen, and it is the same word the Quran uses for the ways of guidance.
Scholars differ over what this modifies. Some read the paths as smoothed for the bee, others the bee as compliant along them, and both readings are preserved in the classical commentaries.
An indefinite noun, so the sentence says healing rather than the healing. Early scholars generally read it as real but partial, describing a genuine remedy rather than a cure for everything.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Medicine in seventh-century Arabia was made of what could be carried. Dates, oil, herbs, cupping, cautery and honey. Honey kept without spoiling on long journeys, which mattered a great deal. It was put on wounds as well as swallowed. Doctors were rare, and households treated themselves. Naming honey as a healing named something already in most tents. It did not bring in a new remedy.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for healing occurs four times in the Quran. Three of those describe revelation itself, healing what is in the chests or given to those who believe. This is the only place where the Quran applies the word to a physical substance, and the substance comes out of an insect.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage puts the obedience of the bee and the use of the honey in one sentence. Following an assigned path is one movement with making something that helps others. They are not two. The passage also refuses to make the healing a reward. It simply comes out, from the bellies of insects doing as they were told. The benefit sits downstream of an obedience that nobody involved understands.

crossReferences.why: Calls revelation a healing, using the very word this ayah applies to honey.
Names a healing for what is in the chests, giving the same word its inward sense.
Carries the instruction that this ayah completes, telling the bee where to build its houses.

studies.applyIt: Think of the smallest useful thing you do that nobody notices, and do it once more this week without mentioning it. The bee here is not praised, thanked, or told what its work becomes. It eats, it travels its route, and something people need comes out of that. Try that shape for one task.
studies.explainEasier: The bee eats from all kinds of fruit and follows the paths its Lord set for it. Out of its body comes a drink of many colours. In that drink there is healing for people.

studies.theme: Time and the Brevity of Life
studies.title: Back To The Frailest Age
studies.meaning: Three movements are packed into one sentence. Created, taken, and for some a return to an age the ayah calls the meanest. The last clause is precise about what is lost. It is knowledge already gained, not knowledge never had. Early scholars note that this is not presented as punishment. It sits among the signs. The two names at the close, knowing and capable, are the frame the passage offers for holding it.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. It stands among the ayat that take their signs from the human life span rather than from crops and animals. The surah has just described milk, fruit and honey. Here it turns the same attention on the body that takes them in. The classical scholars report no particular occasion. They read the ayah as a general statement about the course a human life can take.

keyTerms.note: A verb from the language of settling accounts, meaning to receive in full what is owed. Death is described as a completed collection rather than as a loss, which is a deliberate choice of register.
A superlative for what is lowest in value or condition. The word is blunt, and early scholars observe that the Quran does not soften its description of extreme old age at this point.
The whole allotted stretch of a life rather than a moment within it. Pairing it with the previous word makes the phrase name a stage inside a span, not an accident that befalls someone.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Age was authority. Elders settled disputes, held the family lines, and carried the poetry and treaty terms that nobody had written down. The memory of a community lived inside its oldest members. So the loss described here was not a private matter. When an elder stopped knowing, a tribe lost records it had no other copy of. Everyone understood exactly what that cost.
studies.didYouKnow: The exact phrase for this stage of life appears twice in the Quran and nowhere else. The other occurrence sits inside a long argument for resurrection that runs from a drop of fluid through birth and growth to old age, and then to dry ground stirring under rain. Both uses stand in passages about what God is able to do.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The ayah places the undoing of a person inside the ordinary care it has been describing. That is uncomfortable, and it is deliberate. Knowing and capable are named at the exact point where a human being is neither. So the two names say who holds the account when the person can no longer hold it. And they put dignity somewhere other than in what a person can still do.

crossReferences.why: Uses the identical phrase for this stage, inside a longer argument about being raised again.
Traces the same arc, weakness to strength to weakness and grey hair, as a created pattern.
Says whoever is granted long life is reversed in creation, and asks whether people consider it.

studies.applyIt: Sit with someone old this week, particularly someone whose memory has begun to go. Do not test them and do not correct their dates. Just be there for the length of one cup of tea. This ayah names knowing and capable at the exact moment a person is neither, and that is easier to believe in company than alone.
studies.explainEasier: God made you, and one day he takes you back. Some people live so long that they reach a very weak age. They forget what they once knew. God knows everything and can do anything.

studies.title: They Would Not Level It
studies.meaning: An observation about unequal provision comes first. Then an argument that turns the conduct of the hearers into its starting point. Those given more do not hand their property to the people they own until both stand level. Early scholars read this as exposing an inconsistency. The same people guarded every degree of their own advantage, and yet they were assigning partners to God in what he owns. The closing question names the whole thing as denial.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Bonded service was an ordinary part of the society addressed. The ayah takes the arrangement as its audience knew it and reasons from it. The classical scholars note that the passage is not describing what ought to happen with property. It reasons from what visibly does happen. No specific occasion is reported for it in the sources.

keyTerms.note: A verb for granting a surplus over another. It states the inequality as something given rather than earned, which removes the ground on which the favoured party might otherwise feel entitled.
The word for two things standing at exactly the same height. Its appearance is the hinge of the argument, because levelling is precisely what the property holders would never grant.
A verb for rejecting what you actually recognise. It differs from simple disbelief, so the charge is not ignorance of the favour but refusal to acknowledge something already known.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Households in Mecca included people who were owned. The line between them and the free ran through every detail of daily life. Where you sat. What you were called. Whether your word counted in a dispute. Property was the clearest marker of all, and a man who blurred it lost standing among his peers. Everyone listening knew exactly how firm that line was.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb that closes this ayah is not the usual Quranic word for disbelief. It names a denial made against a person's own recognition. The Quran uses it elsewhere of people who rejected signs. In its words, their own selves were certain of them. Choosing it here turns ingratitude into a claim about what a person actually knows.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The argument makes the hearers apply their own standard to themselves. If you would not share ownership with someone in your household, you have already shown that you understand what owning outright means. So setting partners beside God is not a position you hold in a steady way. Ingratitude is then redefined. It is not a failure to feel thankful. It is a refusal to draw an obvious conclusion.

crossReferences.why: Puts the same argument in almost the same terms, drawn from partners in what people already own.
Uses the same verb for denial, and adds that their own selves were certain of what they rejected.
Returns to the distribution of livelihood and says the ranking between people is itself assigned.

studies.applyIt: Notice one advantage you have that you did not arrange: where you were born, a language you speak, a body that works. Then notice how quickly you defend it as yours. You do not need to give it away. Just say once, in plain words to yourself, that it was handed to you, and let the sentence sit there.
