studies.explainEasier: God gave some people more than others. Those with more would not hand their property over to the servants they own and make them equal partners. The verse asks whether they will then deny what God has given them.

studies.title: Children And Grandchildren
studies.meaning: A list of gifts arrives in a single breath, and its order matters. Partners drawn from among the hearers themselves, then children from those partners, then a further generation, then good things to eat. It moves outward through a household and forward through time. Early scholars differ over the exact reference of one word in the list. Then the sentence turns and asks how people fed by all this can trust what is empty.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The surah has been listing what people receive and then asking what they do with it, and here the list becomes domestic. The classical scholars differ over whether one term names grandchildren, servants or relatives by marriage, and they preserve the range without settling it. No specific occasion is reported. The audience addressed counted lineage as the central form of wealth.

keyTerms.note: A word for one of a matched pair, used of both sexes. Saying they come from among yourselves stresses shared kind rather than difference, and that is where the sentence begins its argument.
The word occurs only here in the Quran. Early scholars read it as grandchildren, as servants, or as those who assist, and all three senses come from a root for swift, willing service.
A plural covering what is pleasant and clean, most often of food. It closes the list by moving from people to provision, so the household and its table are named together as one gift.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A man's standing was counted in his descendants. Sons and their sons meant defence, labour, and a name that outlived him. A line that ended was spoken of with pity. Marriages were negotiated between clans, and they sealed alliances that outlasted the couple. A second generation of children was visible proof that a household had held together. In that world it was an achievement worth naming aloud.
studies.didYouKnow: One word in this ayah, usually translated as grandchildren, occurs nowhere else in the Quran. Its root has to do with speed and eager service. That is why some classical scholars read it as helpers rather than descendants. The early Arabic dictionaries record both senses side by side. They do not resolve which the ayah intends.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage treats family as provision, and that is a specific claim. Partners, children and a further generation sit in the same list as food. All of them are given rather than achieved. That cuts against reading a family line as an accomplishment, which is what the audience assumed. The closing contrast sets falsehood against favour. Misplaced trust and ingratitude are named as one movement.

crossReferences.why: Describes partners made from among yourselves, and names affection and mercy as the sign in it.
Continues the theme of children as something granted, with the choice explicitly not the parents'.
Places wealth and sons together as the adornment of this life, and weighs them against what lasts.

studies.applyIt: Say one specific thank you to a family member this week for something they have simply always done. Not a general appreciation. Name the thing. This ayah lists people alongside food as provision, and the point of that ordering is that the nearest gifts are the first ones to stop registering.
studies.explainEasier: God gave you partners from among your own people. From them he gave you children and grandchildren. He also gave you good things to eat. Yet some people trust what is empty and turn away from all of it.

studies.title: God Knows And You Do Not
studies.meaning: The first ayah describes what people serve besides God by two denials. It owns no provision, from sky or earth. It has no power to get any. The second ayah draws out the instruction. Do not coin likenesses for God. The reason given is a bare contrast between his knowing and their not knowing. Early scholars note that the ban falls on the act of comparing, not on one particular comparison.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. It comes straight after the surah has listed what people actually receive. Rain, milk, honey, partners, children. The instruction follows from that list, since the things being served had added nothing to it. The classical scholars report no specific occasion. They read the pair as the hinge into the long comparisons that fill the next several ayat.

keyTerms.note: The verb for holding legal possession, which in that society implied the ability to give away. Denying it says the thing served cannot transfer anything, for the simple reason that it holds nothing.

Literally to strike, used both of minting coins and of framing a comparison. The idiom treats a likeness as something manufactured, which suits an argument about people fashioning descriptions of God.
A plural with the definite article, so the prohibition covers the practice rather than a single instance. The same word returns immediately afterwards with God as the one doing the striking.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Comparison was the standard tool of Arabic thought. Family lines, poetry and the settling of disputes all worked by likening one case to another. A man who produced the right comparison in an assembly won the argument outright. Telling that audience to stop coining likenesses in one area meant something specific. It told skilled people to set down the tool they trusted most.
studies.didYouKnow: The ban here is followed at once by three likenesses that God strikes in the ayat just after. Each is introduced by the very verb the hearers were told not to use. The surah forbids the activity and then does it within two lines. Classical scholars read that as a statement about who is qualified to do it.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The reason attached to the ban is unusual. It is not that comparison is disrespectful. It is that the people doing it lack the information. A likeness works by drawing on what you already know. So any comparison a person invents for God is built out of what that person happens to have met. The ban is therefore about method. The ayat that follow show the method done properly.

crossReferences.why: Begins the comparisons God strikes, immediately after the hearers are told not to strike their own.
Supplies the principle behind the prohibition, that nothing whatever resembles Him.
Sets out a likeness about what is served besides God, which cannot create even a fly.

studies.applyIt: Catch yourself the next time you explain God with a comparison, especially one that begins with a person. A parent, a judge, a friend. You do not have to abandon it. Just add a sentence afterwards naming where the comparison breaks down, and notice how much of your picture was resting on the part that broke.
studies.explainEasier: People serve things beside God that own nothing in the sky or on the earth. They cannot give anything, and they have no power to get any. So do not make up pictures of God. God knows, and you do not.

studies.title: Are They Equal In Comparison
studies.meaning: The first of the likenesses arrives, built entirely out of the social world of the audience. A bonded man with power over nothing is set beside someone given generous provision. That second man spends from it in private and in the open. The question that follows is never answered directly. Early scholars note that the praise breaking into the comparison stands in place of the answer. The closing clause says most people do not know this.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The surah has just forbidden people to coin their own likenesses. This is the first that God strikes in reply. The comparison uses bonded service as a plain fact of that society, not as approval of it. The classical scholars report no particular occasion. They read the two figures as standing for what is served besides God, and for God himself.

keyTerms.note: A passive participle from the verb to own, so the man is defined entirely by another's possession of him. The word leaves him with no capacity of his own that the sentence could describe.
From a root for a thing passing out and away. The verb covers all giving out of what one holds, and the surrounding words make the giving continuous rather than occasional.
Paired here with openly, so both are approved together. The two describe giving that is not managed for an audience, since someone doing both is not calculating who happens to be watching.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Bonded service was visible everywhere in Mecca. The powerlessness described here was legal, not a figure of speech. A bonded man could not own, could not give, could not enter a contract. Against him the audience would have pictured a merchant of standing. His generosity was known in the market, and by reputation he practised it where nobody saw. Both figures were people they could name.
studies.didYouKnow: This is the first of three comparisons in this surah introduced by the identical phrase about God striking a likeness. The other two follow within forty ayat, one about a man who cannot speak and one about a town that had been secure. Together they form the surah's longest sustained sequence of parables.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The comparison turns on the power to give. That is a precise way to argue about what deserves worship. What is served besides God is not called evil. It is called unable, and being unable is what rules it out. Putting praise in the middle of the question does something too. The right response is supplied before the reader has finished working the comparison out, as though the answer were never in doubt.

crossReferences.why: Forbids the hearers to strike likenesses immediately before this one is struck for them.
Commends spending by night and day, secretly and openly, in the same paired phrasing.
Says that what is called upon besides God does not own the skin of a date stone.

studies.applyIt: Give something away this week that nobody will find out about. It does not need to be money and it does not need to be large. The comparison here praises giving done openly and unseen together, and the unseen half is the part that tells you whether the open half was really about giving at all.
studies.explainEasier: God gives a picture. One man is owned by someone else and has no power over anything. Another has been given plenty and gives from it, both in secret and out in the open. The two are not the same.

studies.title: A Burden On His Guardian
studies.meaning: The second comparison sharpens the first. One man cannot speak, has power over nothing, and is a weight on whoever answers for him; sent anywhere, he brings back nothing good. The other commands justice and is himself on a straight road. Early scholars note that the second figure is described twice over, by what he tells others to do and by where he stands, so his speech and his position are made to agree.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. It is the second of three likenesses struck in reply to hearers who had been coining their own. The classical scholars read the mute figure as standing for what was served besides God, unable to answer or to help anyone. They read the other as standing for God, or in some readings for the person who calls to him. No specific occasion is reported for the ayah.

keyTerms.note: A form describing someone without speech from birth rather than someone silent by choice. The related plural is used elsewhere in the Quran of people who possess speech but will not use it for truth.
A word for something that must be carried and returns nothing. It is blunt about dependence, and early scholars apply it to the object of worship in the comparison rather than to any human being.
A word covering both the one who owns and the one who protects. Its double sense keeps the figure inside a relationship of care, so the burden is being carried by someone obliged to carry it.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A household took full responsibility for the people who depended on it. That included those who could not work or speak for themselves. Nobody was turned out. The clan carried the cost, and it was a point of honour. The sums were still talked about, though. Sending a man on an errand and having him come back with nothing was a familiar annoyance, in an economy where every journey cost water and days.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for the mute man occurs in this exact singular form only once in the Quran. Its plural is used several times elsewhere, always of people described as deaf, mute and blind while their faculties in fact work. The singular is reserved for a comparison, and the plural for an accusation.
studies.theologicalSignificance: This comparison adds speech to the capacity the previous one weighed. What cannot answer cannot be in a relationship. So the objection to serving it is not that it is weak. It is that nothing passes in either direction. The other man commands justice and stands on a straight path. That joins two things people usually keep apart. Telling others what is right, and being where you say they should be.

crossReferences.why: Strikes the first of these comparisons, weighing capacity to give rather than capacity to speak.
Presses the same point, that what is called upon does not answer and possesses no faculties.
Uses the plural of this word for people whose senses work but who bring nothing back.

studies.applyIt: Think of one place where what you tell other people is right and where you actually stand have drifted apart. Do not announce it to anyone. Just close the gap by a single visible step this week, in the direction of the thing you already say. This comparison praises the man who commands justice only alongside where his own feet are.
studies.explainEasier: God gives another picture. One man cannot speak and can do nothing. He is a weight on the man who looks after him, and he brings back nothing good. The other tells people to be fair and walks a straight road.

studies.title: As A Blink Or Nearer
studies.meaning: Two claims are joined by a small word doing more work than it looks. Everything hidden in the heavens and the earth belongs to God. The arrival of the Hour is a blink of an eye, or quicker. Early scholars read that second claim as describing the speed of the command, not the length of the event. A third clause closes with power. So hiddenness, speed and capacity are stated as one thought.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. It comes after the comparisons and before the surah turns to the birth of the human being. The audience had demanded again and again to know when the Hour would come. The surah opened by saying the command of God had already drawn near. The classical scholars treat this as part of that running answer, not as a reply to a question asked on one particular day.

keyTerms.note: What is absent from perception rather than what is mysterious in itself. Placing it in a possessive relationship with God makes hiddenness relative, since a thing unseen has to be unseen by someone.
The ordinary word for a portion of time, used as a name for the end. Its plainness is deliberate, so the event is referred to by a term for something short rather than something vast.
The flick of the eye, the fastest movement a person could point to. The comparison takes its unit from the body rather than from the sky, which keeps an unimaginable speed measurable.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Time in Arabia was measured by things that took a while. A moon, a season, the days a caravan needed to reach Gaza, the years of a boycott. Fast events were reckoned by the body, a breath or a glance. Choosing the blink as the measure meant reaching for the shortest span anyone in the audience had a name for. It was also one they could test on themselves.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase comparing something to the blink of an eye occurs twice in the Quran. It is here, and in a much shorter later surah. Both times it describes the speed of the command of God, not the scale of what the command achieves. The two places use slightly different grammar for the same image.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Joining the unseen to the speed of the Hour answers a specific objection. People cannot say when the end will come. That is because knowledge of it is held elsewhere, not because it is far away. The second clause takes distance out of the question altogether. What is left is capacity, named at the close. So the passage leaves the reader with the one fact that does not depend on timing.

crossReferences.why: Repeats the same image of a blink, applied there to the singleness of God's command.
Opens this surah by saying the command of God has come, so it should not be hastened.
Lists knowledge of the Hour among the things kept with God and with nobody else.

studies.applyIt: Blink once, deliberately, and notice how little time that was. This ayah uses your own eye as its unit of measure, which means the comparison is available to you at any moment and needs no equipment. Reach for it the next time something feels too far off to be worth preparing for.
studies.explainEasier: Everything hidden in the sky and on the earth belongs to God. When the last Hour comes, it will take no longer than a blink of an eye, or less. God can do anything.

studies.title: Not Knowing Anything
studies.meaning: You are born knowing nothing. The empty state comes first in the ayah. What follows then reads as equipment, not as nature. Hearing, sight and the inner faculty are given, in that order. Early scholars note that this order matches how a newborn meets the world. The closing clause does not say so that you may understand. It says so that you may give thanks. The same instruments are pointed at a different end.
studies.historicalContext: This is a Meccan ayah. It belongs to the surah's long list of what people are given. Just before it, the surah described extreme old age and the loss of knowledge already gained. Here it turns to the other end of a life. It describes the moment before there is any knowledge at all. The classical scholars report no particular occasion for it. They read it as finishing the arc that the ayah before it began.

keyTerms.note: Given in the singular while the words beside it are plural. Classical grammarians discussed the difference at length, most reading hearing as one undivided capacity where seeing is many separate acts.
A plural, which commentators connect to the many distinct things a person looks at. Its pairing with a singular word for hearing is among the ayah's most discussed features.
The lexicons connect this root to an animal that yields well on little pasture. Gratitude in that image is a return larger than what came in, rather than a bare acknowledgement of it.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Infant mortality was high, and birth was attended by the women of a household without physicians. A child who lived was named on the seventh day and its arrival announced through the clan. Nothing about a newborn was assumed, least of all that it would hear and see. Families watched for the first response to a sound and remembered afterwards when it came.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for hearing here is singular. The words for sight and for the inner faculty are both plural. The gap is sharp enough that classical grammarians wrote about it again and again. Most of them explained it this way. Hearing is one whole capacity. Seeing is many separate acts, each with its own object.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Putting the purpose clause at gratitude rather than at knowledge changes what the faculties are for. They are not described as tools for working out the truth, though they can be used that way. They are described as gifts whose proper use includes noticing that they were given. That makes ingratitude the misuse of an instrument rather than merely an omission of good manners.

crossReferences.why: Lists the same three faculties as given after the shaping, and closes on how little thanks follows.
Repeats the three and adds the same complaint, that thanks is rarely given for them.
Describes the other end of the same life, when knowledge already acquired is taken away.

studies.applyIt: Pick one of the three named here. Use it on purpose for five minutes today. Listen to something without looking at a screen. Or look at something without narrating it to yourself. The ayah ties these faculties to thanks rather than to knowledge. Thanks usually needs the equipment noticed first before it works at all.
studies.explainEasier: God brings you into the world knowing nothing at all. Then he gives you ears to hear, eyes to see, and a mind to think with. He gives them so that you will say thank you.

studies.title: Nothing Holds Them Up
studies.meaning: A question again, and a scene anyone can check. Birds are suspended in open air, and the sentence lets a negative do the work: nothing holds them except God. The commentators note that the word describing their state means made subject rather than free, so the flight is presented as an arrangement instead of an achievement. The closing clause then names signs in the plural, which nothing else in this long sequence does.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The surah resumes its sequence of signs here, after the passage of comparisons. Arabians watched bird flight closely. They read birds for omens and watched them as signs of water. The classical scholars report no particular occasion for the ayah. They read it as part of the surah's method, which points at what its hearers already looked at every day.

keyTerms.note: A collective noun rather than a plural, so it names birds as a category and not a countable group. The sentence is looking at flight itself rather than at any particular flock overhead.
A passive participle used elsewhere in the Quran of the sun, the moon and the sea. It places birds among things arranged for a purpose rather than among things acting on their own account.
The word occurs only here in the Quran. It names the empty space between ground and sky, so the ayah is precise about where the birds are: in nothing at all.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Birds were read professionally. Diviners took omens from the direction a startled bird flew, and travellers watched for species that meant water within a day's ride. Falconry was known among the wealthy. A society that attentive to birds had never asked what kept them up, because the question does not arise while you are using an animal as an instrument.
studies.didYouKnow: This is the only ayah in the surah's long sequence of signs that uses the plural. Five others close with the same phrase about a single sign for a people who reflect, remember, listen or understand. This one alone says signs, and it alone names its audience as people who believe rather than people who think.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The ayah puts the wonder in what keeps going, not in what began. It does not ask who made birds. It asks what is holding them right now. That turns an argument about creation into an argument about upkeep. The change matters. A world that has to be held at every moment is not a machine that was wound once and left. That difference is the whole distance between two ideas of God.

crossReferences.why: Asks the same question about birds spreading and folding their wings, and gives the same answer.
Says God holds the sky from falling on the earth, using a related verb of holding.
Describes God holding the heavens and the earth from slipping, extending this to everything.

studies.applyIt: Watch a bird stay up without flapping for as long as it lasts. Gulls and crows do it on any windy afternoon. The ayah asks what is holding it, not what built it, and that is a different question from the one most arguments about God get stuck on. Ask the ayah's version once, outdoors.
studies.explainEasier: Look at birds staying up in the open sky. Nothing is holding them there except God. For people who believe, that is one of the signs that he is looking after the world.

studies.title: Homes That Travel With You
studies.meaning: Two kinds of dwelling are named in a single sentence and neither is ranked above the other. Built houses give rest; tents made from hides are light enough to move on the day of departure and raise again on the day of settling. Then the list runs on into wool, camel fur and goat hair. The commentators note that everything named comes from animals the surah introduced earlier, so the inventory closes a circle.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The audience held settled townspeople and families who still moved with their herds. The ayah speaks to both. It prefers neither way of living. The classical scholars note how precise its words are, since it names three different animal fibres separately. No specific occasion is reported. The ayah belongs to the run of favours the surah has been setting out.

keyTerms.note: From the root for stillness. It names what a house is for rather than what it is made of, so the gift being described is the quieting rather than the structure that produces it.
The word occurs only here in the Quran. It is the technical term for a household moving with its herds, and its presence marks the ayah as spoken to people who actually did that.
One of three fibres named separately, alongside sheep wool and goat hair. The distinction belongs to a herder rather than a poet, and this word too occurs nowhere else in the Quran.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A black tent was woven from goat hair. The hair swells when it gets wet, so the roof turns the rain. A tent could be struck and loaded in under an hour. Wool went into clothing and bedding. Camel fur went into rope and coarse cloth. A family's tent was often made by its women over years, and repaired panel by panel. The dwelling was the household's own work.
studies.didYouKnow: Two words in this one ayah appear nowhere else in the Quran. One is the term for a household striking camp. The other is the word for camel fur. Both belong to the working vocabulary of herding life. Finding them together in one sentence shows how closely this surah tracks the daily work of its hearers.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The ayah names a fixed house and a moving one in the same breath. So it refuses to make settling down the mark of a blessed life. Both are described as given. The closing phrase then sets a limit on all of it. It says enjoyment for a time. That short clause does quiet work. The comfort is real, and the holding is short. The ayah leaves that tension standing.

crossReferences.why: Introduces the same animals earlier in this surah, before their hides and fibres are itemised here.
Describes houses God permitted to be raised, where His name is remembered, adding another sense.
Weighs what is given for enjoyment for a time against what remains with God instead.

studies.applyIt: Look around the room you are in and find one thing that came from an animal or a plant, then trace it back two steps in your head. Wool, cotton, leather, wood. This ayah names its fibres separately because the giver of a thing is easier to see while the thing has not yet become a category.
studies.explainEasier: God gave people homes to rest in. He also gave them tents made from animal hides, light enough to carry when they travel and set up when they stop. Their wool and fur became blankets and warm things.

studies.title: Garments Against Heat And Harm
studies.meaning: Four provisions in one sentence, and every one is about shelter. Shade out of what has been created. Hollows in the mountains. Garments against the heat. Garments against each other's violence. Early scholars note that last pair, since one word covers cloth for the sun and armour for battle. The sentence closes on completion, and then on a purpose. The purpose named is submission, not thanks.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The ayah closes the surah's inventory of favours, just before it turns to those who refuse them. What it lists belongs to travel and to conflict. Those were the two conditions in which a Meccan felt most exposed. The classical scholars report no specific occasion. They observe that this ayah completes the list the earlier ones had been building.

keyTerms.note: The word occurs only here in the Quran. It names natural cavities in rock used as refuge from sun and storm, so the shelter being described is found rather than built by anyone.
A word for a garment worn over the body. It appears twice in this ayah and once more in the Quran, where it describes garments of pitch worn by the guilty.
A word for force and hardship in war. Saying the garments protect you from your own violence places the danger among the hearers themselves rather than somewhere outside them.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Travellers timed their journeys around shade, resting through the worst hours under a rock overhang or a solitary tree. Caves in the hills around Mecca served as shelter and as retreat. Armour was expensive, mostly mail brought from the north, and a coat of it could be the most valuable object a family owned. Every item on this list was survival rather than comfort.
studies.didYouKnow: The word used twice here for a garment appears only once more in the Quran. There it describes garments of pitch. So one term covers what protects the body in this life and what covers the guilty in the next. Classical scholars noticed the echo. They read it as meant, not as chance.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Ending a list of favours with armour is unexpected. It treats human violence as a lasting condition to be guarded against. It does not treat it as a problem the passage means to solve. That is unusually plain. The purpose named at the close is submission, not thanks. So a favour completed is offered as an argument. A person provided for this fully has no case left for holding back.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same word for garments, there made of pitch, in a description of the guilty.
Names the making of armour as something taught, to protect people from their own violence.
Uses the same language of a favour completed, there of a way of life brought to perfection.

studies.applyIt: Put on a coat this week and notice, for one second, that it is doing a job. Most protection works by being unremarkable. This ayah lists shade, caves and clothing as favours precisely because they are the things a person stops seeing, and it asks you to complete the list yourself before the weather turns.
studies.explainEasier: God made shade for you out of the things he created. He gave you caves in the hills to shelter in. He gave you clothes that keep out the heat, and shields that keep you safe in a fight.

studies.title: They Know It Then Deny It
studies.meaning: Three short movements. The messenger's duty is limited to delivering the message plainly. That lifts the outcome off him entirely. Then comes the surah's sharpest finding. They recognise the favour, and then they deny it. So the problem was never that they missed it. Then the scene jumps forward. A witness is raised from every community, and no plea is let in. Early scholars read the three as cause and result.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Here the surah turns from its list of favours to the response that list received. The classical scholars connect the first ayah to the distress the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) felt at the rejection he was meeting. They present it as general comfort, not as a reply to a named event. The passage belongs to the surah's later Meccan argument.

keyTerms.note: A noun for getting a message all the way to its destination. It defines the task by arrival rather than by acceptance, which is exactly where the responsibility is being cut off.
A verb for knowing something by acquaintance, the way one knows a face. It makes the denial that follows a refusal rather than an error, since what is denied has already been identified.
From a root for seeking to remove another's displeasure. The passive denies them not forgiveness but the opportunity to plead for it, which is a narrower and colder refusal.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: An envoy between tribes carried words he had not written. He was not answerable for how they landed. He was answerable only for delivering them exactly. His safety rested on that understanding. Harming an envoy was among the worst offences a group could commit. The audience knew the role well. So limiting a messenger's duty to clear delivery drew on a category they already had.
studies.didYouKnow: The line about raising a witness from every community appears twice in this surah, five ayat apart. The second time, one preposition changes and a clause is added. The first leaves the witness unnamed and ends with excuses refused. The second names the addressee himself as a witness against the people before him.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Splitting delivery from result protects two things at once. It keeps a messenger from judging himself by how many accept. And it keeps the refusal from being anyone else's fault. The middle ayah then makes that refusal a choice, not a mistake. That is what lets the last ayah close off excuses without being unfair. Once a thing has been recognised, no excuse is left.

crossReferences.why: Repeats the raising of a witness from every community, adding the messenger as a witness there.
States the same limit on the messenger's duty, that only conveying is upon him.
Shows communities acknowledging that messengers came, and testifying against themselves.

studies.applyIt: Think of something you keep telling someone who does not want to hear it. Say it once more, plainly and kindly. Then stop keeping score. This passage separates delivering a message from securing a result. Most of the tiredness in a relationship like that comes from quietly taking on the second job.
studies.explainEasier: If people turn away, the messenger's only job is to say the message clearly. They know the good things God gave them, but they still say no. One day someone from every nation will stand up and speak.

studies.title: Surely You Are Liars
studies.meaning: Two scenes, each opening with the same word for seeing. In the first, those who wronged see the punishment and two things are denied together: reduction and delay. In the second, those who associated partners see those partners and immediately point at them, presenting them almost as evidence. What comes back is one flat sentence calling them liars. The commentators note that the accused do not defend themselves; they reject the account.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The surah has been building towards this scene since it described people giving shares to what they did not know. The classical scholars read the exchange as a general picture of that day. They do not read it as a report about named people, and they record no occasion for it. Those addressed dealt daily with go-betweens they expected would speak for them.

keyTerms.note: A verb for making a load lighter. Denying it addresses a specific hope, that a sentence once passed might still be negotiated downward, which was ordinary practice in tribal arbitration.
From the root for looking, used idiomatically for allowing someone more time. It closes off the second thing a debtor would ask for, so both usual concessions are refused together.
A commercial word for those who share in a venture. Calling them ours keeps the possessive relationship intact even at this moment, which commentators read as the habit outlasting the belief.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Business in Mecca ran on partnership. Several investors paid for a caravan, and profits were split by an agreed share. Disputes went to arbitration, where each side named backers to speak for it. The word used here belonged to that world. So did the scene it describes: a man finding out in front of an arbiter that his partners will not stand with him.
studies.didYouKnow: The two ayat open with exactly the same three words. Only the description of who is seeing changes: those who wronged, then those who set up partners. The matching build makes the second sight continue the first. So the punishment and the partners come into view in one movement, not two.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The exchange shows something about false attachments. They do not survive the moment they were meant to be useful. What was served is not shown to lose the argument. It is shown to have no interest, which is colder than losing. Refusing to lighten or to delay makes the day a settlement, not a bargain. Whatever a person brings into it is already fixed on arrival.

crossReferences.why: Puts the same question about their partners, and reports the denial that immediately follows.
Has the associates disown their followers, and the call made to them go unanswered.
Continues this scene directly, with submission offered once the partners have gone.

studies.applyIt: Name one thing you are relying on that has never actually been tested. A relationship, a reputation, a plan. You do not need to abandon it. Just ask, in one honest sentence, what it would do if you needed it tomorrow, and notice whether you already know the answer.
studies.explainEasier: On that day the people who did wrong will see their punishment. Nothing will make it lighter or come later. Those who prayed to other things will point at them. Those things will call them liars.

studies.title: Punishment Above Punishment
studies.meaning: The passage adds a second count to the charge. Submission is offered, and then the inventions desert their makers. In that order, the surrender lands at the moment nothing is left to hold instead. The sentence then narrows to a smaller group. These did not merely refuse. They also kept others off the path. Their punishment is described as stacked on top, and the reason given is the damage done, not the belief held.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The surah has just shown the partners disowning those who called on them. This completes that scene. The classical scholars connect the second ayah to the organised effort in Mecca to keep people away from the message. That effort included pressure on individuals and on pilgrims arriving for the season. The scholars describe the practice in general. They do not tie the ayah to one episode.

keyTerms.note: A noun from the root for peace and for handing something over. It names the act with no word for regret attached, which is why commentators distinguish it from turning back in repentance.

keyTerms.gloss: went astray, was lost to them
keyTerms.note: The verb ordinarily used of a person losing their way. Applied here to the inventions, it reverses the usual direction: what was followed is now the thing that has gone missing.
A verb for spoiling something that was sound. It names outward damage rather than inward refusal, which is why the added punishment attaches to it and not to disbelief on its own.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Access to the sanctuary at Mecca was controlled. The men who controlled it also decided who could speak to the pilgrims each season. Warnings were given on the roads in. Anyone who showed interest could be pressed through his family and through his trade. Obstruction was not an idea. It was a working business, run by people whose income depended on the arrangement.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase used here for the extra penalty, punishment above punishment, occurs only once in the Quran. Elsewhere the language of increase is more general. Classical scholars noted that this stacking matches the double charge in the same ayah. The charge is refusal and obstruction, with one laid literally on top of the other.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage draws a line between surrender that is chosen and surrender that is merely left over. It puts the value of faith firmly on the near side of that line. Then it separates two kinds of wrong. Refusing for yourself is one thing. Standing between other people and a road is treated as a further act, with its own result. That makes obstruction a separate category, not a stronger degree of the same thing.

crossReferences.why: Describes belief professed once the punishment is seen, and says it did not benefit them then.
Sets up this scene, with the partners disowning those who used to call upon them.
Names those who disbelieved and turned others from the path, exactly as this ayah does.

studies.applyIt: Think of a time you gave in only when there was nothing left to hold, and notice how different that felt from choosing. Then pick one small thing you have been holding out on and let it go now, while it still costs you something. That difference is the entire subject of this passage.
studies.explainEasier: On that day they will finally give in to God. The things they made up will be gone. People who refused, and also stopped others from coming, will get punishment on top of punishment.

studies.title: An Explanation Of All Things
studies.meaning: The witness scene returns. This time the addressee himself is named as a witness over the people in front of him. The sentence then turns to the book and gives it four descriptions in a row. It is an explanation of everything, guidance, mercy, and good news. Early scholars differ over how widely to read the first. Most limit it to what concerns religion rather than to every subject. The list ends on good news, not on warning.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. This ayah repeats an earlier one in the surah and adds to it. The classical scholars read the repeat as deliberate, not accidental. The scene of witnesses answers an audience that expected figures it had honoured to speak up for it before God. No specific occasion is reported. The ayah works as the summary just before the surah's most quoted instruction.

keyTerms.note: A legal word for someone who testifies to what they saw. Used twice in this ayah, it frames the day as a hearing at which testimony comes from inside each community rather than from outside.
An intensive noun from the verb to make plain, which this surah has already used twice of the messenger's own task. Here the quality is transferred from the person to the book itself.
From the same root as the birth announcement earlier in this surah. Placing it last means the description of the book ends on the note that the earlier passage showed a man refusing.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Testimony was everything in a society with no archives. Contracts, marriages, debts and blood settlements lived in the memory of named witnesses. A man's worth as a witness was a real form of standing. Taking a witness from inside a community rather than a stranger matched the practice exactly. An outsider's account of a clan's affairs carried very little weight.
studies.didYouKnow: This ayah repeats the opening of one five ayat earlier, changing a single preposition and then continuing differently. The earlier version leaves the witness unnamed and closes with excuses refused. This one names the addressee as a witness and closes with guidance, mercy and good news. The same sentence is turned twice within one page.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Putting the book's description right after the courtroom scene links the two. A text that explains is what makes testimony fair. A community cannot be witnessed against over something never made clear to it. Naming mercy and good news beside guidance then resists one reading of scripture. It will not let the book be mainly a legal tool, even in a passage set in a hearing.

crossReferences.why: States the same raising of witnesses five ayat earlier, without the additions made here.
Puts the same scene as a question, each community brought a witness and the messenger over them.
Calls the Book sent down something explained in detail, close to the description used here.

studies.applyIt: Read the surah you know best in translation, from beginning to end, in one sitting this week. Not to study it. The claim in this ayah is that the book explains, and explanation needs continuity, which is exactly what reading in fragments removes. Give one surah its whole shape once and see what changes.
studies.explainEasier: One day God will bring someone from every nation to speak about what that nation did. He has given you this book. It makes things clear, it shows the way, and it brings kindness and good news.

studies.title: Three Commanded, Three Forbidden
studies.meaning: Six things in one sentence, set out as three and three. Justice is giving what is owed. The second term goes past that. It means doing what is excellent, whether or not it is due. The third narrows to relatives, so kindness starts where it is hardest to keep up. Against these stand gross indecency, what people commonly know to be wrong, and grabbing more than your share. The sentence closes with the word for counsel, not with a threat.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, near the end of a surah that has spent its length on blessings, argument and how groups of people act. Early sources report no occasion for the ayah itself. They do keep accounts of its effect on hearers. One well-known report tells of a Meccan opponent moved by it. It sits just before orders about keeping deals and oaths. That gives the general statement something to bite on.

keyTerms.note: From a root meaning to make two things equal in weight. It is the balance point rather than generosity, which is why the next word is needed to carry the sentence past mere fairness.
From the root for beauty and goodness. It covers both doing a thing well and doing well by someone, and it names a surplus above what justice requires rather than a softening of it.
The root means to seek or desire, and in this form it names wanting past your share at someone else's cost. It is the social form of the arrogance the surah has already been describing.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Mecca had no court and no police. Disputes were settled by clan pressure, by a respected figure hearing both sides, and by the threat of feud. So a strong family could take more than its share, and a weak one had little redress. Duties to relatives were the strongest social bond there was. They were also the easiest to abuse. Naming justice, excellence and kinship in one line spoke to exactly where that system broke.
studies.didYouKnow: A companion of the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) is reported to have called this the widest verse in the Quran for good and evil. In many places it is recited from the pulpit at the close of the Friday address. That custom goes back centuries. The ayah names six things. Not one of them concerns ritual.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The ayah gives right and wrong as something commanded, not as something worked out. It then makes no case for it. What it shows is that the moral part of revelation is not a separate department from belief. The same voice that has spent the surah describing rain and cattle now describes conduct, in the same tone. The final word matters too. The teaching is given as counsel aimed at remembering. That assumes the hearer already knows.

crossReferences.why: Takes justice to its hardest case, standing for it against yourself and your own family.
Warns that hatred of a people must not push you off fairness towards them.
Names the same claim of the relative, set beside the poor and the traveller.

studies.applyIt: Take the third item on the list, the relative. Pick the family member you have the least warmth for and give them something this week that justice does not require: a call with no agenda, a small errand, an unprompted piece of praise. The ayah puts kinship next to justice for a reason. It is where being merely fair stops being enough.
studies.explainEasier: God tells people to be fair. He tells them to do more good than they have to. He tells them to look after their relatives. He also tells them not to do shameful things, not to be unfair, and not to push others around.

studies.title: You Made God Your Guarantor
studies.meaning: An instruction about covenants comes first. Then a ban on breaking oaths. Then the sentence that gives both their weight. When you swear, you have already named God as the party standing surety for the deal. Early scholars note that this is not a threat. It is a description of what an oath actually is. The closing clause about knowledge sits exactly where a human witness would otherwise be named.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The classical scholars note that the surah's closing section deals with how a community actually behaves. It reads naturally beside the pledges given to the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him). They report no single occasion for this ayah. Oaths and treaties held Arabian life together. That is why a passage about them needs no introduction.

keyTerms.note: A verb from the language of completing a payment. It treats a covenant as a debt that can be partly discharged, so falling short is described as underpayment rather than as betrayal.
From a root for making something firm. It names the deliberate strengthening of an oath, so the prohibition covers promises the speaker took extra trouble to make binding.
The legal term for a third party who answers for a debt if the principal defaults. It occurs only here in the Quran, and it describes the oath's structure rather than adding a penalty.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: With no courts and no written records, an oath was how a deal was enforced. Alliances, safe passage, debts and the ending of feuds all rested on a sworn word. Behind that word stood a guarantor, who would pay or fight if the swearer failed. Finding a guarantor was itself a bargain. A man who could not find one could not make agreements at all.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for a guarantor occurs only once in the Quran, and it is here. Its ordinary use in that society was commercial: the person who accepts liability if a debtor defaults. So an oath is described using the exact legal term a Meccan trader would have used in a contract, with the roles left unchanged.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage makes an oath a three-party deal rather than a two-party one. That changes what breaking it is. It is not only a wrong done to the other person. It is a claim made against a guarantor who was named without being asked. That is why the instruction needs no penalty clause. The shape of the act supplies the seriousness. The ayah only has to describe it accurately.

crossReferences.why: Returns to the same subject three ayat later, with the consequence of deceit spelled out.
Opens with the same instruction to fulfil covenants, at the head of a surah about agreements.
Says the covenant will be asked about, adding the accounting this ayah leaves implicit.

studies.applyIt: Find the smallest promise you have let slide, the kind nobody would ever hold you to, and keep it this week. Reply to the message. Return the thing. This ayah puts the weight on the structure of a promise rather than on its size, which means the small ones are not a different category, only a quieter one.
studies.explainEasier: Keep the promises you make to God. Do not break an oath once you have made it firm. When you swear, you have made God the one who stands behind your word, and he knows what you do.

studies.title: She Unravelled Her Own Yarn
studies.meaning: A comparison arrives without introduction: a woman who spins thread up to strength and then pulls it back into loose fibre. What makes it sting is that nobody did this to her. Then the application, which is oaths used as a way in, and a motive named plainly, one group being wealthier than another. The commentators note that the closing clause reframes the entire situation as a test rather than as a temptation.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan by placement. The classical scholars note that the ayah is concerned with agreements between groups. Some report a proverbial woman in Mecca who spun thread and then unspun it. Others read the comparison as made up rather than drawn from a real person. The sources keep both readings and do not settle between them. No single occasion is agreed.

keyTerms.note: The same verb used in the ayah just before for breaking oaths. Applying it first to thread and then to promises makes the comparison structural rather than decorative, since one word does both jobs.
The word occurs only here in the Quran. It names spun thread taken back to the state it held before spinning, so what has been lost is the work rather than the material itself.
From a root for entering. It names something slipped into an agreement to leave the swearer a way in, and it occurs only in this surah, twice within three ayat.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Spinning was constant work for women. They did it while walking, talking and watching children, and a household's cloth depended on it. Thread was spun on a drop spindle over days, then woven or traded. Undoing spun yarn needed no explanation to anyone. It was the plainest waste of work anyone could show, and everyone had handled a spindle's worth of it.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for the undone fibres occurs only here in the Quran. The verb for what she does to them is the same one used in the ayah before for breaking an oath. So the comparison is built by repeating one verb across two objects, thread and promise. Nothing in the text says the two are alike.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Naming the motive as one community being richer than another is very exact. It points at the pressure that really breaks agreements, which is gain rather than spite. And it says so without preaching. Calling the whole thing a test then puts the gap itself inside the design. What is tested is not whether you were offered a better deal. It is what you did when you were.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same verb for breaking oaths that this ayah applies to unravelling spun thread.
Describes a people who broke their oaths after agreement, and asks whether they will be feared.
Sets those who keep the covenant against those who cut apart what should be joined.

studies.applyIt: Think of one relationship you have quietly downgraded because a better option appeared. A friend, a supplier, a commitment. You do not have to undo the newer arrangement. Just tell the older party the truth about where things stand, this week, rather than letting it fray. Unravelling is slower than cutting and looks less like a decision.
studies.explainEasier: Do not be like a woman who spins strong thread and then pulls it all apart. Do not use promises to trick each other just because one group has more money. God is testing you with this.

studies.title: One Community If He Willed
studies.meaning: A condition that is deliberately not carried out. God could have made everyone one community, and did not. What follows is put in the shortest possible form. He leaves astray, and he guides, and both are attached to his will. Early scholars are careful here. They read the leaving astray in the light of a turning away that comes first. The last clause then restores answering for what you do. That is what stops the ayah falling into fatalism.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, inside the section on oaths and communities. The surah has just named one group's wealth as the pressure that breaks agreements. The classical scholars read this ayah as speaking to the many kinds of people around those agreements. They report no particular occasion. The surah raised a similar condition earlier. There it was put in the mouths of objectors rather than stated directly.

keyTerms.note: A group defined by something shared rather than by descent. Its use lets the sentence be about religious division rather than tribal division, which the audience heard as two separate matters.
A causative that the commentators consistently qualify. They read it alongside ayat describing the turning away that comes first, so the leaving follows a movement the person has already made.
An emphatic passive carrying two separate markers of certainty. Its position at the very end holds the ayah in balance, since a questioning implies an answer belonging to the one questioned.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Arabia held many communities at once. There were tribes with their own gods, Jewish settlements in the north, and Christian towns to the south. There were also people who had rejected all of it. Trade meant dealing across every one of those lines. Nobody in that audience thought of one single religious community as the natural state of things. That is what makes this condition so pointed.
studies.didYouKnow: This surah raises the same conditional twice, and the two occurrences sit in different mouths. Earlier it is quoted from objectors arguing that had God willed, they would not have served anything besides Him. Here it is stated directly, and what follows is a questioning rather than an excuse.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The ayah puts God's will and answering for what you do in one sentence. It does not reconcile them. That refusal is the position, not a dodge. What it rules out is using either half against the other. You cannot plead the will as an excuse, because the questioning is stated outright. And you cannot claim your own guidance as an achievement, because the guiding is given to God. Both moves close at once.

crossReferences.why: Quotes objectors making the same conditional, and answers that the messengers' duty was delivery.
States the same possibility and adds that people will not cease to differ from one another.
Asks whether the messenger would compel people, once the same point has been made.

studies.applyIt: The next time you are certain about why someone else has not been guided, stop at the certainty. This ayah attributes both directions to God's will and then says you will be asked about your own conduct, not theirs. Spend the energy you were about to spend diagnosing them on one thing you have been putting off yourself.
studies.explainEasier: If God had wanted, he could have made everyone one single group. He did not. He lets some people go the wrong way and he guides others. You will be asked about the things you did.

studies.title: A Foot That Slips
studies.meaning: The ban returns, with its consequences laid out. Oaths used as a way in make a foot slip after it had been steady. The harm is described as tasted, which makes it personal before it is a penalty. Then the reason widens to holding others back from the path. The second ayah names the trade underneath the whole business. It is swapping a covenant for a small price, and no price is said to be large enough.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The surah's closing instructions speak to a community that had to trade and travel among people who did not share its commitments. There a broken oath was two things at once. It was a practical betrayal, and it was a public argument against the message. The classical scholars report no specific occasion. They read the pair as continuing an instruction given a few ayat earlier in the same section.

keyTerms.note: The verb for a foot losing purchase on smooth ground. It makes the failure look sudden and involuntary, although the ayah has just described the deliberate act that brought it about.
A noun for standing fixed. Naming the security before the slip means what is lost was already held, which is a different injury from never having had it in the first place.
The commercial word for what is paid in an exchange. Calling it small names no amount; it says that whatever the figure was, the thing given up was not of that order.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A merchant's name for keeping his word was his working capital. It decided whether he could take goods on credit in the north. It decided whether a tribe would guarantee his passage. It decided whether anyone would partner with him next season. Selling that name for one profitable lie was a known temptation and a known folly. People discussed it in the market like any other bad trade.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase for oaths used as a means of deception occurs twice in the Quran. Both times are in this surah, three ayat apart. The instruction is given first. Then the comparison about unravelled thread is set between them. Then the same phrase returns, this time with its consequences attached.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Framing the matter as a purchase is the real move here. It grants that breaking a covenant is done for something. It grants that the something is real and can be weighed. What it denies is that the weighing was ever done honestly. What is with God was left out of the sum. So the argument is about arithmetic, not about resisting a temptation.

crossReferences.why: Gives the instruction this passage restates, naming the guarantor rather than the consequence.
Describes those who exchange the covenant of God and their own oaths for a small price.
Uses the same phrase about not selling what has been revealed for a small price.

studies.applyIt: Look at one thing you have gained recently by shading the truth, even slightly. Price it honestly: what you got, and what you spent to get it. This passage does not ask you to be above the trade. It asks you to do the sum properly, which most people avoid because the answer turns out to be obvious.
studies.explainEasier: Do not use promises to trick people. A foot that was standing firm can slip, and you will taste trouble for keeping others away from God. Do not sell what you promised God for a small price.

studies.title: What Runs Out And What Stays
studies.meaning: A comparison put as plainly as Arabic allows, with no image and no argument. What you hold is described by a verb of running dry. It is the emptying of a well or a purse. What is with God is described by a participle of remaining. Then a promise is attached, and its terms are a surprise. The patient are repaid by the best of what they did. Not by the average, and not by the worst.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The ayah closes a passage about oaths and covenants, where the temptation named is exchanging an agreement with God for a small price. Early scholars read this as addressing people under pressure to renounce their faith for money, protection or standing, which was a live situation in Mecca. No particular occasion is reported. The preceding ayah has already said that what is with God is better, and this one says why.

keyTerms.note: A verb used of supplies that finish and of a well that gives no more. It says nothing about how much there was, only that the quantity is of a kind that ends.
An active participle from the root behind one of the divine names, the Everlasting. Using it of what is with God ties the durability of the reward to the durability of the one holding it.
A superlative, not a general word for good. The reckoning is described as taking the highest point of a person's record as the rate for the whole of it, which is a specific and unusual arrangement.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Wealth in that economy spoiled in plain sight. Grain went to weevils. Dates fermented. Camels died of thirst or were driven off in a raid. A merchant's whole capital could be one caravan crossing hostile country. Nobody had to be talked into believing that goods run out. They watched it happen. What the ayah adds is a second column in the same ledger, held somewhere raiders cannot reach.
studies.didYouKnow: The closing clause of this ayah is repeated almost word for word at the end of the next one. That next ayah promises a good life to whoever acts rightly. Repeating an ending across two ayat in a row binds them into a pair. So the reward for patience and the reward for righteous work are given the same terms. The device appears elsewhere in the Quran, but rarely this tightly.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage sets two holdings side by side. Then, instead of saying what the lasting one contains, it says who receives it. The withholding is deliberate. The reward is marked out by how long it lasts and by its rate, not by its content. And the rate is mercy put as arithmetic. Being repaid at the level of your best moments, rather than your usual ones, says something about how the account is meant to come out.

crossReferences.why: States the same contrast, adding that what is with God is better and more lasting.
Everything on earth passes away, and only the face of your Lord remains.
Calls wealth and children the ornament of this life and lasting deeds the better hope.

studies.applyIt: Look at your bank balance and then at your calendar for this week. One of those runs out and one of them is where the other column gets filled. Find twenty minutes in the calendar you were going to spend on nothing much, and give it to something that will still matter in ten years. A person, usually, rather than a project.
studies.explainEasier: Whatever you own will run out one day. What God has does not run out. He will pay back people who keep going through hard times, and he will pay them for the very best things they did.

studies.title: The Promise Of A Good Life
studies.meaning: The condition is stated three ways, and each way does work. Righteous action is required. Male or female is spelled out, so nobody is let in by group. Belief is named as the state that goes along with the action, not as a separate act. What is promised is a good life. Early scholars differ on where that life sits. Some read it of this world, as contentment, enough to live on, and lawful provision. Others read it of the grave or the hereafter. Most allow both.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, in the closing part of the surah, among orders about oaths, deals and how to bear pressure. Among the first hearers were women who had accepted the message against their households. There were also men who had lost trade and cover for it. To state the promise for male and female in one clause was not abstract there. Early sources report no set occasion for the ayah.

keyTerms.note: The adjective means wholesome, clean and pleasant, the same word used of good soil and good speech. It describes the quality of a life rather than its length or its comfort, which is why the commentators could locate it in either world.

The verb is to give life, not to grant or provide. Coupled with an oath particle and an emphatic ending, it reads as a guarantee, and it implies the good life is something conferred rather than achieved.

From a root meaning to be fit, whole and in good repair, used of a mended tool or a reconciled quarrel. Righteous action in Arabic is action that repairs something, which is a more concrete idea than being good.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A woman's standing in that society came through her father, her husband and her sons. Her religious life was largely her household's. A slave's was his owner's. So a sentence that gives the same promise to male and female on the same terms cut across the usual way merit was handed out. Some of the earliest believers were women and slaves. The sentence would have been heard by them first.
studies.didYouKnow: The pairing of male and female in a promise of reward occurs several times in the Quran. In each case the wording is matched rather than added on. The same condition, the same repayment, no separate clause. Here the ayah also switches from singular to plural halfway through. It moves from him to them. That widens the promise from the one person to the group.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Two things are being fixed. The first is that the standing of a human being before God does not run through sex, lineage or social position, since the qualifying terms are action and belief and nothing else. The second is quieter: the reward begins with a life rather than a place. Whatever the good life is, it is described as something God gives now, in the same sentence as the reward that comes later.

crossReferences.why: Lists ten qualities twice over, once for men and once for women, in the same terms.
Whoever does good, male or female, and is a believer, enters the garden.
Names the opposite condition, a life made narrow by turning from the reminder.

studies.applyIt: Pick one action today that repairs rather than adds. Fix the drawer that sticks. Answer the message you have been avoiding. Say sorry for a small thing no one else recalls. The word this ayah uses for righteous action is built on the idea of putting something back in working order. It is simpler to start there than with something bigger.
studies.explainEasier: Anyone who does good and believes in God will get a good life. It does not matter whether they are a man or a woman. God will also pay them back for the very best of what they did.

studies.title: Seek Refuge Before You Read
studies.meaning: An instruction about how to come to recitation. Two ayat then explain why it is needed and why it works. The seeking of refuge comes before the reading, not during it. Then the reach of what is guarded against is described twice. Once by denial, and once by limit. Both descriptions turn on relationship rather than on strength. Early scholars note that no power to compel is given anywhere in the three ayat.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. It sits just after the surah's instructions on oaths and just before its answer to the charge of forgery. The classical scholars read that position as deliberate, since the ayat that follow concern people misreading the revelation. They report no particular occasion. The practice of saying these words before reciting comes from this ayah, and it is attested very early.

keyTerms.note: A verb for going to someone stronger and placing yourself under their cover. In that society it named a formal act with obligations attached, so the word describes entering a protection rather than making a request.
A passive form from a root for stoning and casting away. It describes a status already imposed rather than a threat still open, so the adversary is named by his expulsion.
A word for delegated power backed by proof. Denying it says the influence described has no standing rather than no force, which is why the next ayah defines it by who accepts it.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Seeking refuge was a legal act with a name. A man in danger could go to a stronger clan and formally put himself under its protection. Once he was accepted, an attack on him became an attack on his protectors. Refusing such a request damaged a chief's good name. Everyone who heard this instruction knew exactly what entering a protection involved.
studies.didYouKnow: The name used here for the adversary, the driven-out one, occurs only twice in the Quran. The other time sits inside the prayer of a woman. She places her newborn daughter, and that child's children after her, under God's protection. So both uses of the phrase fall inside an act of seeking refuge.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Together the three ayat describe an adversary with no standing to act. Authority is denied over those who believe and trust. It is then granted only over those who take him as an ally. So the tie is chosen on the human side. That puts the responsibility somewhere uncomfortable and reassuring at once. Nothing is forced, so nothing can be blamed. And the protection asked for is already there.

crossReferences.why: Gives the same instruction for the moment a prompting arrives, using the identical verb.
Holds the only other use of this name for the adversary, inside a mother's prayer of protection.
Has him admit at the end that he held no authority over anyone, only an invitation.

studies.applyIt: Say the words of refuge aloud the next time you open the Quran, and then pause for one breath before you begin reading. The pause is the point. The instruction places the asking before the reading rather than inside it, which makes it a way of arriving rather than something done while already moving.
studies.explainEasier: Before you read the Quran, ask God to keep you safe from Satan. Satan has no power over people who believe and trust their Lord. He only has power over people who choose to follow him.

studies.title: A Sign In Place Of A Sign
studies.meaning: A practice is described and an accusation quoted in one sentence. When one revealed passage is put in place of another, the objection raised is not confusion. It is forgery. Early scholars read the charge as being about consistency. A man making things up would keep his story straight. The bracket in the middle answers the charge before it is even reported. The closing clause names the real shortfall, which is knowledge.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The classical scholars differ over what exactly is being replaced. Some read it of rulings. Others read it more widely, of whole passages. That discussion is long and was never settled. What is agreed is the objection reported here. It was raised in Mecca against the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him), as proof that the revelation was his own work.

keyTerms.note: An intensive verb for putting one thing in place of another. The grammar makes God the agent, which is the whole answer to the charge, since a substitution with a known author is not a slip.
The same word covers a revealed passage and a sign in creation. Its double sense keeps this sentence connected to the signs the surah has been listing for dozens of ayat before it.
An active participle from a root for cutting something to shape. The accusation is of manufacture rather than of error, so what is alleged is deliberate work and not a mistake.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Poetry was the memory of that culture, and audiences watched it closely. A reciter who changed a line between performances was corrected from the floor. Catching a man out that way was the usual method. It showed that he was making it up rather than passing it on. The objection quoted here used a test the audience trusted. They applied it to a text that arrived across years rather than all at once.
studies.didYouKnow: The word used here for what is replaced is the same one the surah has been using for the signs in creation. Those signs are rain, cattle, birds and the turning of shadows. So the objection and the argument share one vocabulary. A passage replaced and a bird held up in the air are named by the same term.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The bracket carries the weight, and it does not defend any particular replacement. It says that the one revealing knows what he sends down. That moves the question from the content to the sender. It is a claim about revelation as an act rather than as a text. And it makes telling over time a feature of teaching, not a sign of a changing mind.

crossReferences.why: States the same principle directly, that nothing is replaced except with something like it or better.
Says God erases and confirms what He wills, and that the source of the book is with Him.
Reminds the messenger that what was given could be taken away entirely, had God willed it.

studies.applyIt: Think of an instruction you were given as a child that was later replaced with a better one, by a parent or a teacher who knew more than you did at the time. Notice that you did not conclude they had been lying. Hold that experience beside this ayah once, and see whether the objection still feels as strong.
studies.explainEasier: Sometimes God puts one verse in place of another one. He knows best what he sends down. When that happens, some people say the message was made up. Most of them simply do not know.

studies.title: Brought Down In Truth
studies.meaning: A reply is dictated rather than argued. The answer to the charge of invention is a claim about how the message travelled. It was brought down by a named bearer, from the hearer's own Lord, and truthfully. Then three purposes follow. The first is unexpected. It is to make firm those who already believe. So the reply is addressed as much to a community under pressure as to the objectors outside it.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. It answers the accusation reported in the ayah just before. The classical scholars identify the bearer named here with the angel Gabriel. They note that the same title is used elsewhere in the Quran of Jesus. The setting is the late Meccan period. The small community was under steady pressure, and the charge of forgery was being made in public.

keyTerms.note: A title the classical commentators identify with the angel Gabriel. It occurs four times in the Quran, and this is the only occurrence that concerns the descent of the revelation itself.

keyTerms.gloss: so that He may make firm
keyTerms.note: An intensive verb for planting something so it will not shift. It names an effect on people who already believe, which is why the ayah reads as support rather than as proof.
A phrase covering both accuracy and rightful entitlement. Attached to the bringing down, it says the transmission was faithful and also that it was authorised, answering two objections at once.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A message carried weight in that world because of its chain. A tribal messenger was asked who sent him, and by whose hand the words had travelled. A claim with no named carrier was worth nothing. So answering a charge of invention by naming the bearer was exactly the form of reply the audience expected. They refused this particular answer, but not the form of it.
studies.didYouKnow: The title used here for the bearer occurs four times in the Quran. The other three all concern Jesus, who is described as strengthened by this same Spirit. This is the only place where the title is attached to the sending down of the revelation to the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him).
studies.theologicalSignificance: Naming a bearer puts revelation inside a chain rather than inside a private moment. That has results. What is claimed can be described, argued over and tested against itself. The ayat around this one go on to do exactly that. Putting the making firm of believers first also grants something honest. The nearest work of revelation is often to hold the people who already accepted it.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same title of the one who strengthened Jesus, in a passage about messengers rejected.
Describes the same descent, naming the trustworthy spirit and a clear Arabic tongue.
Reports the accusation of invention that this ayah is dictated in order to answer.

studies.applyIt: When something you believe is challenged, notice whether your first move is to defend the content or to check where you got it. This ayah answers a charge by naming a source rather than by arguing the point. Try that order once this week on something small, and see how much of the argument it quietly removes.
studies.explainEasier: Say that the Holy Spirit brought this message down from your Lord. It came down true. It came to make believers strong. It came to guide them and to bring good news to those who obey God.

studies.title: A Clear Arabic Tongue
studies.meaning: A rumour is quoted and answered with one observation about language. Someone had suggested a human teacher. The reply does not deny that the man existed, or that conversations took place. It points instead at the distance between his speech and the text in question. Early scholars report several names for the person hinted at. They keep the whole range, since the argument does not depend on which one is right.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The classical sources name several possible people, generally a non-Arab living in Mecca. They differ over which one is meant.
