What they agree on is the shape of the accusation. It granted the quality of what was being recited, and then went looking for a human source for it. No single name is settled in the sources.

keyTerms.note: A verb for deviating from a straight line, used of leaning towards something. The word carries a sense of bending away from the obvious, so the allusion is described as a swerve rather than a claim.
A word describing speech that is hard to follow rather than merely a foreigner. It names the man by how he sounded, which is precisely the ground on which the reply stands.
An active participle, so the tongue does not merely happen to be clear but makes things clear. It is the same form the surah has used of the messenger's task and of the book's function.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Mecca was full of foreigners. There were enslaved people from Abyssinia and Persia, traders from Syria, and craftsmen who had settled and married. Several spoke Arabic poorly and worked at trades near the sanctuary. A rumour that one of them was the real source travelled easily. A foreign teacher was an easier answer for people who had already granted how good the recitation was.
studies.didYouKnow: The word used here for the non-Arab tongue appears three times in the Quran. One of those places imagines the opposite case. It asks what people would have said had the revelation come in a foreign tongue to Arab hearers. So the same word carries the accusation in one place and the answer to it in another.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The reply argues from craft rather than from rank. That is unusual, and it is meant. It invites the doubter to compare two samples of language and draw the obvious answer. It accepts in advance that anybody can make that test. So part of the case for where the book came from is open to the public. That matters for a claim that could otherwise rest entirely on the one making it.

crossReferences.why: Imagines the reverse case, a foreign recitation to Arab hearers, and the objection that would follow.
Says that had a non-Arab recited it to them, they would not have believed in it.
Reports a related charge, that others helped him and that these were old legends written down.

studies.applyIt: Notice the next time you reach for an answer because it is comfortable rather than because it fits. The rumour answered here was not stupid. It was convenient. Take one thing you believe lightly and ask yourself, once this week, whether you took it up because it was true or because the other option was harder.
studies.explainEasier: Some people said that a man was teaching him all this. But the man they pointed to did not speak Arabic well. What was being recited was clear Arabic.

studies.title: Who Actually Invents Lies
studies.meaning: The charge of forgery is turned around without heat. Two matching sentences do the work. Those who do not believe in the signs are not guided. And it is those same people who invent. Early scholars note that the argument turns on motive and habit rather than on logic. Someone with nothing at stake beyond this world has a reason to make things up. Someone staking everything on an account of the next has the strongest possible reason not to.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, right after the charge that a human teacher stood behind the recitation. The surah has spent several ayat answering that charge. Here it hands it back. The classical scholars read the pair as closing the exchange rather than opening a new subject. They report no specific occasion. The ayat around them all concern the same public dispute in Mecca.

keyTerms.note: The same verb used against the messenger a few ayat earlier. Repeating it with a different subject is the whole argument, since the charge is returned in the vocabulary in which it arrived.
Definite rather than indefinite, so the sentence names lying as a category rather than a particular untruth. What is being described is a practice, not an isolated incident.
A definite plural in the emphatic final position. Arabic uses this construction for restriction, so the sentence does not merely say that they lie but that they are the ones who do.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: In a society without documents, character was the evidence. Disputes were settled by weighing the standing of the two sides. A man known for accuracy could beat one known for dressing things up, and neither had to produce a thing. Turning a charge around by pointing at who had a record of inventing was a known move. The audience knew how to weigh it.
studies.didYouKnow: The root for fabricating runs through this surah in both directions. It is used first of what people invent about God, then in the objectors' accusation against the messenger, and then twice of the objectors themselves. One word carries the charge out and brings it back within a few pages.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage makes truthfulness a matter of what a person has staked rather than of temperament. It does not claim that believers cannot lie. It claims that someone who does not believe the signs has removed the only consideration that would make inventing about God costly. That reframes the dispute entirely: the question is not who sounds more sincere but who has anything to lose.

crossReferences.why: Holds the accusation of invention that these two ayat answer by returning it to the accusers.
Asks who does greater wrong than one who invents a lie about God after truth has reached him.
Puts the same question, pairing invention about God with denial of His signs.

studies.applyIt: Ask what a claim would cost the person making it. Not whether they seem honest, which is easy to perform, but what they lose if it turns out to be false. Apply that test to one thing you were told this week and one thing you said. It is the test this passage uses, and it works in both directions.
studies.explainEasier: People who do not believe God's signs will not be guided, and a hard punishment waits for them. They are the ones who make up lies. They are the real liars here.

studies.title: A Heart At Rest In Faith
studies.meaning: A general statement opens and is cut off before it can close. The break is the point. An exception is put in for the person who is forced, whose heart stays settled. Only then does the sentence resume. It describes the other case, someone who opened his chest to it willingly. Early scholars read the contrast this way. On one side is what a mouth says under force. On the other is what a person has actually made room for inside.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, from the years of persecution before the emigration. The classical sources report an occasion behind it. A man in the early community was tortured until he spoke words of denial. He came afterwards in distress and was put at ease. The sources tell that story the same way in outline. The ayah is read as setting out a general principle, not a one-off case for one man.

keyTerms.note: A passive from the root for aversion, so the word already contains the person's unwillingness. The grammar removes agency, which is exactly the ground on which the exception is standing.

A word for something that has come to stillness after motion, used of a heart and of a town at peace. It describes a condition rather than an assertion, so it is not something a person can simply claim.
A verb for cutting something open and making it broader. Used of the chest it describes making interior room, which is why commentators treat it as the opposite of speech extracted under pressure.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: The early community in Mecca included people with no clan behind them. They bore the worst of it. Violence against a protected man brought payback. Violence against an unprotected one brought none at all. Those without patrons could be held and beaten, with no help anywhere. The line this ayah draws mattered most to exactly those people.
studies.didYouKnow: The word used here for the heart at rest comes from the same root as a word used a few ayat later. That later word describes a town that was safe and settled before it turned ungrateful. So one idea of stillness covers an inner state under torture and a city living in comfort. In this surah it is the city that fails.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The exception shows that faith sits in the heart rather than in the mouth. The second half stops that from becoming a licence. What is condemned is not weakness under force. It is having made room. On one side is a person overwhelmed from outside. On the other is a person changed within. The passage insists these are different things, even when the words spoken are the same.

crossReferences.why: Uses a word from the same root for settled security, there of a town rather than a heart.
Allows for outward caution in a situation of danger, while locating the reality elsewhere.
Describes a man of faith concealing it among people who would have harmed him for showing it.

studies.applyIt: Think of a place where what you say and what you hold have come apart, not under threat but out of ordinary social ease. The severity of this ayah falls on the widening rather than on the words. Notice whether you have started to make room for something you would once only have said, and name it accurately to yourself.
studies.explainEasier: If someone is forced to say words denying God, he is not blamed. His heart is still calm and full of faith. The warning is for the person who opens his heart to leaving faith.

studies.title: They Preferred This Life
studies.meaning: A reason is given for what the previous ayah described. It is not stated as unbelief but as preference. They loved this life more than the next. That makes the failure a matter of ranking rather than of information. Then a seal is described over three faculties. The passage closes on a verdict, introduced by a phrase this surah has used twice before. Early scholars read the sealing as a result of the preference, not its cause.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, following the passage that told compulsion apart from willing change. These ayat take up the second case and explain it. The classical scholars note that the explanation given is about attachment rather than about doctrine. They read that as typical of the surah's whole approach. No specific occasion is reported for any of the three ayat.

keyTerms.note: A verb for choosing between two things a person loves. The form makes it comparative, so the sentence does not accuse them of hating the next life, only of ranking this one above it.
The verb for pressing a seal into clay or wax to close something. It describes a closure that follows a decision to close, which is why commentators tie it to the preference named just before.
From a root for letting something slip out of attention. It names an absence rather than an act, so the passage ends by describing people who are not noticing rather than people who are fighting.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A seal was how a document or a container was closed and its contents guaranteed. Merchants sealed goods before a journey, and a broken seal meant tampering. The image carried a finality everyone understood. What is sealed is not merely shut. It is declared shut, with someone's name pressed into the closing for anyone to read.
studies.didYouKnow: The three faculties sealed here, the heart, the hearing and the sight, are the same three this surah earlier described as given to a newborn who knew nothing at all. One passage names them as gifts issued at birth and this one names them as closed later. The surah opens and shuts the same list.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Making preference the cause matters, because it puts the failure in something ordinary. Nobody here is described as rejecting evidence or as hating God. They chose the nearer good over the further one, again and again. The sealing is presented as what that finally produces. So the danger builds up rather than arriving all at once. And the cure is a matter of ranking rather than of argument.

crossReferences.why: Names the same three faculties as given at birth, before this passage describes them closed.
States the same preference plainly, that you prefer this life while the next is better and lasting.
Describes a seal on hearts and hearing and a covering over sight, in the same order.

studies.applyIt: Track one choice today where you took the nearer good over the further one. Not a large moral decision. An hour, a purchase, a conversation avoided. This passage explains a sealed heart by an accumulation of small preferences, which means the accounting has to be done at that scale before it means anything.
studies.explainEasier: They loved this life more than the next one, so God sealed their hearts, their ears and their eyes. They stopped noticing. In the life to come they will be the ones who lose.

studies.title: Forgiving After All That
studies.meaning: A sentence that keeps restarting. The Lord is named, then a long clause about those who emigrated after being persecuted, then struggled, then held out, and only after all of it does the sentence close with two names. The commentators note the repeated opening, which holds the subject in place while the conditions pile up. Then the scene moves to a day when every soul argues its own case and is paid exactly.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The classical scholars connect the first ayah to those who had left for Abyssinia under pressure. Others read it of the later emigration. They differ over which is meant, and the wording covers the pattern rather than one departure. The surah described emigrants settled in a good place much earlier. So the subject is not new here.

keyTerms.note: A passive from a root for putting metal in fire to separate it. The word covers both trial and torture, and its passive form places what happened firmly outside the sufferers' control.
A verb for restraining oneself and staying in place under pressure. It is listed last, after emigrating and struggling, so the sequence ends on the least visible of the three.
A verb for contesting back and forth. Applied to a soul on that day, it makes the scene a hearing in which each party speaks only for itself, which the following clause then renders unnecessary.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Leaving Mecca meant leaving three things: the protection of a clan, the sanctuary, and the trade that fed a family. Emigrants arrived elsewhere as clients who depended on a host's goodwill. They had no standing of their own. The three verbs in this ayah describe an order people in the audience had lived. Pressure at home, then the departure, then the long plain holding on afterwards.
studies.didYouKnow: The opening words of the first ayah are repeated inside it. So the phrase naming the Lord appears twice in one sentence, with the long list of conditions set between them. Classical scholars read the repeat as a device. It holds a promise open across a clause that had grown too long for a listener to carry.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The two names at the end are unexpected after a list of hardships. A reader expects a reward and gets forgiveness instead. That quietly grants something. People under that kind of pressure do not come through it clean. Pairing it with the next ayah then balances the account. Mercy is named first and exactness second, and neither is allowed to cancel the other out.

crossReferences.why: Describes the same emigrants earlier in this surah, promising them a good place in this world.
Names those who emigrated and were then killed or died, with provision promised to them.
Lists emigration, expulsion and harm suffered, and answers with forgiveness and gardens.

studies.applyIt: Think of a hard season you came through and the things you did in it that you are not proud of. The exhaustion, the sharpness, the corners cut. This passage ends a list of endurance with forgiveness rather than with a medal. Let that be the shape of how you remember it, and stop re-litigating your own conduct under pressure.
studies.explainEasier: Your Lord forgives and shows mercy to people who left home after being hurt. They struggled and they kept going. One day every person will speak up for themselves. Each one will be paid in full for what they did.

studies.title: The Robe Of Hunger
studies.meaning: The third comparison, and the only one shaped as a story. A town has everything. It has safety, calm, and provision arriving in plenty from every direction. Then a single verb turns it. What follows is described as clothing rather than as an event. Hunger and fear are worn like a garment. Early scholars differ over whether a real town is meant or the example was built. Both readings are old and widely held.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Some classical scholars read the comparison as pointing at Mecca itself. Mecca was safe through its sanctuary and fed by trade arriving from every direction, and they connect the story to a period of hardship there. Others read it as a built example with no place in mind. The sources give both. The surah itself presents it simply as a likeness struck.

keyTerms.note: From the same root as a word used a few ayat earlier for a heart at rest under compulsion. Applied to a town it names undisturbed calm, which the surah has already shown matters less.
A word for provision arriving without effort. The Quran uses it of the garden given to Adam, so the phrase places this town among the most generously supplied cases it names anywhere.
Applying it to hunger and fear makes them worn rather than merely suffered. Clothing is close, constant and visible to others, which is what the image adds to a plain statement of scarcity.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Mecca grew nothing. Its safety came from the sanctuary, which made raiding it unthinkable. Its food arrived by caravan from Yemen and from Syria. That arrangement was the whole economy of the city, and its pride. It also depended completely on the goodwill of other people. Everyone there understood how fast hunger would follow if the roads closed.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase describing hunger worn as a garment occurs only here in the Quran. The word for the rich provision this town received appears in only two other places. One describes what was given in the garden. The other describes what a people were told to eat on entering a settled town. So this town is placed in very select company.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The comparison puts the failure after the provision rather than before it. That reverses the usual shape of a warning. This town is not tested by scarcity. It is undone by having enough. The verb describing what it did is the ordinary word for covering something over. So ingratitude here is an active hiding of what is in plain view, not a lapse of feeling.

crossReferences.why: Names the same two gifts, food against hunger and safety against fear, given to a trading people.
Tells a longer version, a well-supplied people whose provision was taken after they turned away.
Continues this comparison directly, adding the messenger who came to them and was denied.

studies.applyIt: Name three things about your life that are working right now and that you have not thought about this month. Say them out loud, one sentence each. This comparison describes a place undone by having enough. The only guard it points to is noticing. Nobody does that without deciding to.
studies.explainEasier: Think of a town that was safe and calm, with plenty of food coming in from every side. Then it stopped thanking God for all of it. So God let it taste hunger and fear.

studies.title: A Messenger From Among Them
studies.meaning: One sentence completes the comparison. It adds the element that turns the story from misfortune into judgement. A messenger came, and he came from among them. So the message arrived in a familiar voice, through a known person. They denied him. What followed is described as seizing them while they were in the middle of wrongdoing. Early scholars note the order. The denial comes before the seizure, and the wrongdoing runs right through it.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, closing the comparison of the secure town. The classical commentators who read that comparison as pointing at Mecca read this ayah the same way, since the audience was hearing a messenger from among themselves. Others keep it general. The sources report no separate occasion for this ayah, treating it as part of the likeness begun in the one before.

keyTerms.note: Two short words carrying the argument. A messenger from outside could be dismissed as a stranger; one from inside removes that defence, since his life before the message was known to everyone.
An intensive verb meaning to declare someone a liar rather than to disagree with him. It names a verdict passed on a person, which is why the ayah treats it as the decisive act.
An active participle, so the state is ongoing at the moment described. The grammar places them mid-action when it arrives, which answers in advance any claim of having been taken by surprise.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Sending a message through one of a group's own members was standard practice. An insider could not be accused of misreading the situation. It also raised the cost of refusal. Turning him down meant turning down someone whose family, trade and history everyone could recite. In Mecca the messenger's name for honesty before the message began was widely known and often mentioned.
studies.didYouKnow: This surah said much earlier that a messenger was raised in every community. It used the same word for community that the comparison here applies to a town. The general claim comes near the beginning. The worked example comes near the end. So the surah shows in a short story what it had stated some eighty ayat before.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Adding the messenger changes what the comparison is about. Without him the story is a place losing its provision. That could be read as bad luck. With him it becomes an answer to something offered and refused. That is a different kind of account altogether. It also shows that warning comes before consequence as a standing pattern, not as a courtesy given in particular cases.

crossReferences.why: States the general principle that a messenger was raised in every community, which this exemplifies.
Sets up the town this ayah completes, secure and well provided before it turned.
Says no community is punished until a messenger has been sent to it first.

studies.applyIt: Think about who in your life is closest to you and most likely to tell you something true you do not want to hear. Then notice how often their closeness is exactly what you use to discount them. Ask that person one direct question this week and let the answer stand without a rebuttal.
studies.explainEasier: A messenger came to them from their own town, so they knew him well. They called him a liar. So the punishment caught them while they were still doing wrong.

studies.title: Eat And Be Thankful
studies.meaning: Two instructions and a condition. Eat from what God has provided. Two adjectives describe it, and the tradition has spent centuries telling them apart. Then be grateful for the favour. Then a clause that reframes both: if it is him you serve. Early scholars note that this condition does not threaten. It ties ordinary eating to worship. A table and an act of devotion are treated as one continuous thing rather than two.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, right after the comparison of the town that lost its provision. So the instruction reads as the bright side of that story. The classical scholars connect the passage that follows to Arabian food customs. Those customs set certain animals aside on the authority of tribal gods. The scholars treat this ayah as the general statement that the next one narrows.

keyTerms.note: From a root for loosening a knot or setting down a load. The word describes what has been let go rather than what has been granted, so the default in view is openness rather than restriction.
A word covering what is pleasant, clean and nourishing. Pairing it with the previous term adds a quality of the thing itself alongside the question of whether it was ever set apart.
An imperative placed beside eating rather than after it. The grammar puts the two on one level, so gratitude is described as part of the meal rather than as a response that follows it.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Food in Arabia was closely governed by custom. Certain animals were set aside by tribal decision and never eaten. Others were kept for special times. Much of this was tied to the shrines. So deciding what a household could eat was a question of authority as much as of appetite. Everyone knew whose name was being called on at any given table.
studies.didYouKnow: The word here for wholesome runs through this surah in several places. A few dozen ayat earlier it describes the good things provided to households. Near the surah's start it describes the state of the righteous as the angels take them. So one term covers food, family life and the manner of a death.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Tying gratitude to eating rather than to rescue changes where devotion is practised. The ayah does not ask for thanks after a rescue. It asks for thanks at the most ordinary act a person performs. It is also the most repeated. The closing condition then makes the object of worship readable from the table. What you treat as the source of your food is already a claim about who provides.

crossReferences.why: Gives the same instruction to eat of good things and give thanks, addressed to those who believe.
Shows the same provision withdrawn from a town that covered over the favour instead.
Asks who set apart the adornment and good provision that God produced for His servants.

studies.applyIt: Say something before your next meal, even one sentence in your own words, and mean it. Then eat slowly enough to notice the first three mouthfuls. This ayah puts gratitude beside eating rather than after it, and the only way to test that arrangement is to try it at a meal you would otherwise not have registered.
studies.explainEasier: Eat the food God has given you, the food that is allowed and good for you. Say thank you to God for it. Do this if he is really the one you serve.

studies.title: Unless Driven By Necessity
studies.meaning: A short list is given and then qualified at once. Four things are named as set apart. The last of them is defined by what was spoken over it rather than by what it is. Then the sentence opens a door for anyone driven by need. That door is for someone not seeking it out and not going beyond the need. It closes on two names rather than on a penalty. Early scholars stress how narrow the list is.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The classical scholars note that these four items appear in several places in the Quran with almost the same wording. Arabian food custom at the time set aside many more animals than these, on tribal authority. The surah has just asked who granted that authority. The shortness of the ayah is read against that background. It is not read as a complete account of the subject.

keyTerms.note: An animal that died without being slaughtered. The word names a condition rather than a species, which is part of why the list is described as short: it turns on how something came to be food.
From a root for raising the voice, originally the shout at the sighting of a new moon. It names the act of speaking a name over an animal, so what is at issue is the dedication rather than the meat.
A passive from a root for harm and constraint. The grammar removes agency again, matching the exception made a few ayat earlier for a person compelled to speak against his own faith.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Meat was scarce and mostly eaten at gatherings. Slaughter was a public act, and a spoken dedication went with it. Animals were also set aside for shrines by tribal decision, their ears slit to mark them. Eating such an animal carried social meaning. A traveller crossing empty country could face real hunger with nothing but a carcass before him. That is the situation the exception addresses.
studies.didYouKnow: The same four items are named in four separate places in the Quran. They appear in Meccan and Medinan passages alike, with the wording nearly the same each time. Classical scholars noted the repeat. They also noted that the list does not grow between its earliest place and its latest. That is unusual for a subject raised more than once.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The structure here teaches as much as the content. A short list is given, an exception follows at once, and the passage closes on forgiveness and mercy rather than on consequence. That ordering does real work. It presents the limits as narrow and the room around them as wide, and it names the character of the one setting the limits before a reader has any chance to picture severity.

crossReferences.why: Gives the identical list and the same exception for necessity, in a Medinan setting.
Turns on the dedication spoken over an animal, which is the final item in this list.
Follows immediately, warning against tongues that describe things as set apart or released.

studies.applyIt: Read this ayah once slowly and notice its shape: a short list, an immediate exception, and then two names for God at the end. Most people remember the list and forget the ending. Sit with those last few words for a moment, and let them be part of what you carry away from a passage about limits.
studies.explainEasier: God has told you not to eat animals that died on their own. He has told you not to eat blood, or pork, or meat offered to something other than God. If you are starving and have no choice, God forgives.

studies.title: Do Not Say This And That
studies.meaning: The instruction is not really about food. It is about a sentence, and the ayah puts that sentence in the reader's own mouth. This thing is released, that one is set apart. What makes it wrong is named in the purpose clause, which is attributing an invention to God. Early scholars note that the ban falls on the speaking itself. The second ayah then measures what such speech buys, calling it a brief enjoyment.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, following the short list of items the previous ayah named. Arabian tribes set many animals aside from use by their own decision. They marked those animals and credited the arrangement to the gods of the shrines. The classical scholars read this ayah against that practice and report no separate occasion. The surah has spent its second half asking who granted such authority.

keyTerms.note: The same verb the surah used much earlier of tongues uttering a lie about their own outcome. Its return binds the two passages, so speech about God and speech about oneself become one habit.
Repeated three times within a single ayah, which is unusual density even for the Quran. The repetition holds attention on the false attribution rather than on the categories being announced.
A word for provisions carried on a journey and used up along the way. It measures the gain from such speech by its duration rather than its size, so what is denied is permanence.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Setting animals aside was a public act with visible marks. A camel's ear was slit. A she-camel was released to graze untouched after a certain number of births. The decisions were made by men of standing and defended as inherited. Everyone could see which animals were marked. Nobody asked to see the authority, because the authority was the age of the practice itself.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for falsehood appears three times in this single ayah. That is unusual even by the Quran's standards of repetition. It attaches first to the tongues doing the describing, then to the attribution being made, and then to the people making it. So it follows the lie from its speaker to its target and back.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The offence named is not getting a label wrong. It is putting a decision into God's mouth. That difference has results. It makes speaking for God a serious act, whether or not the content happens to be correct. And it puts the danger in confidence rather than in error. The brief enjoyment named afterwards then names what such speech is usually for, which is standing.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same phrase about tongues describing a falsehood, there concerning their own outcome.
Describes the same practice at length, animals set aside by claim and children lost to it.
Asks directly who gave leave for the categories people announce about their own provision.

studies.applyIt: Notice how often you say what God wants in a sentence about someone else's life. Not in a formal setting. In the ordinary ones, about a decision a friend made or a choice you disapprove of. Try going a week without that construction, and see what you find yourself saying instead.
studies.explainEasier: Do not say that this food is allowed and that one is not, and then claim God said so. People who make up things about God will not do well. What they get lasts only a short time.

studies.title: They Wronged Their Own Selves
studies.meaning: One sentence connects this passage to an earlier one. Then it adds a clause that removes a likely misreading. Restrictions given to an earlier community are recalled, and the addressee is pointed back to where the account was already set out. Then the sentence turns. What happened was not a wrong done to them. Early scholars read the closing clause as naming a result rather than laying a general charge.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The details referred to are given in an earlier surah. The classical scholars treat this ayah as a cross-reference rather than as fresh information. The surah has been asking who holds the authority to set things apart. This ayah supplies a case where that authority was used. So it belongs to the argument rather than standing as a separate subject.

keyTerms.note: A verb from the root for following a track. It presents the earlier account as something a hearer can go back and trace, which is why commentators read this ayah as pointing elsewhere rather than summarising.
From a root for putting something out of its proper place. Denying it rules out arbitrariness, since the word describes a misallocation rather than mere harshness or severity.
Placed before its verb, which in Arabic marks emphasis. The word order puts the weight on who received the harm rather than on the act, so the sentence is really about direction.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Mecca's traders knew the Jewish communities of Yathrib and the northern oases. They dealt with them often. They knew that those communities kept limits on food and on days. These facts were common knowledge, not a matter of dispute. A Meccan audience could follow a reference to them with nothing needing to be explained.
studies.didYouKnow: This ayah does not repeat the restrictions it refers to. It points the hearer back to a passage in another surah where they were set out. That makes it one of the clearest cases in the Quran of a text treating itself as a body a reader can navigate, rather than as a sequence of separate announcements.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The denial in the middle of the sentence carries the weight. It rules out the idea that a limit is punishment for its own sake. It does so before a reader can reach that thought. What replaces it is a statement about harm they did to themselves. That keeps the blame with the one acting. And it leaves the history itself in the earlier passage, where it belongs.

crossReferences.why: Sets out the restrictions this ayah refers back to, with the same explanation attached to them.
Connects restrictions given to an earlier community with wrongdoing that had occurred among them.
Notes food set apart by a community for itself before the earlier scripture was sent down.

studies.applyIt: Look up the passage this ayah points to, in a translation, and read the two together. It will take four minutes. The ayah assumes a reader who can follow a reference, and most of us read the Quran in a way that makes that impossible. Try being the reader it assumes, once.
studies.explainEasier: God told the Jewish people not to eat certain things. That story is already told in another part of the Quran. God did not treat them unfairly. They were the ones who had hurt themselves.

studies.title: A Whole Community In One Man
studies.meaning: Forgiveness is promised to those who did wrong out of ignorance, then turned back and put things right. Three conditions are given in sequence. Then, with no transition at all, Abraham is described in four words. Each does separate work, and the last of them denies something rather than asserts it. Early scholars dwell on the first word, which calls a single man a community. They preserve several readings of what that means.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Abraham was claimed by everyone in the argument. The Meccans traced the sanctuary to him, and the Jewish and Christian communities to the north held him as a founder. The classical scholars note that describing him without reference to any of those later communities is deliberate. No specific occasion is reported for the three ayat.

keyTerms.note: Applied here to one man. Commentators read it as a leader whom a community follows, or as a man who stood for a whole people when nobody stood with him, and they preserve both.
The word occurs in this exact form only here in the Quran. It describes sustained standing devotion rather than a single act, so it names a posture held across a lifetime.
A word for turning aside from what is crooked. It appears twice in this surah and belongs to no later community, which is why it can describe Abraham without placing him inside one.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Mecca's whole standing rested on Abraham. The sanctuary was said to have been raised by him. The pilgrimage was traced to him, and the tribes that guarded the site claimed descent from him. Naming him and then denying that he associated anything with God struck the arrangement where it was strongest. It used the audience's own founder against their practice.
studies.didYouKnow: The word describing Abraham as devoted occurs in this exact form only once in the whole Quran. The word calling him a community, applied to one man, is the same term the surah uses everywhere else for whole peoples. That includes the peoples to whom messengers were sent. A single man is given a plural's noun.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Placing repentance right before this portrait is not for show. The ayat that follow describe a man. He is built out of the very qualities the previous one asks for. So an example arrives where an argument might have. And the passage calls him thankful for favours, in a surah that has spent a hundred ayat listing favours. That quietly names gratitude as the thing that made the rest possible.

crossReferences.why: Asks who would turn from the way of Abraham except someone who has fooled his own soul.
Denies that he belonged to any later community, using the same word for upright.
Records his own turning towards the one who made the heavens and the earth, upright.

studies.applyIt: Think of one person you know who is, by themselves, holding up something that ought to have more people behind it. A neighbourhood, a family, a project. Tell them you have noticed. This passage counts a single man as a community, and people in that position are usually the last to be told what they are carrying.
studies.explainEasier: God forgives people who do wrong without knowing, and then turn back and make things better. Abraham was like a whole nation in one man. He thanked God, stayed away from idols, and God chose him.

studies.title: Follow The Way Of Abraham
studies.meaning: Two more things are given to Abraham, one in this life and one in the next. Then the sentence turns to the addressee with a single instruction. Follow that way. Early scholars note what is not said. No new content is named, only a person to follow. And the description of him is repeated word for word from three ayat earlier, including the denial that closes it.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The instruction places the message being delivered in line with a figure the audience already honoured. That was a claim about lineage rather than about novelty. The classical scholars read the repeated description as answering the objection that this was something newly made. No specific occasion is reported. The pair closes the surah's argument about founders.

keyTerms.note: Left indefinite and unspecified. The commentators give a range, from reputation to descendants to the sanctuary itself, and read the vagueness as deliberate breadth rather than as an omission.
A word for the road a community travels, distinct from the terms for law or for creed. It names a direction rather than a set of doctrines, which suits an instruction to follow a person.
Repeated from the earlier description, so the instruction carries the same word that characterised the man. Its second appearance within three ayat is what makes the two passages one argument.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Descent was the master argument in Arabian dispute. Claims to land, to office and to honour were settled by family line. A man who could trace his line to a great ancestor had standing. He had it before he opened his mouth. Framing this message as following an ancestor everyone claimed used the strongest form of argument in that society.
studies.didYouKnow: The word describing Abraham as upright appears ten times in the Quran. Two of those are in this surah, three ayat apart. Both times it is followed at once by a denial that he associated anything with God. So the term and its explanation travel together as a fixed pair.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Telling a messenger to follow an earlier figure makes revelation a restoring. It is not a new invention. That is a real claim, not just a turn of phrase. It also sets a limit on the messenger's own standing. He is told to follow, in the same passage where opponents accused him of inventing. So the answer to a charge of novelty turns out to be an instruction to imitate.

crossReferences.why: Gives the description of Abraham that this instruction repeats almost word for word.
Issues the same instruction to follow the way of Abraham, upright, in a different setting.
Asks who is better in religion than one who submits and follows the way of Abraham.

studies.applyIt: Pick one person, living or from the past, whose way of being religious you actually want to imitate, and name one specific thing they do. Not their beliefs. A habit. Then do that thing once this week. This passage answers a large question by pointing at a person, which is a method as much as an answer.
studies.explainEasier: God gave Abraham good things in this life. In the next life he will be with the good people. Then God gave this message: follow the way of Abraham, who never worshipped idols.

studies.title: Appointed For Those Who Differed
studies.meaning: A short ayah with a restrictive particle at its head, which limits rather than explains. The day of rest is said to have been appointed for those who differed about it, and the commentators give a range of readings for what that differing was. Then the sentence moves the whole matter forward to a judgement still to come. What is striking is that no verdict is offered here, only the promise that one will be given.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, following the passage about Abraham. His practice came before the later communities entirely. The classical scholars read the ayah against that background. The observance under discussion came after him. So it is not part of what the previous instruction points to. They give several accounts of the differing referred to. They keep the range without settling it.

keyTerms.note: A particle that restricts whatever follows it. Its position at the head narrows the whole sentence, so the ayah reads as a limitation on scope rather than as an account of origins.
The same verb used earlier in this surah for what scripture was sent down to clarify. Its return links the passages, since both concern disagreement that a later judgement is said to resolve.
An emphatic form of the verb for deciding between parties. It belongs to arbitration language, so what is promised is a ruling between disputants rather than the punishing of one side.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: The Arabian week was set by markets and by caravan departures. It was not set by a day of rest. Meccans knew the idea of one day set aside mainly through contact with the Jewish communities to the north. Traders adjusted their schedules around it. The practice was familiar as a fact of business. It was familiar long before it became a subject of argument.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for this day of rest appears five times in the Quran. The others all sit inside accounts of one particular community and its history. This one alone steps back from that history. It says something about the scope of the observance. And it hands the disagreement forward to a day of judgement instead of settling it.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The method of the ayah teaches more than its content does. A disputed matter is raised. Instead of deciding it, the passage names the one who will decide and the day on which it will happen. That models a way of holding disagreement. What belongs to a final judgement is not to be settled in advance. And the surah has just spent several ayat warning against speaking for God.

crossReferences.why: Says the scripture was sent down to clarify what people differed about, using the same verb.
Ends with the same promise, that what people disputed will be made clear on that day.
Refers whatever people differ about to God for judgement, in closely similar terms.

studies.applyIt: Take one religious disagreement you have strong feelings about and, this week, decline to settle it. Not out of indifference. Out of the recognition this ayah models, that some things are handed forward. Notice how much energy comes back when a question stops needing an answer from you today.
studies.explainEasier: The day of rest was set for people who argued about it. Your Lord will settle it on the Day when everyone is raised. He will judge between them about the things they disagreed on.

studies.title: The Better Way To Argue
studies.meaning: Three modes are named and ranked by situation, not by taste. Wisdom is the argument that fits the person in front of you. Good exhortation is the appeal that moves someone already willing. For those who push back, argue in the way that is best. The last clause takes away the pull that usually bends an argument. Who is astray and who is guided is known by God. That knowledge sits outside the speaker entirely.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, in the final passage of the surah. It comes straight after a mention of the religion of Abraham. It comes straight before orders on answering injury. Early scholars mostly read the run as one unit. The unit is about how a small, pressured group should behave. Some report that the ayat which follow came down after a certain loss at Uhud. The sources differ, and the surah is otherwise Meccan.

keyTerms.note: The root also gives the word for a bridle. Wisdom in Arabic is the faculty that restrains and steers, so it names the judgement about what to say and when, not a body of knowledge.

Speech that appeals to the heart rather than to the intellect, usually with a reminder of consequence. The qualifier attached to it here matters: it must be the beautiful kind, which rules out shaming.

A superlative, so the instruction is not to argue acceptably but to argue in the very best available manner. The same form appears in the two ayat about reward a little earlier, tying the surah's close together.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Public argument was a competitive art in Arabia, closer to a contest than to a talk. Tribes kept speakers and poets who fought on their behalf with satire and boast. A defeat in that arena was a real loss of standing. The point of arguing was to shame the other side. To be told to argue in the best manner was to be asked to give up the usual prize.
studies.didYouKnow: The ayah does not say what to argue. Every one of its terms concerns manner: with wisdom, with good exhortation, in the best way. The only content it supplies is the destination, the way of your Lord. Early scholars reading it as a template for calling others to faith have noted that it spends all its words on the caller and almost none on the message.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The closing clause does theological work that is easy to miss. By reserving to God the knowledge of who has strayed and who is guided, it takes the outcome of the conversation out of the speaker's hands, which is what makes gentleness sustainable. A person who believes he can tell who is beyond reach will eventually stop being careful with them. The ayah removes that certainty, and with it the licence it grants.

crossReferences.why: Applies the same instruction to argument with the People of the Book.
Moses and Aaron are sent to Pharaoh and told to speak to him gently.
Attributes the gathering of people to gentleness, and warns what harshness would have done.

studies.applyIt: The next time someone disagrees with you about something that matters, try one thing. State their position back to them until they agree you have it right. Do that before you say anything of your own. It usually takes two tries. It also removes most of the reason the talk was going to go badly. That is the whole point of the instruction here.
studies.explainEasier: God tells the Prophet to invite people to his Lord's way with wisdom and kind advice. If someone argues back, he should answer in the nicest way he can. Only God knows who is lost and who is guided.

studies.title: Equal, Or Better Than Equal
studies.meaning: A conditional with a ceiling built into it. If an injury is answered, the answer is matched to what was done and goes no further. Then the sentence changes register entirely and commends something else, without withdrawing what it has just allowed. The commentators note that both halves stand together, so the passage sets a limit and then, separately, points past it. Which of the two it prefers is stated in the final word.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan by the surah's placement. The classical scholars report that some held the final ayat to have come later, connecting them to grief after a battle. The sources differ over this. Several present the ayah as a general principle, whatever the occasion. What is agreed is that it addresses a community already injured and weighing how to answer.

keyTerms.note: From a root for what comes along behind. The verb names a response that follows something rather than an initiative, which is why the whole sentence depends on having been injured first.
The word for a matching equivalent, from the same root as the likenesses struck earlier in this surah. It sets an exact ceiling, so a response is measured from the injury rather than from the anger.
A verb for restraining oneself and staying in position. Here it names not passivity but a choice made while still holding the capacity to act, which is what gives the recommendation weight.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Feuds in Arabia grew by design. An injury was answered with more than had been received, to show that the responding clan was stronger. A killing could set off exchanges lasting generations. Poets kept the tally in verse. Setting an exact ceiling on a response cut against the whole logic of that system, where matching an injury was read as weakness.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase setting the measure of a response occurs in this exact form only here. Its key word comes from the same root the surah used for the likenesses that God strikes. So the vocabulary of comparison that ran through the middle of the surah returns at the end. It returns to measure an answer to injury.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage does two things usually kept apart. It sets a maximum, which grants that answering an injury is real and that limits are needed. Then it commends something better, without cancelling the first. That shape refuses both extremes. One treats restraint as unrealistic. The other treats any response as wrong. And the choice is left with the injured party.

crossReferences.why: Repeats the same balance, an equal answer allowed and forgiveness commended above it.
Follows immediately, telling the addressee to be patient, with his patience attributed to God.
Applies the same measure of an equivalent response in a quite different setting.

studies.applyIt: Think of the last time someone wronged you and you answered. Ask honestly whether your answer was equal, or equal plus a little, for the message. That little extra is what this ayah rules out first, before it says anything at all about patience. Start there, before you attempt the harder half.
studies.explainEasier: If someone hurts you and you answer back, do not do more than what was done to you. But if you hold back and stay patient, that is better for you.

studies.title: Your Patience Is From God
studies.meaning: Three restraints, and then a reassurance. The order to be patient is at once qualified. A clause takes away any credit for it: patience is only by God. Early scholars read that as saying the power to endure is itself given. Then grief over the opponents is forbidden. So is the tightening in the chest that their scheming brings on. The last ayah answers all three at once by saying where God is.
studies.historicalContext: These are the last two ayat of a Meccan surah. They close it on instruction rather than on argument. The passage before them allows an answer to injury that matches it exactly, then says patience is better. So this is the second half of that thought. Some early reports connect the run to grief after Uhud. The sources differ, and the surah is otherwise placed in the Meccan period.

keyTerms.note: The noun is attached to the hearer and then immediately reassigned. The root means to bind or confine, so patience is holding yourself in place, and the ayah says even the grip is supplied.

A physical word for narrowness, used of a road or a room. Applied to a person it names the squeezed feeling in the chest under pressure, which is being addressed as a bodily state rather than a moral failing.
From the same root as the word for beauty and for doing well by others. Placed at the very end of the surah, it names the second group God is with, alongside those who are mindful.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Scheming in that world was concrete and legal. A clan could withdraw protection, boycott a family's trade, refuse marriages, or block access to the wells and the market. None of it required violence, and none of it could be answered by force. Believers in Mecca lived under exactly that kind of pressure for years, which is why the ayah names the physical symptom rather than the injury.
studies.didYouKnow: The surah's last word names those who do good, and its first movement opened with God's command arriving. Between them the chapter has run through creation, cattle, bees, honey, trade, oaths and argument. Ending a hundred and twenty-eight ayat on a two-part statement of where God is, with no further instruction, gives the chapter an unusually quiet close.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The clause about patience changes what the virtue is. If the power to endure is itself given, then endurance is not a store a person spends down and runs out of. Asking for more of it is the natural response to finding you have none. That makes exhaustion a reason to turn towards God, rather than proof of failing Him. The closing statement then offers presence rather than rescue.

crossReferences.why: Names patience and prayer together and gives the same assurance that God is with the patient.
Addresses the same tightness in the chest and answers it with praise and prostration.
The assurance of God's company spoken in the cave at the hardest moment.

studies.applyIt: When your chest tightens next about something someone is doing to you, do not try to talk yourself out of the feeling. Say instead, simply, that you are asking for the patience rather than producing it. Then put the phone down for ten minutes. This ayah treats the constriction as real and locates the supply outside you, which is worth testing.
studies.explainEasier: God tells the Prophet to be patient. The patience itself comes from God. He tells him not to be sad about the people who reject him. He tells him not to let their plots make him feel tight inside.
